questions.question: "Tell me about yourself" (technical version, 90 seconds)

answer.label: Who I am
answer.text: I'm an AI systems architect and engineering leader, with 10+ years in production software. I co-founded a company that EY acquired, and I led engineering at EY for five years. Since 2025 I've designed and shipped multi-agent systems and agentic RAG for clients in regulated domains.

answer.label: Now: MITCON
answer.text: Right now I'm at MITCON, an environmental consultancy, as a forward-deployed AI engineer through People Equation. I led discovery and found 10 use cases for human-in-the-loop agentic workflows. The first two, long-form regulatory and feasibility reports, are in build. The contract covers 7 deliveries and 307 pages. I'm also automating the statutory clearance chain: CAD to KML site boundaries, a 97-row consolidated statement filled automatically, and EIA chapter drafting with expert checkpoints.

answer.label: The engineering I'm proudest of
answer.text: The extractor runs under a grounding contract. The model proposes a value only if the document states it, and it quotes the sheet and cell. If a value is ambiguous it shows both readings. If it can't ground a value it leaves a gap. A gap on screen is recoverable. An invented number in a signed document isn't.

answer.label: Before that
answer.text: At Fresh Tracks Canada I built a multi-agent payment system on LangGraph and AWS Bedrock. Deterministic code computes every amount. The agents read payment history, decide the next action and write every mail in the brand voice. At AML SoftServe I designed agentic RAG over 800+ AUSTRAC documents. It screens every onboarding and transaction, and every finding cites its source clause.

answer.label: How I deliver
answer.text: I also build the delivery practices that make teams faster. At TekMindz I introduced an AI-enabled delivery method with an LLM-maintained project wiki on every project. Sprint velocity rose 40 to 50% on the pilot project. People Equation's fde plugin and fde-os template now turn the method into versioned skills, pinned per engagement.

questions.throughLine: Grounded AI where a wrong answer costs something, with evals and guardrails built in from the start, and systems the client can run after I leave.
questions.remember: MITCON grounding contract, Fresh Tracks payment agents, AML agentic RAG, the delivery method.
questions.deliveryTip: Stop at 90 seconds even if they look interested. Leave the grounding contract as the hook they will ask about. After the Fresh Tracks and AML SoftServe lines, stop and let the interviewer choose which engagement to open.
questions.steer: Pause after the grounding contract line. Most interviewers will ask how it works, which is your strongest ground.
questions.trap: Say MITCON is an agentic workflow, never "agents". Don't say an LLM computes money at Fresh Tracks. Deterministic code computes every amount. Don't walk through four engagements in sequence. Don't end with "I hope I gave you the general idea". Don't call the whole period freelance or contract work. Keep to 90 seconds and let the interviewer choose where to go. TekMindz was five months, full-time and salaried, January to May 2025. Never call it a contract of three and a half months. Fresh Tracks ran from December 2025 to August 2026. Never say it lasted seven months.

followUps.question: Was the AI in the product at Fresh Tracks and AML SoftServe?
followUps.answer: Yes, at both. At Fresh Tracks the payment agents ran in the shipped product, on LangGraph and AWS Bedrock. Deterministic code computed every amount, and the agents read payment history, chose the next action and wrote the mail. At AML SoftServe an agent ran retrieval over 800+ AUSTRAC documents on every onboarding and transaction, then decided whether to flag it. MITCON is an agentic workflow with model calls at named steps.
followUps.remember: AI is in the shipped product at Fresh Tracks and AML SoftServe, and in the MITCON workflow.
followUps.trap: Don't name an agent framework for AML SoftServe. You don't remember it. Don't quote outcomes for Fresh Tracks beyond refunds moving from about two business days to one.

checks: MITCON is live. Check how many of the 7 contracted deliveries have gone out by the interview date, and say "scoped" or "delivered" to match.
Fresh Tracks and AML SoftServe: know the flows in the story bank. Braintrust's tracing role at AML SoftServe is our reading, so confirm it. You don't remember the AML agent framework, so name none.

questions.question: "Tell me about yourself" (HR version, 60 seconds)

answer.label: Background
answer.text: I studied at IIT Kharagpur and I've 10+ years in production software. I co-founded an ed-tech company called Spotmentor and ran its engineering. EY acquired it in 2020, and I spent about five years at EY, finishing as Senior Manager, Engineering.

answer.label: What I do now
answer.text: Since 2025 I've worked directly with clients as an AI systems architect. I sit with their teams, learn how the work is done, and design and build the AI system that automates the safe parts.

answer.label: Recent clients
answer.text: My clients have been in travel in Canada, compliance in Australia and environmental consulting in India.

answer.label: What I want next
answer.text: I'm looking for a full-time, permanent role designing and shipping AI systems for customers, where I can do this inside one company for the long term.

questions.throughLine: Founder, then manager, then a hands-on AI architect working with clients. Now I want a permanent home for that work.
questions.remember: IIT Kharagpur, 10+ years, Spotmentor acquired by EY, five years at EY, AI systems since 2025, want full-time.
questions.deliveryTip: Keep it plain. No stack names. Smile at the last line, because it answers their next question for them.
questions.steer: The last line sets up "why are you leaving contract work", which you have a clean answer for.
questions.trap: Don't list every engagement by name. HR wants the shape, not the detail.

questions.question: "Walk me through your most impactful project"

answer.label: The problem
answer.text: MITCON prepares environmental clearance reports in India. The documents are statutory and they get signed. A wrong number in one is a legal problem. The inputs are CAD drawings, spreadsheets and PDFs.

answer.label: Discovery
answer.text: I led discovery through value chain analysis and hotspot identification across the client's clearance process. We mapped the chain and split it into steps an expert must check and steps that are safe to automate. That found 10 use cases. The contract covers 7 deliveries, 307 pages of reporting, and MITCON provides the scope for each use case.

answer.label: What I built
answer.text: I built CAD to KML boundary conversion, a 97-row consolidated statement filled automatically, and EIA chapter drafting. Every gate has an expert checkpoint. It runs on Django, DRF and Celery with a React front end.

answer.label: The grounding contract
answer.text: The model may only propose a value the document states. It must quote the exact sheet and cell. If a value is ambiguous it proposes both readings. If it can't ground a value, it leaves the field empty.

answer.label: Two calls I made
answer.text: Five days in, I re-cut my own architecture from a FastAPI monolith into Django and React repos, because the shape stopped fitting the delivery plan. I also changed models on evidence. Anthropic's document block accepted only PDF among binary files, so workbooks failed with a 400. I moved to OpenAI, then to a two-stage route through OpenRouter. A lightweight decision model narrows each document before Gemini Flash-Lite extracts from it. On 110 uploads, the rebuilt pipeline raised recall from 28% to 62% and cut wrong values from 27% to 11%, against the old pipeline on gpt-4o-mini.

questions.throughLine: A gap on screen is recoverable. An invented number in a signed document isn't.
questions.remember: 7 deliveries, 307 pages, 97-row statement, 773 commits in about 10 days, grounding contract, wrong values 27% to 11% on a golden set.
questions.deliveryTip: Lead with the stakes: a signed legal document. Then the contract. Keep the architecture for when they ask.
questions.steer: Offer the model-routing story. It shows you test the provider and the route, not just the prompt.
questions.trap: Don't claim time saved at MITCON. No such figure is on record yet. The 27% to 11% figure is from a golden set, so say that.

followUps.question: How fast did you build it?
followUps.answer: The first cut went in fast: 773 commits across 3 repos in about 10 days. Most of that pace came from the delivery method and coding agents I run.
followUps.remember: 773 commits, 3 repos, about 10 days.

followUps.question: What did it save the client?
followUps.answer: I don't have a measured saving to quote yet. The engagement is still live. What I can say is what it covers: 7 deliveries and 307 pages.
followUps.remember: No saving figure yet. Say so.
followUps.trap: Never estimate a percentage saving on the spot.

checks: MITCON is live. Check how many of the 7 contracted deliveries have gone out by the interview date, and say "scoped" or "delivered" to match.
No measured time saving exists for MITCON in the profile. The only measured outcome is the golden-set extraction eval. Add a client-side figure to work-portfolio.md once you have one.

questions.question: "Why AI systems architecture and forward-deployed work? How did you move from engineering management back into hands-on AI delivery?"

answer.label: Why this role
answer.text: AI systems work joins two things I've done for years. I've worked with clients since Spotmentor, and I've written production code throughout. These roles ask for both at once: design the system, then stay with the customer who runs it.

answer.label: Where client work started
answer.text: At EY I owned delivery across 8 enterprise accounts. That meant rollout, integration and per-client customisation, working directly with client stakeholders. Discovery and embedding aren't new to me.

answer.label: The move
answer.text: In January 2025 I left EY. I joined TekMindz as Director, Technology, and led AI adoption across delivery and day-to-day operations. Then I took contract work as AI Systems Architect at AML SoftServe and Fresh Tracks Canada. Now I'm Forward Deployed AI Engineer at MITCON.

answer.label: Proof I'm hands-on
answer.text: I was top contributor at AML SoftServe, with 327 of 986 commits on the team of 8 I headed. At Fresh Tracks the record is 218 merged commits across 10 repos for our team of two. At MITCON the repos recorded 773 commits across 3 repos in about 10 days. A share of the later two were written by coding agents under my direction. The systems shipped too: payment agents at Fresh Tracks and agentic RAG at AML SoftServe.

questions.throughLine: I did client delivery as a manager. Now I design and build the AI system myself.
questions.remember: 8 EY accounts, then 327 of 986 commits, 218 merged commits, 773 commits. The last two include agent-written work.
questions.deliveryTip: Answer the "why" in one sentence, then let the commit numbers prove you're hands-on.
questions.steer: The commit numbers usually end the "are you still technical" doubt. Say the agents wrote a share of them before anyone asks, then move straight to a technical story.
questions.trap: Don't apologise for the manager years. They are where the client skills came from.

followUps.question: Will you miss managing people?
followUps.answer: No evidence yet. Decide your honest answer before the interview. Until then, say: "I haven't decided how I'd put that in one line, and I'd rather be straight than rehearsed. I did enjoy growing the team at Spotmentor, and I get that from mentoring now."
followUps.remember: Prepare this one yourself.

checks: Your personal motive for leaving EY and choosing AI systems work is not recorded. The "why this role" point is our framing from the facts. Confirm or replace it.

The commit counts are repo totals. Authorship is not recorded, and a share was written by coding agents under your direction. Know the split between agent-written and hand-written commits before you quote a count as your own work.

questions.question: Cross-engagement progression story: how the FDE method grew from Fresh Tracks to MITCON

answer.label: TekMindz
answer.text: At TekMindz I led AI adoption across delivery and day-to-day operations. I introduced an AI-enabled development method and designed a repeatable way to set up an LLM-maintained project wiki on every project. It gives engineers and their coding assistants shared, persistent context. Sprint velocity rose 40 to 50% on the pilot project, which shipped major enhancements to a 2,000+ daily-user platform in 3 months. The method then rolled out to the company's other time-and-materials projects.

answer.label: AML SoftServe
answer.text: At AML SoftServe the AI was in the product, so the discipline was evals and grounding. DeepEval scored retrieval and faithfulness on each change, and Guardrails AI blocked ungrounded output. The platform was regulated and multi-tenant, with row-level security as the tenant boundary.

answer.label: Fresh Tracks Canada
answer.text: At Fresh Tracks I wrote five Claude Code skills, a root CLAUDE.md with a verified service graph, and a ROUTER.md that maps ticket keywords to starting files. I added hooks that block the agent from running pytest, because the containers pointed at the dev database. They also block it from changing data under the staging profile.

answer.label: MITCON and the fde plugin
answer.text: By MITCON the method was a product. fde is People Equation's Claude Code plugin, versioned and tagged. fde-os is the engagement template: three repos, eight skills and an init that refuses to run twice. Each engagement pins a plugin version, so a skill can't change under a running build.

questions.throughLine: Each engagement turned the last one's habits into tooling. By MITCON the method installs in one step.
questions.remember: Project wiki, then evals on every change, then five skills and blocking hooks, then a pinned plugin.
questions.deliveryTip: Tell it as four short steps. End on "pinned per engagement", because it shows you think about reproducibility.
questions.steer: If they ask "isn't this just prompts in markdown?", talk about the hooks and version pinning.
questions.trap: fde and fde-os belong to People Equation. Say "People Equation's plugin", never "my product".

followUps.question: Did it make delivery faster?
followUps.answer: At TekMindz, sprint velocity rose 40 to 50% on the pilot project after I rolled out the method. Fresh Tracks ran as a 2-engineer, AI-accelerated team.
followUps.remember: 40 to 50% sprint velocity at TekMindz, 2-engineer team at Fresh Tracks.

followUps.question: Has anyone else used the method?
followUps.answer: It's applied the same way across the MITCON repo, the earlier MITCON monolith and a broker-triage scoping engagement. That last one is still early and mostly empty.
followUps.remember: Three engagement repos. broker-triage is early.
followUps.trap: Don't present broker-triage as a delivered engagement.

checks: The TekMindz project wiki is described on the resume as shared, persistent context for engineers and their AI coding assistants. Confirm how it was set up in practice.
The 40 to 50% figure was measured on the TekMindz pilot project only. Be ready to say how it was measured.
The progression story is our reading of how the method grew. The portfolio records each piece separately, not the order you built them or why. Confirm the chain is true before you tell it as a story.

categories.title: MITCON environmental clearance, via People Equation

questions.question: "Tell me about the MITCON engagement"
questions.simple: MITCON is an Indian environmental consultancy. Getting a project environmental clearance means a chain of statutory documents. I'm building a human-in-the-loop agentic workflow that automates that chain, with an expert approving every gate. Every model call sits at a named step.

answer.label: The problem
answer.text: MITCON prepares environmental clearance filings in India. Each one is a chain of statutory documents. There's a site boundary, a consolidated statement and an EIA report. Experts were building them by hand from emails, WhatsApp chats, scanned documents, photos and AutoCAD files.

answer.label: What I built
answer.text: I'm building the workflow that automates the chain. CAD drawings become a KML site boundary. A 97-row consolidated statement fills itself from the source documents. The system drafts the EIA report chapters. An environmental expert signs off at every gate.

answer.label: My role
answer.text: I'm the Forward Deployed AI Engineer, on contract since 09/2026. People Equation is the vendor and MITCON is the end client. I led discovery through value chain analysis and hotspot identification. I identified 10 use cases for human-in-the-loop agentic workflows. The first two, long-form regulatory and feasibility reports, are in build. I'm the only engineer. People Equation provides a product manager.

answer.label: The part I'd lead with
answer.text: The extractor works under a grounding contract. The model may propose a value only when the document states it. It must quote the citation verbatim, and code accepts the value only if that citation is found in the source. If a value is ambiguous, it shows both readings. If it can't ground a field, it leaves it blank.

answer.label: Impact
answer.text: The scope is 7 contracted deliveries covering 307 pages of statutory reporting. On 110 uploads the rebuilt pipeline raised recall from 28% to 62% and cut wrong values from 27% to 11%, against the old pipeline on gpt-4o-mini. The repos recorded 773 commits across 3 repos in about 10 days. A share of them were written by coding agents under my direction.

questions.remember: Statutory chain, an agentic workflow with an expert at every gate, and a model that may only say what the document says.
questions.steer: The interesting part is what the model is not allowed to do. Can I walk you through the grounding contract?
questions.trap: Don't call MITCON a direct client. It's delivered through People Equation, and a reference check will find that. Never say "agents" or "train" for MITCON. It's an agentic workflow with model calls at fixed steps, and images go to Gemini whole. Nothing was trained.

followUps.question: Who was the client, exactly? Were you working for MITCON or for People Equation?
followUps.answer: People Equation is the vendor and MITCON is the end client. I lead with MITCON because that's the work. The contract sits with People Equation.
followUps.remember: Client first, vendor named.

questions.question: "Walk me through the architecture"
questions.simple: It's a Django API with Celery workers, a Postgres database and a React front end. The front end talks to the API through a client generated from the API's own schema. A model reads the source documents, and python-docx writes the report chapters.

answer.label: Three repos
answer.text: The engagement follows the fde-os template. There's a docs repo that holds the engagement record. There's a Django back end with Celery and an openapi.json. There's a React front end that uses a generated API client.

answer.label: Back end
answer.text: The API is Django 5.1 with Django REST Framework. Postgres holds the data. Celery runs the slow work, with Redis as the broker. Orchestration is hand-written on Celery. There's no agent framework, and ADR-001 chose a deterministic pipeline with model calls at seven named steps.

answer.label: Reading documents
answer.text: Plain code reads the formats: PDFs, workbooks, Word files, mail, WhatsApp chat logs and CAD. Images and scans go to Gemini whole. Every model call goes through OpenRouter. Model names live in per-task TOML files, never in Python. Gemini Flash-Lite extracts under the contract in model-tasks/extract.toml, after a decision model narrows each document.

answer.label: Writing documents
answer.text: gpt-4o-mini drafts each chapter section by section, from seed templates that carry the agency wording. Every change is a pending proposal that a person accepts, rejects or refines. python-docx and openpyxl produce the output documents.

answer.label: Front end
answer.text: React, in pnpm workspaces. The API client is generated from openapi.json, so the front end can't drift from the back end's contract.

answer.label: The human gates
answer.text: An environmental expert checks the output at every gate before it moves on. Nothing reaches a signed document without that review.

questions.remember: Django and Celery behind, React in front, a generated client between them, and an expert at every gate.
questions.steer: The architecture is deliberately boring. The care went into the extraction contract, and I'm happy to go there.
questions.trap: Don't describe the Celery task layout or queue design in detail. The profile doesn't record it, so confirm it first.

followUps.question: Why a generated API client?
followUps.answer: The back end publishes openapi.json, and the front end's client is generated from it. If the API changes, the client changes with it. A mismatch shows up at build time instead of in front of the expert.
followUps.remember: The schema is the contract between the back-end and front-end repos.

followUps.question: Why Celery? Why not do the extraction inside the request?
followUps.answer: Reading a workbook or a long PDF and calling a model takes far longer than a web request should. Celery takes that work off the request path. The user gets a job back and the result arrives when it's done.
followUps.remember: Slow work goes to a worker, never into the request.
followUps.trap: This is the general reason. If they ask for timings, say you don't have a measured figure to quote.

followUps.question: Where does the CAD-to-KML step fit?
followUps.answer: It's the first link in the chain. The site boundary comes in as a CAD drawing and goes out as KML. The boundary file carries legal liability, so an expert checks it before anything downstream uses it.
followUps.remember: The boundary file is the first gate and the one with legal weight.

checks: The Celery task layout and queue design are not recorded. Confirm them against the repos before you describe them in detail.
Confirm that the 3 repos behind the 773 commits are the fde-os docs, back-end and front-end repos for MITCON.

questions.question: "What were the key technical decisions?" (re-cutting the architecture, dropping Anthropic, gpt-4o-mini to Gemini)
questions.simple: Four decisions shaped MITCON. I threw away my first architecture after five days. We dropped Anthropic because its document block took only PDFs. A spike on 110 uploads showed the rebuilt pipeline on Gemini beat the old one on gpt-4o-mini, so Gemini took extraction. And I put a strict grounding contract on every model call.

answer.label: Re-cutting the architecture
answer.text: I started with a FastAPI monolith. Five days in, its shape no longer fitted the delivery plan. So I re-cut it into a Django and React multi-repo on the fde-os template.

answer.label: Dropping Anthropic
answer.text: Anthropic's document block accepted only PDF among binary files (ADR-003). Our inputs include workbooks, and those returned a 400 before they ever reached the model. So we dropped it and moved all model access to OpenRouter. I filed the reproduction as a session note, so the reason is on record.

answer.label: gpt-4o-mini to Gemini
answer.text: We began with gpt-4o-mini for extraction. A spike on 110 uploads set the old pipeline on gpt-4o-mini against the rebuilt pipeline on Gemini, and the rebuild won on wrong values, recall and repeatability. On the same first stage, Gemini alone also beat gpt-4o-mini. I chose Gemini Flash-Lite plus the narrowing step, and the extra decision-model call added no net cost per file. So Gemini took extraction. gpt-4o-mini stayed for authoring, answers and chat.

answer.label: The grounding contract
answer.text: This was the decision that mattered most. The model may only propose what the document states, with a citation. An ambiguous value gets both readings. Anything it can't ground stays blank.

questions.remember: Re-cut early, drop a provider on a reproduced fact, pick the model on a spike, and constrain the model instead of trusting it.
questions.steer: The provider switch is a good example of deciding on a reproduction. I can tell you exactly what failed.
questions.trap: Don't say Anthropic's models were worse. The reason was input format: workbooks were rejected with a 400 before reaching the model.

followUps.question: What exactly didn't fit about the monolith?
followUps.answer: The shape stopped fitting the delivery plan five days in, so I moved to the Django and React multi-repo. That's the record. Prepare the specifics before you're asked.
followUps.remember: Five days in, cheap to change.
followUps.trap: Don't invent a reason. The profile records only that the shape stopped fitting the delivery plan.

followUps.question: Couldn't you have converted the workbooks to PDF and stayed on Anthropic?
followUps.answer: You'd lose the cell addresses. The contract asks for sheet and cell as the citation. A rendered PDF of a workbook gives you a page, and the expert can't check a page against a cell.
followUps.remember: The citation needs the cell, so the workbook has to stay a workbook.

followUps.question: Why did you move extraction off gpt-4o-mini?
followUps.answer: I ran a spike on 110 uploads. The old pipeline on gpt-4o-mini had a wrong-value rate of 27.2%, recall of 27.9% and repeatability of 46.0%. The rebuilt pipeline on Gemini scored 10.9%, 61.9% and 87.2%. On the model alone, gpt-4o-mini scored 24.0% wrong values and 36.1% recall, against 11.1% and 57.3% for Gemini. Voting over three gpt-4o-mini reads cost the same as one Gemini read and scored worse.
followUps.remember: The rebuild won on every measure, Gemini alone beat gpt-4o-mini too, and voting didn't rescue it.
followUps.trap: Quote the figures with the 110-upload count. Don't claim a benchmark you didn't run.

checks: The reason for comparing gpt-4o-mini with Gemini, and not another model, is not recorded. Prepare it.
Prepare one concrete example of what stopped fitting in the FastAPI monolith.

questions.question: "How do you stop the extractor inventing numbers?" The grounding contract in depth
questions.simple: The model works under four rules. It may only propose a value the document states. It must quote where it found it. If the document is ambiguous, it shows both readings. If it can't ground a value, it leaves the field empty for an expert.

answer.label: The principle
answer.text: My comment above the contract says it best: "a gap on screen is recoverable and an invented number in a signed document is not." Every rule follows from that.

answer.label: Rule one: stated only
answer.text: The model may propose a value only when the document states it. It doesn't calculate, estimate or fill in from general knowledge.

answer.label: Rule two: cite it
answer.text: Every value carries the exact fragment it came from. For a spreadsheet that means the sheet and the cell. The expert can check any number in seconds.

answer.label: Rule three: both readings
answer.text: When the source is ambiguous, the model proposes both readings. It doesn't choose. The choice belongs to the expert who signs.

answer.label: Rule four: omit what it can't ground
answer.text: If the model can't ground a field, it leaves it out. A blank on screen tells the expert where to look. A confident wrong number hides.

answer.label: Where it lives
answer.text: The contract is a file, model-tasks/extract.toml. It's a file in the repo, so a change to it is visible in the history. Hand-written gates in code enforce it after the model replies.

questions.remember: A gap on screen is recoverable. An invented number in a signed document is not.
questions.steer: This is the part of my work I'd most like to be judged on, because the cost of a wrong answer is legal.

questions.question: "Tell me about your work at Fresh Tracks Canada"
questions.simple: Fresh Tracks Canada is a Vancouver travel business. I was AI Systems Architect there on a contract, working across their booking platform of 10 repos. I built a multi-agent payment system on LangGraph and AWS Bedrock, where code computes every amount and agents decide and write. I also built a tool that tells sales agents what trains and hotels are free during a live call.

answer.label: The problem
answer.text: Fresh Tracks sells rail and hotel trips across Canada. Their sales agents need availability during a live call, before an itinerary exists. The sources don't make that easy. One has a live API, one has a B2B feed, one has no API at all.

answer.label: What I built
answer.text: The Trip Availability Assistant. It puts four different availability sources behind one adapter model. It fetches ahead of time, so the agent's screen never waits on a scrape. It shipped with an operator dashboard and a feature-flagged Excel fallback.

answer.label: The payment agents
answer.text: Payments were manual. Sales staff made one payment link per instalment, plans varied per customer, and errors and late refunds were common. I built a multi-agent payment system on LangGraph and AWS Bedrock, with a Django payment service underneath. A salesperson now sets the itinerary and the payment plan and saves. The agents handle requests, reminders, refunds and instalment changes.

answer.label: My role
answer.text: I was AI Systems Architect on a direct contract, from 12/2025 to 08/2026. We were a 2-engineer, AI-accelerated team. The record shows 218 merged commits across their 10 repos for our team of two.

answer.label: Impact
answer.text: Refund turnaround went from about two business days, with a human checking the values, to one business day from the nightly run. There's no manual review on the cases the agents handle, an estimated 95%. The other 5% go back to sales staff the old way. Coverage started at an estimated 80% and reached an estimated 95% after root-cause analysis of the failed cases.

questions.question: "Walk me through the Trip Availability Assistant architecture"
questions.simple: Each supplier gets an adapter, and each adapter has an acquisition method: live call, scheduled sweep or existing sync. Scheduled jobs scrape or fetch in the background and drop results on a queue. The booking system stores snapshots, and the agent's screen reads those snapshots.

answer.label: Four sources, one model
answer.text: BIM is a live HTTP lookup. VIA Rail comes through its authorised Sqills B2B API in a daily sweep. Rocky Mountaineer has no B2B API, so it's an anonymous scrape every 20 minutes. Jonview comes through an existing sync. All four sit behind one adapter and acquisition-method model.

answer.label: The pipeline
answer.text: An EventBridge cron starts a Fargate task. The task runs Playwright through a Canadian residential proxy. Results go onto SQS. A consumer in the PMS reads them and writes AvailabilitySnapshot and AdapterRunLog rows.

answer.label: The read path
answer.text: The agent's screen reads snapshots. It never waits on a scrape. If a sweep is slow or fails, the agent still gets the last good answer.

answer.label: Manual override
answer.text: There's a break-glass path for a manual Excel upload. I modelled it as an override, MANUAL_UPLOAD, and kept it out of the source list.

answer.label: Operator surface
answer.text: It shipped with a scrape-run dashboard, run history and per-config verdicts. A run passes only if every valid config passes.

questions.remember: Cron, Fargate, queue, snapshot. The agent reads the snapshot and never waits.

The reason for the proxy isn't written down anywhere I can point to. My reading is that it makes the sweep look like an ordinary Canadian visitor, and I'd confirm that before saying more.
followUps.remember: No API, anonymous read, stealth and a Canadian proxy. The reason is my reading.

questions.simple: Four decisions. Every supplier fits one adapter model. A manual upload overrides a source instead of becoming one. The agent's screen reads stored snapshots, so it never waits. And the scraper began as a throwaway prototype with a seam that let it graduate cleanly.

answer.label: One adapter model
answer.text: The sources differ in how we get the data. So the adapter has an acquisition method: live call, scheduled sweep or existing sync. The rest of the system doesn't care which.

answer.label: Manual upload is an override
answer.text: Someone sometimes has to upload a spreadsheet by hand. If that were a fifth source, it would compete with the real ones. As an override, it sits beside the sources and doesn't compete with them.

answer.label: The read path never blocks
answer.text: A sales agent is on the phone. A browser scrape can take a while or fail. So we fetch ahead of time and the screen reads the last snapshot.

answer.label: Throwaway first, then graduate
answer.text: The scraper began as a feasibility prototype under NB-10708. It was deliberately not a git repo, so nobody would mistake it for production. The browser logic sat behind an output.py seam. At graduation we swapped writing JSON to disk for writing to SQS, and the browser code didn't change.

questions.remember: One model, override not source, never block the read, and a seam that lets the prototype graduate.
questions.steer: The output.py seam is a small thing that saved a rewrite. It's worth a minute.
questions.trap: Don't call the prototype production code. It was explicitly throwaway until it graduated.

followUps.question: Why not just call every supplier live?
followUps.answer: Rocky Mountaineer has no API, so a live call means a live browser scrape during a phone call. That's slow and fragile. Pre-fetching keeps the screen fast and the failures out of sight of the customer.
followUps.remember: You can't scrape live while a customer waits.

followUps.question: What's the trade-off of pre-fetching?
followUps.answer: Staleness. The snapshot is only as fresh as the last sweep: 20 minutes for Rocky Mountaineer, daily for VIA Rail. The run history and verdicts make the age and the failures visible.
followUps.remember: Fast and visible beats live and fragile.

questions.question: "What went wrong, and how did you handle it?" (the BIM data slip and the PostHog flag; a supplier with no API)
questions.simple: Two things went wrong. The client's own BIM data slipped to December, so the live lookup had nothing to read. And one supplier had no API at all. I handled the first with a per-supplier feature flag and the second with a scheduled scrape.

answer.label: The data slip
answer.text: The BIM lookup depended on the client's own data. That data slipped to December. The code was ready and the data wasn't.

answer.label: What I did
answer.text: I shipped a PostHog feature flag per supplier. When it's on, the BIM lookup is replaced by a "Check Excel" link to Confluence. Agents had a working path straight away. When the data arrives, the business flips the flag back. There was no code fork.

answer.label: The supplier with no API
answer.text: Rocky Mountaineer has no B2B API. So we read its public availability every 20 minutes with Playwright, using stealth and a Canadian residential proxy. It ran in Fargate, off the read path.

answer.label: What I took from it
answer.text: A fallback should belong to the business. And when a system won't give you an API, you can still make it reliable if the read path never waits for it.

followUps.answer: A flag is reversible at runtime, per supplier, by the business. A branch is a code fork someone has to merge back. A config change needs a deploy. The flag let them switch back the day the data landed.
followUps.remember: Reversible, per supplier, owned by the business.

questions.question: The payment agents and the payment service
questions.simple: I built a multi-agent payment system on LangGraph and AWS Bedrock. Deterministic code computes every amount. The agents read each itinerary's payment history, decide the next action and write every mail in the brand voice. A Django payment service sits underneath, across Flywire and other systems.

answer.label: Discovery
answer.text: I ran discovery with the client's finance leads. We mapped the as-is processes. Then we split the workflows into human-in-the-loop and safe-to-automate, and scoped a hybrid SaaS and agent roadmap.

answer.label: The payment agents
answer.text: On an instalment's due date at 9 am, an agent makes the payment link and emails the customer, who has about 28 hours to pay. A cron agent queues a reminder for the next day for anything overdue, and repeats until it's paid. A nightly run at midnight compares what was received with what was expected. An overpayment starts a refund with no manual step.

answer.label: Code and model
answer.text: Deterministic code computes every amount: instalment splits, per-country tax and refunds. The model reads the payment history, decides the next step and writes every communication. It's a mix of deterministic and probabilistic. When an itinerary value changes after some instalments are paid, the paid ones stay and the rest are re-spread.

answer.label: Evals and guardrails
answer.text: Guardrails AI checks the mails and DeepEval scores them. LangSmith traces each run end to end. The models run on AWS Bedrock. I built these in from the start, not after launch.

answer.label: The payment service
answer.text: Underneath sits a new Django payment service. It connects Flywire and several other systems and automates payment requests, reminders, refunds and instalment changes.

answer.label: Coverage
answer.text: At launch an estimated 80% of cases went through the agents. At handover it was an estimated 95%. The cases outside the configured rules go back to sales staff and the manual process.

questions.question: "Why freeze the questionnaire into a snapshot?" The snapshot-bound design in depth
questions.simple: Questions change over time, but a regulator may ask years later why a business got its risk rating. So when a business finishes its questionnaire, the exact questions and options it saw are frozen. Every score and every generated document reads that frozen copy.

answer.label: The problem
answer.text: The question bank changes. Wording gets clearer, options get added, scoring rules get sharper. If old programmes read live rows, a past rating could quietly change under them.

answer.label: The design
answer.text: When a programme attempt completes, its questions and options freeze into an immutable snapshot. All scoring and risk mitigation programme generation read the snapshot. They never read the live rows.

answer.label: What hangs off it
answer.text: The risk tier sets the mandatory review date. Options flagged rmp_trigger=true generate risk mitigation programme items automatically, from the snapshot.

answer.label: Templates
answer.text: There are 24 versioned templates: 3 entity types by 4 risk tiers. A generated programme knows which template version it came from.

answer.label: Why it's right
answer.text: A regulated document has to be defensible years later. With a snapshot, the answer to "why this rating?" is always the same as the day it was signed.

questions.remember: Freeze what the customer saw. Score what was frozen. Defend it years later.
questions.steer: This is the same instinct as the MITCON grounding contract: make the system's answer reproducible for the person who has to defend it.
questions.trap: Don't call it versioning alone. Versioned templates and the immutable snapshot are two separate mechanisms.

followUps.question: Why not just version the questions and keep a pointer?
followUps.answer: A pointer works only if nobody ever edits an old version. A snapshot removes that dependency. The completed attempt carries its own copy, so a later edit can't reach it.
followUps.remember: A copy can't be edited from somewhere else.

followUps.question: What does it cost you?
followUps.answer: Storage, and some duplication. Each completed attempt carries its own copy of the questions. For a product whose output must hold up in an audit, that's cheap.
followUps.remember: Duplication is the price of a defensible record.
followUps.trap: Don't quote storage figures. None are recorded.

categories.title: The FDE method: fde and fde-os

questions.question: "Tell me about the FDE plugin and the engagement template"
questions.simple: fde is People Equation's Claude Code plugin. It packages forward-deployed engineering as skills a team installs once and runs on every engagement. fde-os is the matching template: the repos and the record an engagement starts with. answer.label: The problem
answer.text: Every engagement repeats the same work. Discovery, a record of what the client said, decisions, gates and handover. Done from scratch each time, it drifts, and the record stops being trustworthy.

answer.label: What it is
answer.text: fde is People Equation's Claude Code plugin. It packages the FDE method as skills a pod installs once and runs on every engagement. It holds method and shared conventions only. Each engagement owns its own stack in its own repos.

answer.label: The template
answer.text: fde-os is the engagement template. It has three repos: the engagement record, a Django back end and a React front end. It also has a working-memory folder. An init skill renames and sets it up, and refuses to run twice.

answer.label: Where it's used
answer.text: I've applied it the same way across mitcon-eia, the earlier MITCON monolith and the Ashworth Broking scoping. MITCON is the full run.

answer.label: Why it matters
answer.text: It makes the method repeatable. Every claim in the record carries a tag for how strongly it's evidenced. That's what lets a client trust the record.

questions.steer: This is the most on-point thing I work with for this role. I'm happy to walk through how an engagement is structured.
questions.trap: Don't call it your own product, and don't say "I built the method". The repos belong to People Equation. Say "People Equation's plugin".

questions.question: "How is an engagement structured?" (three repos, eight skills, an init that refuses to run twice)
questions.simple: An engagement has three repos and a working-memory folder. One repo is the engagement record, and the other two are the back end and the front end. Eight skills split into two jobs: keeping the record true and building a milestone.

answer.label: The record
answer.text: fde-docs is the engagement record. It has an immutable raw folder with an arrival ledger, so I always know what the client sent and when. It has a wiki with no unsourced facts. It has a charter, gates and ADRs.

answer.label: The code
answer.text: fde-be is a Django API with Celery and an openapi.json. fde-fe is React with a client generated from that schema.

answer.label: Working memory
answer.text: my-sessions holds the working notes for each session. It keeps the scratch work out of the record.

answer.label: Eight skills and init
answer.text: /fde:init takes a slug, renames and sets everything up, and refuses to run twice. The eight skills split between /fde:fdc-session, which keeps the record true, and /fde:aie-session, which builds a milestone.

answer.label: The charter
answer.text: The charter names the executive sponsor, the process owner, the data owner and the security decision-maker. I want those names on day one, before anything is built.

questions.remember: One repo for the truth, two for the code, and skills that keep them apart.
questions.steer: The init that refuses to run twice is small, but it shows the mindset: make the dangerous action impossible.
questions.trap: Don't list skill names beyond the ones on record. Only init, fdc-session and aie-session are named in the profile.

followUps.question: Why does init refuse to run twice?
followUps.answer: Running it again would rename and overwrite a live engagement. Refusing is cheaper than recovering. It's the same instinct as hooks that block an agent from dangerous operations.
followUps.remember: Make the destructive repeat impossible.

followUps.question: Why separate the record from the code?
followUps.answer: They change for different reasons and at different speeds. The record changes when the client tells us something. The code changes when we build. Keeping them apart stops a build from quietly rewriting what the client said.
followUps.remember: The record changes on evidence. The code changes on work.

followUps.question: What's an arrival ledger?
followUps.answer: A log of every input as it arrives: what came in, from whom and when. The raw folder is immutable, so the original is always there. Anything in the wiki traces back to an entry.
followUps.remember: Nothing in the wiki without a source in the ledger.

questions.question: "What were the key design decisions?" (pinned plugin versions, authority tiers, no application code)
questions.simple: Three decisions. Each engagement pins the plugin version and doesn't upgrade mid-milestone. Every fact in the record carries a tag for how well it's evidenced. And the plugin holds method only, never application code.

answer.label: Pinned versions
answer.text: The plugin is versioned and tagged. An engagement records its plugin_version in an .engagement file. It doesn't pull a new version mid-milestone. In the repo's words, "a skill that changes under a running build is a skill that invalidates the record it just wrote."

answer.label: Authority tiers
answer.text: Every claim carries a tag. stated means the client said it. artefact means we read it from a repo, a site or a file. ours means it's our inference and can be challenged. A reader can see at a glance how much weight each fact bears.

answer.label: No application code
answer.text: The plugin holds the method and shared conventions. Each engagement owns its own stack in its own repos. So the method can't drag one client's code into another's.

questions.remember: Pin the method, tag every fact, and keep client code out of the plugin.
questions.steer: The authority tiers are the bit clients notice. They can see which facts are theirs and which are our guesses.
questions.trap: Don't oversell the tiers as a tool. They're a discipline written into the template and the skills.

followUps.question: Isn't pinning just going to leave engagements on old versions?
followUps.answer: Between milestones, an engagement can move up. During one, it stays put. The record a milestone writes has to match the method that wrote it.
followUps.remember: Upgrade between milestones, never during one.

followUps.question: Who decides whether something is stated or ours?
followUps.answer: The tag follows where the fact came from. If the client said it, it's stated. If we read it from a system or a document, it's artefact. If we worked it out, it's ours, which flags it as an inference that can be challenged.
followUps.remember: The source decides the tag.

questions.question: AI-assisted delivery tooling at Fresh Tracks: skills, CLAUDE.md, ROUTER.md, and hooks that block the agent
questions.simple: At Fresh Tracks I set up the coding agent so a two-person team could work safely across 10 repos. Skills ran the routine steps. A context file told the agent how the services fit together. Hooks blocked it from running anything that could touch real data.

answer.label: Five skills
answer.text: I wrote five Claude Code skills: /start-ticket, /session-sync, /ready-for-git, /post-pr and /generate-invoice. Each one runs a routine step the same way every time.

answer.label: Context the agent can trust
answer.text: A root CLAUDE.md holds a verified service graph. Each repo has its own bible. A ROUTER.md maps ticket keywords to the files to start from, so the agent begins in the right place.

answer.label: Hooks that block
answer.text: PreToolUse hooks block the agent from running pytest, because the containers point at the dev RDS database. They also block any data mutation under the staging profile. I designed those guardrails against my own tooling.

answer.label: The rest of the record
answer.text: A RUNBOOK and ADRs sit alongside, so a decision and how to operate it are written down.

answer.label: Why it matters
answer.text: It's what let a 2-engineer team work across 10 repos. Speed came from the skills. Safety came from the hooks.

tabs.title: Forward-deployed practice
tabs.purpose: Discovery, scoping, embedding with a customer and proving the metric moved.

questions.question: What is a forward-deployed engineer, and how is it different from a solutions engineer or a consultant?
questions.simple: A forward-deployed engineer sits with the customer and ships production code against their real problem. A solutions engineer mostly works before the deal, on demos and fit. A consultant mostly advises. The FDE owns a working system and whether it moved the customer's number.

answer.label: Answer first
answer.text: A forward-deployed engineer writes production code inside the customer's world. I own the result, and I'm judged on whether their metric moved.

answer.label: Against a solutions engineer
answer.text: A solutions engineer mostly works before signature. They run demos and prove fit. I come in after, and I live with the system once it's running.

answer.label: Against a consultant
answer.text: A consultant leaves recommendations. I leave a running system, a runbook and a record of why each decision was made.

answer.label: What it looks like for me
answer.text: At MITCON I led discovery myself. Then I built the extraction pipeline, and the first two deliveries are in build. It's the same person from the first meeting to production.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: I've worked this way on three contract engagements since June 2025: AML SoftServe, Fresh Tracks and MITCON. I also packaged the method as a Claude Code plugin and an engagement template for People Equation.

questions.remember: Same engineer from discovery to production, judged on the customer's metric.
questions.steer: I can show you how I turned that way of working into a plugin a pod installs on every engagement.
questions.trap: Don't run down solutions engineers or consultants. Don't call the fde plugin your own product; the repo belongs to People Equation.

followUps.question: Isn't that just a consultant who codes?
followUps.answer: The difference is ownership. I commit to the customer's repos and I stay until the thing runs. At Fresh Tracks that meant 218 merged commits across their 10 repos.
followUps.remember: Ownership of running code is the difference.

followUps.question: Where does product feedback fit in?
followUps.answer: Whatever I learn in one engagement goes back into the method. The fde plugin is that loop: the same skills and conventions run on every engagement, so a fix lands once.
followUps.remember: Field lessons go back into the plugin.

questions.question: How do you run discovery in the first two weeks of an engagement?
questions.simple: Discovery is where you learn how the work really runs before you build anything. You find out who decides what and what the data looks like. You also find which steps are safe to automate. The output is a scoped plan the customer agrees to.

answer.label: Answer first
answer.text: I map the work as it really runs and name who decides what. I do that before I write production code.

answer.label: Name the people
answer.text: The engagement charter names four roles: the executive sponsor, the process owner, the data owner and the security decision-maker. If a name is missing, I'd treat that as my first risk.

answer.label: Map the process
answer.text: At MITCON I led discovery through value chain analysis and hotspot identification. We mapped the statutory clearance chain end to end. At Fresh Tracks I did the same with the finance leads.

answer.label: Split the steps
answer.text: I mark every step as either expert-checkpointed review or safe to automate. That split becomes the shape of the build.

answer.label: Keep the evidence clean
answer.text: Everything the customer sends goes into an immutable raw folder with an arrival ledger. Every claim in the record is tagged stated, artefact or ours, so nobody builds on a guess.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: At MITCON the discovery produced 7 contracted deliveries covering 307 pages.

questions.remember: People, process, split, evidence. Then a scoped plan.
questions.steer: The tagging of every claim as stated, artefact or ours is worth asking me about. It stops a team building on an assumption.
questions.trap: Don't claim a fixed two-week timeline unless you can say how long MITCON discovery actually ran.

followUps.question: What do you do when the stakeholders disagree about how the process works?
followUps.answer: My approach would be to write down both versions and tag them as stated by each person. Then I'd look for an artefact, such as a real filed document, to settle it. The record would show the disagreement until it's settled.
followUps.remember: Tag both versions, settle with an artefact.

followUps.question: How do you know discovery is done?
followUps.answer: When each step has an owner and a review-or-automate label, and the customer has agreed the deliveries. At MITCON that was the list of contracted deliveries.
followUps.remember: Every step owned and labelled, deliveries agreed.

checks: Confirm how long discovery actually ran at MITCON and at Fresh Tracks before you quote a duration.
The missing-name risk and the disagreement handling are how the method is meant to work, not recorded history. Present them as my approach, and confirm any real case before you cite one.

questions.question: How do you decide what to automate and what keeps a human in the loop?
questions.simple: Some steps are cheap to get wrong and easy to undo, so a machine can do them. Others end up in a signed or regulated document, so a person must check them. The decision turns on the cost of a wrong answer and who carries the liability.

answer.label: Answer first
answer.text: I ask what a wrong answer costs and who signs for it. If a person signs, a person checks.

answer.label: The test I use
answer.text: If the output is reversible and cheap to fix, I automate it. If it lands in a signed or regulated document, it gets an expert checkpoint.

answer.label: MITCON
answer.text: Environmental clearance documents carry legal weight. So the model only proposes values with a citation, and an expert checks at every gate. The rule I wrote is "a gap on screen is recoverable and an invented number in a signed document is not."

answer.label: AML SoftServe
answer.text: I mapped the Tranche 2 AML/CTF obligations with the compliance team. Risk-critical items went to human review. The rest became automatable checks.

answer.label: Fresh Tracks
answer.text: With the finance leads I split the workflows into human-in-the-loop and safe to automate. That split shaped the delivery roadmap.

questions.remember: If a person signs it, a person checks it.
questions.steer: The MITCON grounding contract shows this in code. I can walk you through it.
questions.trap: Don't say "we automated everything we could". In regulated work that sounds careless.

followUps.question: Doesn't a human checkpoint at every gate kill the speed gain?
followUps.answer: The model still does the reading and the drafting. The expert reviews a cited proposal, which is much faster than starting from a blank page.
followUps.remember: The expert reviews, the model drafts.

followUps.question: Who decides where the line goes?
followUps.answer: The process owner, with me. I bring the cost-of-error view, and they bring the domain. The charter names the process owner, which is the role I'd expect to hold that call.
followUps.remember: The process owner decides, I inform it.

checks: The process owner holding the automation-line decision is our inference from the charter roles. Confirm how the line was set at MITCON before you say it.

questions.question: How do you scope an engagement into a delivery plan or statement of work?

questions.question: How do you work inside a customer's codebase and constraints?
questions.simple: An FDE usually works in code someone else owns, with rules they set. The job is to move fast without breaking their systems. That means learning the map quickly and putting guardrails on yourself.

answer.label: Answer first
answer.text: I map their system first. Then I put guardrails on myself, so I can move fast without hurting their data.

answer.label: Map it
answer.text: Fresh Tracks had a 10-repo platform with a Salesforce-driven lifecycle. I wrote a root CLAUDE.md with a verified service graph and a ROUTER.md that maps ticket keywords to starting files.

answer.label: Guard it
answer.text: I added PreToolUse hooks that block the coding agent from running pytest, because the containers pointed at the dev database. They also block data changes under the staging profile.

answer.label: Respect their limits
answer.text: One supplier, Rocky Mountaineer, had no B2B API at all. I didn't wait for one. I scraped it on a schedule, kept it off the read path, and fed it into the existing model.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: I landed 218 merged commits across those 10 repos. At AML SoftServe I was top contributor, with 327 of 986 commits on the team of 8 I headed.

questions.remember: Map their system, then guard myself against it.
questions.steer: The hooks are worth a look. I designed guardrails against my own tooling.
questions.trap: Don't claim the Gemini NL-to-SQL feature in the Fresh Tracks PMS front end. It was a colleague's work.

followUps.question: Why block your own agent from running tests?
followUps.answer: The test containers pointed at the dev database on RDS. A careless test run could have changed shared data. A hook that blocks it is safer than a rule I might forget.
followUps.remember: A hook beats a rule I might forget.

followUps.question: How did you learn a 10-repo platform quickly?
followUps.answer: I wrote the map as I learned it: the service graph, a per-repo guide and the keyword router. Then the map was there for the next ticket and the next engineer.
followUps.remember: Write the map as you learn it.

questions.question: How do you prove you moved the customer's metric? Give me a before and an after.
questions.simple: Proving impact means agreeing the metric with the process owner, measuring it before you ship and measuring it the same way after. Without a baseline the after number means little.

answer.label: Answer first
answer.text: I agree the metric with the process owner in discovery, and I measure it the same way before and after.

answer.label: Fresh Tracks
answer.text: Refund turnaround moved from about two business days, with a human checking the values, to one business day. The nightly reconciliation run does it with no manual review on the cases the agents handle, an estimated 95%. The other 5% go back to sales staff.

answer.label: TekMindz
answer.text: Sprint velocity rose 40 to 50% on the TekMindz pilot project after I rolled out the AI-enabled delivery method.

answer.label: MITCON
answer.text: On a 110-upload golden set, the rebuilt pipeline raised recall from 28% to 62% and cut wrong values from 27% to 11%, against the old pipeline on gpt-4o-mini. The 97-row consolidated statement also fills automatically, under the grounding contract.

answer.label: How it was measured
answer.text: The MITCON numbers come from golden-set evals against the old pipeline on gpt-4o-mini. The Fresh Tracks baseline is the two-day human check. For the TekMindz velocity figure there is no evidence yet of the baseline or the period. Prepare that before I quote it.

questions.trap: Fresh Tracks has one outcome figure, the refund turnaround. Don't quote any other Fresh Tracks number.

followUps.answer: About two business days, because a human checked the values. The nightly run now does it in one business day with no manual review on the estimated 95% of cases the agents handle.
followUps.remember: Two business days to one. An estimated 95% handled, 5% to sales staff.
followUps.trap: Don't add a period or a volume. The record has neither.

questions.question: The customer's data or a dependency slips. What do you do?
questions.simple: Customer dependencies slip all the time. A good FDE ships a reversible fallback so the business keeps working, and swaps the real thing in when it arrives. The fallback shouldn't become a code fork.

answer.label: Answer first
answer.text: I ship a reversible fallback so the business keeps working, and I swap the real thing in when it arrives.

answer.label: The BIM slip
answer.text: At Fresh Tracks the client's BIM data slipped to December. I shipped a PostHog per-supplier feature flag. It swapped the BIM lookup for a "Check Excel" link to Confluence. When the data lands, the flag flips back. There's no code fork.

answer.label: The break-glass path
answer.text: I also modelled manual Excel upload as an override, not as another source. So a person can always correct the data without a special code path.

answer.label: A provider limit
answer.text: At MITCON, Anthropic's document block accepted only PDF among binary files, so spreadsheets failed before reaching the model. I reproduced it, filed it as a session note, and moved extraction to OpenAI.

answer.label: No API at all
answer.text: Rocky Mountaineer had no B2B API. I scraped it on a schedule instead of waiting.

questions.remember: A reversible fallback, then flip back. Never a fork.
questions.steer: The feature-flag fallback is a good story. It kept the sales team working while the client's data was late.
questions.trap: Don't blame the customer for the slip. Describe it as a normal risk you planned for.

followUps.question: Why a feature flag and not a code branch?
followUps.answer: A flag is a business switch. It's per supplier, it can be flipped without a deploy, and it can be flipped back. A branch would have to be merged and maintained.
followUps.remember: A flag flips back, a fork has to be merged.

followUps.question: Wasn't switching model providers risky mid-engagement?
followUps.answer: Less risky than the alternative. The workbooks never reached the model. I filed the reproduction so the reason is on record.
followUps.remember: Reproduce it, record it, then switch.

questions.question: How do you hand a system over so the customer can run it after you leave?
questions.simple: Handover means the customer's team can run, fix and change the system without you. That needs a runbook, written decisions, and screens that show operators what the system is doing.

answer.label: Answer first
answer.text: I build the handover into the system from the start: a runbook, written decisions and an operator screen.

answer.label: Operator surface
answer.text: The Trip Availability Assistant shipped with a scrape-run dashboard, run history and per-config verdicts. A run only passes if every valid config passes, so an operator can see a failure without reading logs.

answer.label: Written decisions
answer.text: At Fresh Tracks I left a RUNBOOK and ADRs, plus a root CLAUDE.md with a verified service graph.

answer.label: The record
answer.text: With the engagement template the record lives in its own repo, fde-docs. The API publishes an openapi.json, and the front end uses a generated client, so the contract between them is explicit.

questions.remember: Runbook, ADRs, an operator screen. From day one.
questions.steer: The ScrapeRun pass rule is a nice detail on operability. Ask me about it.
questions.trap: Don't describe a handover meeting or a training session you can't evidence.

followUps.question: What did the actual handover at Fresh Tracks look like?
followUps.answer: At Fresh Tracks, the agents handled an estimated 95% of cases when I left. I handed the system over with a knowledge transfer on how to add rules for new cases. The engagement ended in August 2026.
followUps.remember: Prepare the real handover story.

followUps.question: How do you know the customer can run it?
followUps.answer: The operator can tell a passing run from a failing one on the dashboard. The runbook covers the known failure paths.
followUps.remember: If the operator can read it, they can run it.

questions.question: An executive wants a demo more than a working system. How do you handle it?
questions.simple: Executives often want something to show. The risk is a demo that can't become the real system. The answer is a demo built on the real path, or a spike that is openly labelled as throwaway.

answer.label: Answer first
answer.text: I give them a demo, but I build it on the real path or I label it throwaway.

answer.label: Why
answer.text: A demo that can't graduate costs the customer twice. They pay for the demo and then for the rebuild.

answer.label: How I've done the throwaway version
answer.text: At Fresh Tracks the Rocky Mountaineer scraper began as an explicit throwaway spike. It wasn't even a git repo. The browser logic sat behind one seam, so at graduation I swapped writing to disk for writing to SQS.

answer.label: What I show
answer.text: I show the gaps on screen too. At MITCON a missing value shows as a gap with no guess, and that's part of the demo.

answer.label: The executive story
answer.text: No evidence yet of a specific executive who pushed for a demo. Prepare one before claiming it.

questions.question: How do you turn what you learn in the field into product feedback or reusable assets?
questions.simple: Each engagement teaches you something. An FDE writes it down in a form the next engagement can reuse, such as a template, a skill or a library, so the lesson isn't lost.

answer.label: The plugin

questions.question: How do you work in a regulated or high-consequence domain?
questions.simple: In regulated work, every output must be defensible later to an auditor or a regulator. That shapes the data model, the review steps and how much freedom the model gets.

answer.label: Answer first
answer.text: I design so every output can be defended years later. That decides the data model and the review steps.

answer.label: AML SoftServe
answer.text: The product was built for Australian reporting entities under AUSTRAC AML/CTF rules. It is now live with 70-odd customers and 20,000+ recorded transactions. The risk questionnaire is snapshot-bound. When an attempt completes, questions and options freeze, and all scoring reads the snapshot, never live rows. The agentic RAG over 800+ AUSTRAC documents made every finding cite its source clause, and Guardrails AI blocked ungrounded output.

answer.label: Isolation
answer.text: Row-level security in Postgres was the security boundary between tenants. Templates were versioned: 24 of them, 3 entity types by 4 risk tiers.

answer.label: MITCON
answer.text: Environmental clearance documents carry legal liability. So the extractor quotes its source for every value and omits what it can't ground. A code-level gate accepts a value only when its citation is found in the source. Experts check at every gate.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: Both engagements are on my CV. AML SoftServe ran 06/2025 to 11/2025, and MITCON runs from 09/2026.

questions.sourceRef: Use-case round: research a use case new to you and your team
questions.question: When a use case is completely new to you and your team, what does your research process look like?
questions.simple: You can't automate work you haven't seen. You map how it runs today, find where the effort piles up, and decide which kind of automation each hotspot needs. Then you prove one hotspot with a pilot before you take the rest.

answer.label: Answer first
answer.text: I run it in four steps: map the as-is, mine the process for hotspots, classify each hotspot, then pilot one.

answer.label: 1. Map the as-is
answer.text: I sit with the people who do the work and map how it really runs. In the background I read the domain's rules and documents. At Fresh Tracks I did this with the finance and sales staff.

answer.label: 2. Mine the process
answer.text: I look at the real trail of the work, such as emails, documents and records. I want to see where the effort, the rework and the waiting pile up. Those are the hotspots.

answer.label: 3. Classify each hotspot
answer.text: Each hotspot gets one of three labels. It is full automation, an agentic step with a human in the loop, or deterministic code. At Fresh Tracks deterministic code computes every amount, and the agent only picks the next step.

answer.label: 4. Pilot one
answer.text: I cut a pilot from one hotspot and agree its success metric first, with a baseline from the customer's own documents. The pilot has to show a measurable delta. Once the customer accepts that, I take the rest of the hotspots.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: At MITCON the hotspot analysis led to 7 contracted deliveries covering 307 pages.

questions.remember: Map, mine, classify, pilot. Agree the metric before the pilot.
questions.steer: Counting the steps out loud makes the answer easy to follow. Then give the MITCON example.
questions.trap: Say how many steps you have and count them. Don't claim you ran a process-mining tool unless you did. Don't quote a delta for the pilot until it is measured.

followUps.question: How do you choose which hotspot goes first?
followUps.answer: I pick the one with the clearest value and the lowest risk, where the customer can measure the result in their own documents. A hotspot that is easy but worth little is not a good first pilot.
followUps.remember: Value and risk, not ease.
