tabs.title: Technical
tabs.purpose: The AI and backend questions, each tied back to what you built, evaluated or understand.

followUps.question: Why not just put all the documents in the context window?
followUps.answer: Cost and quality both suffer. Long contexts are expensive and the model misses details in the middle. Retrieval keeps the prompt small and gives me a citation trail.
followUps.remember: Small prompt, cheaper, and traceable.

followUps.question: When is RAG the wrong tool?
followUps.answer: When the task is one supplied document, like my MITCON extraction. There is nothing to search. I ground the model on that file and make it cite the sheet and cell.
followUps.remember: One document in hand means extraction, not retrieval.

questions.question: What is RAG and why do we need it?
questions.simple: RAG stands for retrieval-augmented generation. The system looks up relevant documents first, then gives them to the model along with the question. The model answers from that text instead of from memory. That keeps answers current and checkable.

answer.label: The problem
answer.text: A model only knows its training data. It does not know my client's documents. It also guesses when it is unsure.

answer.label: The idea
answer.text: I retrieve the passages that matter and put them in the prompt. The model answers from those passages.

answer.label: Why it beats the alternatives
answer.text: I can update the knowledge by changing documents. I do not retrain anything. I can also show the source of every answer.

answer.label: The catch
answer.text: The answer is only as good as the retrieval. If the right passage never reaches the prompt, the model fills the gap.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: At AML SoftServe I designed agentic RAG over 800+ AUSTRAC documents. LlamaParse parsed them, OpenAI embeddings went into pgvector on Supabase, and an LLM reranker on o4-mini sorted the shortlist. Every finding had to cite its source clause. At MITCON the pattern is different. The model reads one supplied document, so it is grounded extraction, not retrieval.

questions.remember: Retrieve first, answer from the text, cite the source.
questions.steer: Name the grounding rule early. At AML SoftServe every finding had to cite its clause, and I can talk about that for a while.
questions.trap: Do not say RAG removes hallucination. It lowers it. Also do not quote a retrieval accuracy figure from AML SoftServe. I have none on record.
checks: Be ready for chunking and embedding detail at AML SoftServe. The notes say both were designed for regulatory text. They give no chunk size and no embedding model name.
DuckDB and Elasticsearch come from the earlier CV and were not reconfirmed in the 18-20 Oct session; confirm before naming them.

followUps.question: Where do most RAG failures start?
followUps.answer: Almost always in ingest or retrieval, not in the model. Bad parsing, bad chunks or a missing filter. I check what was retrieved before I touch the prompt.
followUps.remember: Debug retrieval before the prompt.

followUps.question: How do you keep tenants apart in retrieval?
followUps.answer: The tenant goes in the metadata and the query filters on it. The filter belongs in the data layer, not in the prompt. The AML SoftServe platform was multi-tenant, with isolation on Postgres row-level security. I have not confirmed how that applied to the retrieval chunks.
followUps.remember: Filter in the query, never in the prompt.

questions.question: Explain how a RAG system works end-to-end
questions.simple: A RAG system has two phases. Offline, it cleans documents, splits them and indexes them. Online, it turns the question into a search, ranks what it finds and asks the model to answer from the top results with citations.

answer.label: Ingest
answer.text: The source files are parsed and cleaned, and their structure is kept. Then they are split into chunks with metadata such as source, section and tenant.

answer.label: Index
answer.text: The chunks are indexed for lexical search, vector search or both. Metadata goes in as filters.

answer.label: Retrieve
answer.text: At query time the question is rewritten if needed and searched. The candidates are then re-ranked and a small set is kept.

answer.label: Generate
answer.text: The prompt holds the question, the chosen passages and a rule: answer only from these, cite them, and say when they do not cover it.

answer.label: Check
answer.text: The output is validated against the sources, and the retrieval is logged so a bad answer can be debugged later.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: AML SoftServe. LlamaParse parsed the AUSTRAC documents and the chunking was designed for regulatory text. OpenAI embeddings sat in pgvector, and an o4-mini LLM reranker sorted the shortlist. An agent then checked grounding and decided whether to flag the onboarding or transaction. Guardrails AI blocked ungrounded output.

questions.remember: Ingest, index, retrieve, re-rank, generate with citations, check.
questions.steer: Move to the reranker. We built it in-house for cost: no managed platform fee, and the freedom to switch models.
questions.trap: Do not name a chunk size, an embedding model version or a latency figure from AML SoftServe. None is in my notes.
checks: The reason for an LLM reranker over a cross-encoder is my reasoning (ours). Confirm it matches why you chose it. Expect questions on latency and cost per event.
Confirm how tenant isolation applied to retrieval before you link the two.

followUps.question: Fixed-size chunks or semantic chunks?
followUps.answer: Fixed-size is simple and predictable. Structure-aware is usually better for formal documents. I would only pay for semantic chunking if tests showed a clear gain.
followUps.remember: Structure first, cleverness only if tested.

followUps.question: What goes wrong with tables?
followUps.answer: Splitting a table through the middle separates headers from values. I keep tables whole or repeat the header on each piece.
followUps.remember: Never separate a header from its values.

questions.question: How do you choose a chunking strategy?
questions.simple: A chunk is the unit you retrieve. If it is too small it loses context. If it is too large it dilutes the match and wastes tokens. I pick the unit from how the document is structured, then test it against real questions.

answer.label: Start from structure
answer.text: A contract splits by clause. A policy splits by heading. A spreadsheet splits by sheet and row group. I follow what the author already did.

answer.label: Size and overlap
answer.text: I begin with a few hundred tokens and a small overlap. Then I measure. I do not trust a default.

answer.label: Keep the context
answer.text: Each chunk carries its title, section path and source. A fragment with no heading is hard to rank and hard to cite.

answer.label: Test it
answer.text: I build a small set of real questions with known answer passages. I compare strategies on whether the right chunk comes back.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: AML SoftServe. I designed the chunking for regulatory text, because every finding had to cite its clause. I do not have the chunk size or the overlap in my notes, so I won't quote them. At MITCON the model reads one file whole and cites the sheet and cell, which is not chunking.

questions.remember: Chunk by structure, carry the heading, test on real questions.
questions.steer: Bring it back to citations. A chunk I cannot cite exactly is a chunk I do not trust.
questions.trap: Do not claim a chunk size or a tuned overlap from any engagement. I have none on record.

noEvidence.note: The story bank says chunking at AML SoftServe was designed for regulatory text. It gives no strategy, size or test result.
prepare: Recall how you split the AUSTRAC documents at AML SoftServe, by clause, section or size, and write it down.
Prepare one worked example: how you would chunk a policy document and a spreadsheet, and why.
Decide how you will say the honest line: "I designed it for regulatory text, I can't give you the chunk size."

followUps.question: What is reciprocal rank fusion?
followUps.answer: It scores each document by the sum of one over its rank plus a constant, across the lists. A document ranked high in both lists wins. It ignores raw scores, which differ between systems.
followUps.remember: Add reciprocal ranks, ignore raw scores.

followUps.question: Do you always need a re-ranker?
followUps.answer: No. It adds latency and cost. I add one when the first-stage recall is good but the order is poor. At AML SoftServe I used an in-house o4-mini reranker. We built it in-house for cost, because a managed reranker charged a platform fee on top of the LLM cost.
followUps.remember: Add it only when recall is fine and order is not.

questions.question: What's hybrid retrieval and when would you use it?
questions.simple: Hybrid retrieval combines keyword search with vector search. Keyword search is good at exact terms, codes and names. Vector search is good at meaning. You merge the two ranked lists and get the strengths of both.

answer.label: Two signals
answer.text: BM25 finds exact matches such as a clause number or a company name. Embeddings find passages that mean the same thing with different words.

answer.label: Merging
answer.text: I run both, then fuse the lists. Reciprocal rank fusion works well because it needs no score tuning. A re-ranker can then sort the shortlist.

answer.label: When I use it
answer.text: When users mix exact identifiers and natural language. Compliance and legal text is a good case, because people search for a specific term and for a concept.

answer.label: Cost
answer.text: Two indexes to run and a fusion step to maintain. I only add it if the single method fails on real queries.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: No evidence yet of hybrid retrieval itself. At AML SoftServe retrieval used pgvector and an o4-mini LLM reranker, which is the two-stage shape. I have not recorded a keyword leg or a fusion step.

questions.remember: Keywords for exact terms, vectors for meaning, fuse with RRF.
questions.steer: Describe the two-stage shape at AML SoftServe: vector recall, then an LLM reranker. Then explain why clause numbers and entity names would need a keyword leg.
questions.trap: Do not say you ran hybrid search at AML SoftServe. The evidence stops at pgvector retrieval and an LLM reranker.

noEvidence.note: pgvector and an LLM reranker are in the AML SoftServe stack. The profile does not show a keyword leg or fusion.
prepare: Recall whether the AML SoftServe search also ran keyword queries, for example Postgres full-text search. Write the answer down either way.
Prepare a two-sentence example of a compliance query where exact match and semantic match each matter.

checks: The point that an LLM reranker judges applicability is my reasoning (ours). Confirm it matches why you built it. Expect questions on latency and cost per event.
DuckDB and Elasticsearch come from the earlier CV and were not reconfirmed in the 18-20 Oct session; confirm before naming them.

followUps.question: How do you cite a value from a workbook?
followUps.answer: Sheet name plus cell address, quoted with the fragment. A reviewer can open the file and see it in seconds.
followUps.remember: Sheet and cell, always.

followUps.question: What if a merged cell hides the header?
followUps.answer: I resolve merged ranges to their top-left cell before extraction. Where a human could read it two ways, the model returns both and a person decides.
followUps.remember: Resolve the merge, or return both readings.

questions.question: How do you handle documents with tables, spreadsheets or complex formatting?
questions.simple: Flattening a table to plain text loses the link between a header and its value. I keep the structure, address each value by its sheet and cell, and make the model cite that address. Each file type gets its own handling.

answer.label: Do not flatten
answer.text: Plain-text extraction destroys layout. A number loses its column and a total loses its row. I keep the grid.

answer.label: Address every value
answer.text: At MITCON the extractor must quote the exact fragment as citation. For a workbook that is the sheet and the cell.

answer.label: Match the file to the route
answer.text: We moved from Anthropic to OpenAI because Anthropic's document block accepted only PDF among binary files. Workbooks returned a 400 before the model saw them. I read that as a format problem, not a model problem. The route has since moved on: Gemini replaced gpt-4o-mini for extraction after a spike on 110 uploads.

answer.label: Ambiguity
answer.text: When a table supports two readings, the model proposes both. It does not pick one for the user.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: MITCON. The inputs arrive from several stakeholders as workbooks, PDFs, emails, WhatsApp chats, scanned documents, photos and AutoCAD files. Stage 1 readers are plain code: pdfplumber, pypdfium2, python-docx, openpyxl, xlrd, a LibreOffice sidecar, a mail reader, ezdxf and LibreDWG for CAD, and a WhatsApp chat-log reader. Images and scans go to Gemini whole.

questions.remember: Keep the grid, cite the cell, fix the format before blaming the model.
questions.steer: Tell the Anthropic-to-OpenAI story. It shows I diagnosed a real failure and recorded it.
questions.trap: Do not claim the OpenAI move was about model quality. The recorded reason is the document block accepting only PDF among binary files. The later move to Gemini came from measured results.

Confirm which role python-docx, openpyxl and pypdfium2 each play. The portfolio lists the stack and gives no roles.

followUps.question: What is HNSW?
followUps.answer: A graph index. Each vector links to near neighbours across layers, so a search hops from coarse to fine. It trades some recall and memory for speed.
followUps.remember: Layered neighbour graph, fast and approximate.

followUps.question: How do you handle document updates?
followUps.answer: I version documents, re-embed only what changed and retire the old chunks by id. Stale versions are a quiet source of wrong answers.
followUps.remember: Re-embed only what changed.

questions.question: How do you scale a RAG system from 1K to 100K documents?
questions.simple: At that size, brute-force search over every vector can get slow. Where it breaks depends on the hardware, the vector dimension and how many chunks each document yields. You need approximate nearest-neighbour indexes, metadata filters, a re-ranker and incremental ingestion. Quality needs measuring too, because more documents means more near-duplicates.

answer.label: Index
answer.text: Use an approximate index such as HNSW. Exact search over every chunk vector gets slow and costly as the chunk count grows.

answer.label: Narrow early
answer.text: Filter by tenant, type or date before the vector search. Smaller candidate sets give faster and better results.

answer.label: Two stages
answer.text: Cheap retrieval for recall, then a re-ranker for precision on the top 50 or so.

answer.label: Ingestion
answer.text: Make it incremental and idempotent. Re-embedding the whole corpus on every change does not survive 100K files.

answer.label: Measure
answer.text: Track retrieval quality on a fixed question set as the corpus grows. Near-duplicates and stale versions are the usual damage.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: The largest corpus on record is 800+ AUSTRAC documents at AML SoftServe, in pgvector on Supabase. That is well below 100K, so I have not scaled a retrieval system to that size. I can speak to the design at 800+: parsing, chunking for regulatory text, and an LLM reranker on the shortlist.

questions.remember: ANN index, filters first, two-stage ranking, incremental ingest, keep measuring.
questions.steer: Move to grounding and cost per event. Retrieval at AML SoftServe ran on every onboarding and transaction, so the cost of each call mattered.
questions.trap: Do not state a corpus size beyond 800+ documents. Do not quote a chunk count. None is on record.

noEvidence.note: The only corpus on record is 800+ documents at AML SoftServe. There is no project at 100K scale.

followUps.question: How is the graph built from text?
followUps.answer: An LLM or extractor pulls entities and relations from each chunk. Then you merge duplicates. That merge step is where quality is usually lost.
followUps.remember: Extract, then resolve duplicates carefully.

followUps.question: Would you use one at AML SoftServe?
followUps.answer: For ownership chains, possibly. I would prove the multi-hop need first. I never built it there.
followUps.remember: Prove the need first.

questions.question: What is GraphRAG, and when does a knowledge graph beat plain vector retrieval?
questions.simple: GraphRAG builds a graph of entities and relations from the documents and retrieves along those links. It helps when the answer depends on connections across several documents. Plain vector search finds similar passages but misses multi-hop relationships.

answer.label: What it adds
answer.text: Entities become nodes and relations become edges. A query can follow edges, so it gathers evidence that no single passage contains.

answer.label: Where it wins
answer.text: Multi-hop questions. Who owns the company that owns this account? Which obligations apply to every entity under this parent?

answer.label: Where it loses
answer.text: Building and maintaining the graph is costly. Extraction errors become wrong edges. For most lookups, plain retrieval is enough.

answer.label: How I would decide
answer.text: I would first check whether failures are multi-hop. If they are not, a graph is overhead.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: No evidence yet. I have not built a knowledge graph or a GraphRAG system. The nearest idea in my domain is beneficial ownership in AML, which is naturally a graph, but that is my reasoning, not shipped work.

questions.remember: Graphs help multi-hop questions. Otherwise plain retrieval.
questions.steer: Use the AML ownership example only as an example of where a graph fits.
questions.trap: Do not say you built a knowledge graph. The profile shows none.

noEvidence.note: No knowledge-graph evidence in the profile. The knowledge graph tab was dropped for that reason.

Read one GraphRAG overview and keep a two-sentence summary.

followUps.question: How do you change a prompt safely?
followUps.answer: By running old and new prompts over the same saved inputs and scoring both. At MITCON that means the golden answer keys and scorers. At AML SoftServe DeepEval scored each change. Experts also review at every checkpoint, which backs up any prompt change.
followUps.remember: Compare before and after on saved inputs.

followUps.question: System prompt or user prompt?
followUps.answer: Standing rules go in the system prompt. Per-request data goes in the user turn. I keep untrusted document text clearly separate from the instructions.
followUps.remember: Rules in system, data in user.

questions.question: What is prompt engineering and why does it matter?
questions.simple: Prompt engineering is writing the instructions, context and examples that make a model behave the same way every time. It matters because the prompt is part of the system. A vague prompt gives a vague product.

answer.label: What it is
answer.text: I treat a prompt as a specification. It states the task, the allowed inputs, the output format and what to do when the input is unclear.

answer.label: Why it matters
answer.text: The model is a component with no memory of my intent. The prompt is the only place my rules live.

answer.label: Keep it in code
answer.text: I keep prompts in versioned files, not in someone's head. At MITCON the extraction rules live in model-tasks/extract.toml, next to the code.

answer.label: Prefer rules over tone
answer.text: Clear constraints beat clever wording. "Quote the exact fragment" works better than "be careful".

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: MITCON, where the grounding contract is a prompt that sets what the model may propose, how it cites, and what it omits. At Fresh Tracks the agents wrote every customer and sales mail in the company's encoded brand voice, checked by Guardrails AI.

questions.remember: A prompt is a spec, versioned like code.
questions.steer: Go straight to the grounding contract and the line about gaps on screen.
questions.trap: Do not make it sound like wording tricks. My point is that rules and evidence beat clever phrasing.
checks: Be ready to say what the MITCON golden answer keys cover. Scoring prompt changes against them is on record, but the notes do not say how big each set was for every prompt.

followUps.question: Why return both readings?
followUps.answer: Choosing silently hides the ambiguity from the expert who has to sign. Showing both puts the decision with the person who owns it.
followUps.remember: Never decide silently for the signer.

followUps.question: How do you handle a missing value?
followUps.answer: The model omits it. The interface shows a gap. A person fills it from the source or leaves it open.
followUps.remember: Omit, show the gap, a person fills it.

questions.question: How do you design prompts for structured data extraction?
questions.simple: For extraction I define the exact fields, say where each value must come from, and say what to do when the source is silent or unclear. I make the model cite its evidence so a person can check it.

answer.label: Define the schema
answer.text: List each field with its type and meaning. Name the units and formats.

answer.label: Ground every value
answer.text: The model proposes a value only when the document states it. It quotes the exact fragment as the citation.

answer.label: Handle ambiguity out loud
answer.text: When the source supports two readings, the model returns both. It does not choose.

answer.label: Allow silence
answer.text: If a field cannot be grounded, the model omits it. An empty field is a safe answer.

answer.label: Review the gaps
answer.text: Omitted fields show on screen for a person to fill. A gap is recoverable.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: MITCON. The extraction contract returns proposals with a path, value, unit, citation and source file name. Temperature is 0 with a fixed seed. A lightweight decision model first drops the catalogue fields that cannot apply, so the extractor sees less. Expert checkpoints sit after it.

questions.remember: Schema, cite, both readings, omit the ungrounded.
questions.steer: Quote the line: a gap on screen is recoverable and an invented number in a signed document is not.
questions.trap: Do not say the model never errs. The contract reduces invented values and makes errors visible. People still review.

followUps.question: What if the JSON is valid but wrong?
followUps.answer: That is the harder failure. Citations help, because I can check the quoted fragment against the source in code. At MITCON an invented citation fails the gate, because the quote must be found in the evidence text.
followUps.remember: Valid is not true. Check against the source.

followUps.question: Why cap the retries?
followUps.answer: Unbounded retries burn tokens and hide a real bug in the prompt or the input.
followUps.remember: A cap turns a loop into a signal.

questions.question: How do you get reliable structured output out of an LLM?
questions.simple: Reliability comes from layers. A clear contract in the prompt, an output format the provider can enforce, validation in code, and a defined fallback when validation fails. No single layer is enough.

answer.label: Constrain the format
answer.text: Use the provider's structured-output or JSON-schema mode where it exists. It cuts malformed output a lot.

answer.label: Validate in code
answer.text: Parse against a schema. Check types, ranges and required fields. Treat the model's output as untrusted input.

answer.label: Retry with the error
answer.text: If validation fails, retry once with the validation error in the prompt. Cap the retries.

answer.label: Define the fallback
answer.text: After the cap, surface a gap to a person. Do not guess.

answer.label: Make failure safe
answer.text: Design the contract so that omission is allowed. Then the easiest wrong answer is a blank, not an invented number.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: MITCON. The model returns structured proposals with a path, value, unit and citation. Hand-written gates in code reject an unknown path, a blank value, an uncited value, an invented citation and a unit mismatch. Omission is the safe default. I have no retry loop on record, so I won't claim one.

questions.remember: Constrain, validate, retry with the error, then fall back to a person.
questions.steer: Return to the contract. Making omission safe is the design choice I am proudest of.
questions.trap: Do not claim a retry loop at MITCON. Structured output and the code gates are on record. Retries are not.
checks: Confirm whether MITCON retries after a gate rejects a value. The notes show the gates and the structured output, not a retry.

followUps.question: How do you check a citation?
followUps.answer: In code I check the quoted text appears in the source at the stated address. A mismatch fails the value.
followUps.remember: Verify the quote exists at the address.

followUps.question: Can the model still be wrong with a correct citation?
followUps.answer: Yes. It can quote the right cell and misread it. That is why the expert checkpoint stays.
followUps.remember: Citations catch invention, not misreading.

questions.question: How do you reduce hallucinations in LLM outputs?
questions.simple: I cannot remove hallucination, so I design for it. I ground the model on supplied text, require a citation for every claim, let it say nothing, and put a person at the points where a wrong answer costs most.

answer.label: Ground it
answer.text: Give the model the source and forbid facts from outside it.

answer.label: Force citations
answer.text: Every value carries the exact quote. If I cannot find the quote in the source, I reject the value.

answer.label: Allow omission
answer.text: Blank beats invented. I say so in the contract.

answer.label: Show ambiguity
answer.text: Return both readings when the source is unclear.

answer.label: Put people at the gates
answer.text: Experts review at every checkpoint before anything reaches a signed document.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: MITCON, where code gates accept a value only when its verbatim citation is found in the source. AML SoftServe, where every finding cited its source clause and Guardrails AI blocked ungrounded output. Fresh Tracks, where deterministic code computes every amount, so the model never invents money. Statutory reports carry legal liability, so an invented number is the worst outcome.

questions.remember: Ground, cite, allow blank, show ambiguity, review at the gate.
questions.steer: Use the signed-document line to show I think about consequences first.
questions.trap: Do not call 11% a hallucination rate. It is the wrong-value rate of the rebuilt MITCON pipeline on the golden set, against 27% for the old pipeline. I have no hallucination rate for AML SoftServe.
checks: Be ready for the question of what Guardrails AI actually checked at AML SoftServe. The notes say grounding. They give no rule list.

followUps.question: Is a bigger context window the answer?
followUps.answer: It helps but does not fix cost, latency or accuracy on long inputs. I still prefer sending less.
followUps.remember: Bigger window, same discipline.

followUps.question: How do you merge partial results?
followUps.answer: Prefer a deterministic merge in code over another model call. Conflicts go to a person.
followUps.remember: Merge in code, escalate conflicts.

questions.question: How do you handle token limits when context is too large?
questions.simple: When the input will not fit, I shrink it or split it. I retrieve only what matters, summarise carefully, or process the document in parts and merge the results. Each option loses something, so I pick by what I can afford to lose.

answer.label: Cut first
answer.text: Remove boilerplate and repeated headers before anything else.

answer.label: Retrieve, do not stuff
answer.text: Fetch the relevant passages rather than the whole document.

answer.label: Map and reduce
answer.text: Process sections separately, then merge the structured results. Merge in code where I can, not by asking the model.

answer.label: Summarise with care
answer.text: A summary can drop the exact number I need. I avoid it for anything that must be cited.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: MITCON narrows before it extracts. A lightweight decision model scores each catalogue field against each document and drops the weak ones, so the extractor sees less. On 78 uploads recall rose from about 61% to 68%, and the extra call added no net cost per file. That is a focus gain, not a hard token-limit fix. I have no long-document splitting approach on record.

questions.remember: Cut, retrieve, map and reduce. Avoid lossy summaries for cited facts.
questions.steer: Talk about citations. Anything cited from a long document needs its exact source kept.
questions.trap: Do not describe how MITCON splits long files. It is not recorded. The narrowing figures are the only token-budget evidence.

noEvidence.note: Narrowing is on record at MITCON. How long documents are split or budgeted for tokens is not.

Note whether any run hit a token limit and what you changed.

followUps.question: Does fine-tuning add knowledge?
followUps.answer: Not reliably. It teaches patterns and style. For facts, retrieval is the better route.
followUps.remember: Fine-tune for style, retrieve for facts.

followUps.question: What would make you fine-tune a small model?
followUps.answer: A high-volume narrow task where a cheaper model could match a larger one, plus enough labelled examples to prove it.
followUps.remember: Volume plus data plus a measurable gain.

questions.question: When would you fine-tune vs use RAG vs just prompt engineering?
questions.simple: I start with prompting because it is cheapest and fastest to change. I add retrieval when the model needs knowledge it does not have. I fine-tune only when I need a consistent style or behaviour that prompting cannot hold, and I have data to train on.

answer.label: Prompting first
answer.text: Clear instructions and a few examples solve most problems. I can change them in minutes.

answer.label: RAG for knowledge
answer.text: If the answer lives in documents that change, retrieval keeps it current and citable.

answer.label: Fine-tuning for behaviour
answer.text: Fine-tune for a stable format, tone or narrow skill at scale, once there is clean labelled data and a way to measure the gain.

answer.label: Order of cost
answer.text: Prompting is cheapest, retrieval next, fine-tuning most. I climb only when the cheaper step fails on measured cases.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: My shipped work sits on prompting, grounding and model routing. At MITCON the rebuilt pipeline, with its grounding contract, cut wrong values from 27% to 11% against the old pipeline on gpt-4o-mini. Voting over three gpt-4o-mini reads cost the same as one Gemini read and scored worse. I know of no fine-tuning there, and I have not fine-tuned a model.

questions.remember: Prompt, then retrieve, then fine-tune. Climb only when the cheaper step fails.
questions.steer: Make the point that grounding and routing solved the MITCON problem without training anything, and that I measured it.
questions.trap: Do not claim fine-tuning experience. The profile shows none.
checks: "No fine-tuning at MITCON" is my inference from the absence of any evidence (ours). Confirm before you say it.

followUps.question: Would you revisit the choice?
followUps.answer: Yes. Provider limits change. The note records the reason, so I can retest when it does.
followUps.remember: Record the reason so you can revisit it.

followUps.question: How do you compare two models fairly?
followUps.answer: Same inputs, same prompt, same scoring, run more than once. Single runs mislead. At MITCON repeatability was one of the scores: 52.8% for gpt-4o-mini against 70.6% for Gemini on the model alone.
followUps.remember: Same inputs, repeated runs.

questions.question: How do you choose between different LLM models for a task?
questions.simple: I choose by testing on the real task, not by leaderboard. I check accuracy on my own inputs, input format support, cost, latency and any data restrictions. A cheaper model is fine if it passes.

answer.label: Start with the task
answer.text: Define what a correct answer is. Then try candidate models on real inputs.

answer.label: Check the plumbing
answer.text: Format support matters as much as quality. At MITCON, Anthropic's document block accepted only PDF among binary files, so workbooks failed with a 400 before reaching the model.

answer.label: Weigh cost and latency
answer.text: At MITCON I compared the two models on the same first stage. Gemini had the lower wrong-value rate, 11.1% against 24.0%, and the higher recall, 57.3% against 36.1%. Voting over three gpt-4o-mini reads cost the same as one Gemini read and scored worse.

answer.label: Keep the switch cheap
answer.text: OpenRouter is the only model gateway at MITCON, and model names live in per-task config files, never in Python. Changing model is a config change.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: MITCON, where I dropped Anthropic over the document-block limit, moved extraction from gpt-4o-mini to Gemini after a spike, and put a lightweight decision model ahead of it. AML SoftServe used OpenRouter for LLM access and o4-mini for reranking. Fresh Tracks ran its models on AWS Bedrock. ai-gym routes Claude through OpenRouter under cost budgets.

questions.remember: Test on the real task, check format support, then cost.
questions.steer: Tell the 110-upload comparison. It is a concrete, measured decision, and the format-failure story sits next to it.
questions.trap: Do not say one vendor is better than another. The Anthropic drop was a document-format limit. The Gemini move came from measured results on one task.
checks: The 110-upload figures come from spike scorers. Be ready to say what the golden answer keys held and who confirmed the answers.

followUps.question: When is an agent the wrong choice?
followUps.answer: When the steps are known and fixed. A plain workflow is cheaper, faster and easier to test. At MITCON ADR-001 chose a deterministic pipeline with model calls at named steps, so I call it an agentic workflow. At Fresh Tracks the money maths stays in code and the agents decide only the next action.
followUps.remember: Known path means a workflow, not an agent.

followUps.question: How much autonomy do you give it?
followUps.answer: As little as the task needs. Read-only tools by default, and a person approves anything that writes or spends.
followUps.remember: Least autonomy that works.

questions.question: What is an AI agent? What makes it different from a simple LLM call?
questions.simple: A simple LLM call takes input and returns text. An agent runs a loop. It decides what to do next, calls tools, reads the results and carries state until the goal is met or it hands back to a person.

answer.label: The loop
answer.text: An agent observes, decides, acts and repeats. A single call does one step and stops.

answer.label: Tools
answer.text: An agent can act: query a database, call an API, write a file. The model chooses which tool and with what arguments.

answer.label: State
answer.text: It carries state between steps, so it knows what it has already done.

answer.label: Limits
answer.text: More autonomy means more risk. I add step caps, tool permissions and human approval at the steps that matter.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: Fresh Tracks. I built a multi-agent payment system on LangGraph and AWS Bedrock. Deterministic code computes every amount. A payment-request agent sends the link on the due date. An overdue agent queues reminders. A nightly run compares what was received with what was expected and starts a refund with no manual step. techcirkle-agents is my LangGraph prototype, with human-in-the-loop interrupts and Postgres checkpointing.

answer.label: Split of work
answer.text: Deterministic code computes every amount. The LLM reads each itinerary's payment history, decides the next step and writes every mail in the brand voice. No LLM computes money. Agentic AI-assisted delivery with Claude Code skills is a separate, also true, story.

questions.remember: An agent is a loop with tools and state, plus limits.
questions.steer: Lead with Fresh Tracks. It is a shipped multi-agent system with a clean split between code and model. Use techcirkle-agents for the interrupt design.
questions.trap: Do not call MITCON agents. It is an agentic workflow. Do not give Fresh Tracks figures beyond the refund turnaround, two business days to one.
checks: Confirm how the Fresh Tracks agents were triggered and coordinated, by cron and events or by a supervisor, before you name a pattern.

followUps.question: How is it different from plan-and-execute?
followUps.answer: ReAct decides one step at a time. Plan-and-execute writes the plan first, then runs it. The plan is easier to review but less adaptive.
followUps.remember: One step at a time, or plan first.

followUps.question: How do you stop it looping?
followUps.answer: A step cap, a repeated-call check and a fallback to a person. I cover it in detail in the loop question.
followUps.remember: Cap, detect repeats, escalate.

questions.question: Explain the ReAct pattern
questions.simple: ReAct stands for reason and act. The model writes a short thought, picks a tool call, reads the result, then thinks again. It repeats until it can answer. The loop lets it use real information instead of guessing.

answer.label: The cycle
answer.text: Thought, action, observation, then back to thought. Each observation feeds the next thought.

answer.label: Why it helps
answer.text: The model can check facts and recover from a bad first step. It is more transparent than one big answer.

answer.label: Weaknesses
answer.text: It can loop, it can burn tokens, and a wrong observation sends it the wrong way. I cap the steps.

answer.label: Today
answer.text: Modern tool-calling APIs give the same loop with structured calls. I treat ReAct as the idea behind them.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: No evidence yet that I applied ReAct by name. The Fresh Tracks agents read state, decide the next action and act, which follows the same loop. I have not recorded a specific ReAct implementation.

questions.remember: Think, act, observe, repeat, and cap the steps.
questions.steer: Move to graph-based control, where I can show state and interrupts in techcirkle-agents.
questions.trap: Do not claim you implemented ReAct. Say you understand it and that tool-calling agents build on it.

noEvidence.note: The profile shows LangGraph agents at Fresh Tracks and in techcirkle-agents. It does not name a ReAct implementation.

Prepare an honest one-liner: "I use tool-calling loops, which come from ReAct."

followUps.question: What do you log to debug a loop?
followUps.answer: Every step with the tool, arguments and result, tied to a run id. A trace tool such as LangSmith makes it readable.
followUps.remember: Trace every step under one run id.

followUps.question: Where does the cap live?
followUps.answer: In the graph or the runner, not in the prompt. A prompt asks the model to behave. A cap forces it.
followUps.remember: Enforce in code, not in the prompt.

questions.question: How do you prevent agents from getting stuck in loops?
questions.simple: I cap the steps, watch for repeated calls and give the agent a way out. A hard limit stops runaway cost. A repeat check catches near-identical calls. A hand-off to a person covers what the agent cannot solve.

answer.label: What I ran
answer.text: A run that went past 5 minutes was force-closed and sent to the sales agent. That caught unusual calculations where the agent couldn't find a next step. A run that stopped after the calculated status was recalculated and checked before anything went out. Nightly reconciliation then picked up anything not closed and took it through another run.

answer.label: Hard limits
answer.text: Token and iteration limits are options I'd add: a maximum number of steps and a token or cost budget per run. I didn't run those.

answer.label: Detect repeats
answer.text: Compare each tool call with recent ones. Same tool with near-identical arguments is a loop signal.

answer.label: Give an exit
answer.text: Let the agent say it cannot finish. That should end the run with a clear status, not a retry.

answer.label: Escalate
answer.text: On a trip wire, stop and hand the state to a person with the history attached.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: The 5-minute force-close at Fresh Tracks is the loop guard I ran. Human-in-the-loop interrupts in techcirkle-agents pause the graph for a person.

questions.remember: Lead with what I ran: 5-minute force-close, recalculation, nightly reconciliation. Limits are options.
questions.steer: Point to the force-close and the hand-off to the sales agent as my route for escalation.
questions.trap: Don't say "X amount of time". Say 5 minutes. Don't say token or iteration limits are something I ran. Don't claim you debugged a production loop. None is recorded.

followUps.question: How do agents share state?
followUps.answer: Through one typed state object in the graph, checkpointed, not by passing free text around.
followUps.remember: One typed state, checkpointed.

followUps.question: Supervisor or peer-to-peer?
followUps.answer: Supervisor for control and audit. Peer-to-peer only when the agents truly negotiate, which I rarely need.
followUps.remember: Supervisor for control.

questions.question: How do you design a multi-agent system? What patterns exist?
questions.simple: I split work across agents only when the roles are truly different. Common patterns are a supervisor that routes to specialists, a pipeline where each agent hands off to the next, and a debate or review loop. I keep the number of agents small.

answer.label: Why split
answer.text: Separate prompts, tools and permissions per role. A reviewer should not hold the same tools as a writer.

answer.label: Supervisor
answer.text: One agent routes work to specialists and merges the results. Easy to control, but the supervisor is a bottleneck.

answer.label: Pipeline
answer.text: Fixed stages: plan, build, review, test. Predictable and easy to trace.

answer.label: Review loop
answer.text: One agent produces and another critiques. Cap the rounds.

answer.label: Cost of more agents
answer.text: Each hand-off adds latency, tokens and places for state to go wrong. I start with one agent and split when it hurts.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: Fresh Tracks, a multi-agent payment system on LangGraph and AWS Bedrock, with specialised agents for payment requests, overdue reconciliation, nightly reconciliation, mailers, invoices and per-country tax. techcirkle-agents is a smaller LangGraph prototype that exposes the software development lifecycle as callable agents. In that system it's a deterministic LangGraph graph: code routes between the steps, and the model only chooses the next step from a fixed set. The agents share one state, keyed by the instalment ID.

questions.remember: Split by role and permission. Supervisor, pipeline or review loop. Start small.
questions.steer: Lead with Fresh Tracks. Each agent had one job, and deterministic code did the money. Use techcirkle-agents only for the plan, build, review and test stages.
questions.trap: Say Fresh Tracks was a production multi-agent system. Say techcirkle-agents is a prototype. Do not call MITCON multi-agent.

That code routes between the steps and there's no free-running supervisor are from your account on the 3 November call. The portfolio holds the saved state and the fixed-step choice. Confirm the routing wording.

followUps.question: Where do you store checkpoints?
followUps.answer: In Postgres in techcirkle-agents. A database gives durability and lets me query run history.
followUps.remember: Postgres for durability and history.

followUps.question: What goes wrong with state?
followUps.answer: It grows without bound, or a schema change breaks old checkpoints. I keep state small and version it.
followUps.remember: Keep it small and versioned.

questions.question: What's the role of state management and checkpointing in agentic workflows?
questions.simple: State is everything the workflow knows at a point in time. Checkpointing saves that state after each step. If the run crashes, waits for a person or needs a replay, I resume from the last checkpoint instead of starting over.

answer.label: Explicit state
answer.text: I keep state in one typed object: inputs, intermediate results, decisions. It is not hidden in the prompt.

answer.label: Checkpoint each step
answer.text: The graph saves state after every node. A crash loses at most one step.

answer.label: Pause and resume
answer.text: A human-in-the-loop pause is a checkpoint with a wait. The run can sit for hours and then continue.

answer.label: Audit and replay
answer.text: Saved states let me see exactly how a decision was reached, and replay from an earlier point.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: techcirkle-agents uses LangGraph with Postgres checkpointing. It is a working prototype, deployed on Railway. At Fresh Tracks the instalment plan and payment history live in the Django payment service and the agents read them. Rebalancing leaves paid instalments untouched and re-spreads the rest. On the payment system, the whole LangGraph state was saved to the database after every action, keyed by the instalment ID. A plain run moved through about five statuses, and nightly reconciliation picked up anything not closed.

questions.remember: Typed state, save every step, pause and resume, replay for audit.
questions.steer: Connect it to audit. Saved state is what makes a decision explainable later.
questions.trap: Do not claim thread-scale or multi-tenant checkpoint stores. It is a prototype.

followUps.question: How do you avoid approval fatigue?
followUps.answer: Gate only the high-consequence steps. Batch the rest and show the evidence so a review takes seconds.
followUps.remember: Few gates, strong evidence.

followUps.question: What if the reviewer is unavailable?
followUps.answer: The run stays paused at its checkpoint. I add a timeout and a clear owner so it does not stall unnoticed.
followUps.remember: Paused, owned, with a timeout.

questions.question: How do you put a human in the loop inside an agent graph?
questions.simple: I put an interrupt node in the graph before the risky step. The graph saves its state and stops. A person reviews, approves or edits, and the graph resumes from the checkpoint with their decision.

answer.label: Choose the gates
answer.text: I place a gate wherever a wrong action is costly or cannot be undone. Spending money and writing to a signed document are examples.

answer.label: Interrupt
answer.text: The graph checkpoints, then waits. Nothing runs while it waits.

answer.label: Show the right thing
answer.text: The reviewer sees the proposed action, the evidence and what changes if they approve.

answer.label: Resume with the decision
answer.text: Approve, edit or reject goes back into state, and the graph continues down the right branch.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: techcirkle-agents has human-in-the-loop interrupts on LangGraph with Postgres checkpointing. At MITCON every AI change to a report waits as a proposal for a person to accept, reject or refine. At Fresh Tracks I took the person out on purpose. Code computes every amount and Guardrails AI checks each mail, so the flows run without manual review.

questions.remember: Gate the costly step, interrupt, show evidence, resume with the decision.
questions.steer: Move to how I decide which steps are safe to automate. Fresh Tracks automated fully because code owns the money. MITCON keeps a person at every change.
questions.trap: Do not suggest a person approving everything. Too many gates train people to click through.

followUps.question: How do you handle non-determinism?
followUps.answer: Run several times, score pass rate and look at variance. Lower temperature where I can. I never judge on one run.
followUps.remember: Judge on a rate, not a run.

followUps.question: How do you test the whole graph?
followUps.answer: End to end on scenarios, with the human-in-the-loop steps stubbed to fixed decisions.
followUps.remember: Stub the human, run the graph.

questions.question: How do you test and evaluate agent behaviour?
questions.simple: I test at three levels. Unit tests for the tools and the plain code. Scenario runs that replay saved inputs through the agent and score the outcome. Production traces that I read for new failure modes. Agents vary run to run, so I judge them over many runs.

answer.label: Test the tools
answer.text: Tools are plain code. I test them like any other function. At Fresh Tracks every amount comes from deterministic code, so the money logic is ordinary testable code and only the decisions need scoring.

answer.label: Replay scenarios
answer.text: Keep a set of realistic inputs with expected outcomes. Run the agent on them and score the result, not the exact wording.

answer.label: Check the path
answer.text: Look at the tool calls, not only the answer. A right answer reached by a wrong call is a bug waiting.

answer.label: Repeat runs
answer.text: Run each scenario several times. A pass rate tells me more than one pass.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: Fresh Tracks: DeepEval scored the agents, Guardrails AI checked every mail and LangSmith traced runs end to end. AML SoftServe: DeepEval scored retrieval and faithfulness on each change. MITCON: golden answer keys and scorers compared models and prompts.

questions.remember: Tools by unit test, behaviour by scenario replay, many runs, read the traces.
questions.steer: Talk about why deterministic money code makes the agents easier to test: the amounts are checkable, so scoring covers decisions and wording.
questions.trap: Do not give pass rates, dataset sizes or scoring methods for Fresh Tracks or AML SoftServe. None is on record. Do not call Braintrust an eval tool.

Braintrust at AML SoftServe was used outside evals. Reading it as tracing is ours, so confirm before you say it.

followUps.question: Why LangGraph over a plain loop?
followUps.answer: Checkpointing, interrupts and tracing come built in. For a short script, a plain loop is better. MITCON uses no agent framework: it is hand-written on Celery and Redis, because the path is known.
followUps.remember: Use a framework when you need its features.

followUps.question: Does the framework matter?
followUps.answer: Less than the design. Typed state, small tools and clear gates carry across frameworks.
followUps.remember: Design transfers, syntax does not.

questions.question: When would you use LangGraph vs CrewAI vs AutoGen vs Google ADK?
questions.simple: I have built with LangGraph, and I choose it when I want explicit control over state, branching and interrupts. CrewAI is quicker for role-based crews. AutoGen suits conversational multi-agent setups. Google ADK fits teams on Google Cloud. I know the last three by reading, not by shipping.

answer.label: LangGraph
answer.text: A state graph with checkpointing, interrupts and conditional edges. I pick it when the flow needs control and audit.

answer.label: CrewAI
answer.text: Role-based crews with less setup. It is a quick start, with less fine control over state and flow.

answer.label: AutoGen
answer.text: Built around agents that converse with each other. As I understand it, Microsoft has since moved the line towards its Agent Framework, so I would check the current status before choosing it.

answer.label: Google ADK
answer.text: Google's agent toolkit. It makes most sense with Gemini and Vertex AI.

answer.label: How I decide
answer.text: By how much control I need, which cloud the customer runs on, and what the team can maintain.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: LangGraph at Fresh Tracks, where the payment agents run on it, and in techcirkle-agents. MITCON uses no framework: the orchestration is hand-written on Celery and Redis. I won't name the agent framework at AML SoftServe. I have not shipped CrewAI, AutoGen or Google ADK.

questions.remember: LangGraph for control. The other three I know, I have not shipped.
questions.steer: Say plainly that I am a LangGraph builder and explain why control mattered.
questions.trap: Do not claim hands-on experience with CrewAI, AutoGen or Google ADK.
checks: Prepare your answer if asked which agent framework ran at AML SoftServe. The notes do not have it, and the design mattered more than the framework.
The remark on AutoGen and the Microsoft Agent Framework is general knowledge as of 2026. Check the current status before the interview.

followUps.question: What do you score?
followUps.answer: Correctness against the source, groundedness, format validity and, where it matters, refusal when the source is silent.

followUps.question: Who writes the criteria?

questions.question: What is LLM evaluation and why can't we just use unit tests?
questions.simple: LLM evaluation scores model behaviour on a set of realistic inputs. A unit test expects one exact output. An LLM gives different valid wording each time, and quality is a matter of degree, so I score outcomes over many cases instead.

answer.label: Why unit tests fall short
answer.text: The output is not exact. Two correct answers can share no words. The input space is also open-ended.

answer.label: What I do instead
answer.text: Build a set of realistic inputs. Score each result against criteria such as correct, grounded and complete.

answer.label: Use unit tests where they fit
answer.text: Parsers, validators, tool code and citation checks are deterministic. I test those normally.

answer.label: Track over time
answer.text: Run the same set on every change and compare. A drop is a regression.

answer.text: Fresh Tracks: DeepEval scored the agents and LangSmith traced every run. AML SoftServe: DeepEval scored retrieval and faithfulness on each change. MITCON: golden answer keys and scorers measured wrong-value rate and recall, and showed the rebuilt pipeline on Gemini beat the old one on gpt-4o-mini.

followUps.answer: Use a specific rubric, randomise order in pairwise tests and use a different model family to judge than the one being judged.

questions.question: What is LLM-as-judge and how does it work?

answer.label: How it works
answer.text: The judge gets the question, the answer, any reference and a clear rubric. It returns a score and a short reason.

answer.label: Why use it
answer.text: Humans cannot read thousands of outputs on every change. A judge gives a quick signal.

answer.label: Known biases
answer.text: Judges favour longer answers, favour their own style and can be inconsistent. Position matters in pairwise comparisons.

answer.label: Calibrate
answer.text: Label a sample by hand. Measure how often the judge agrees. Fix the rubric until it does.

questions.question: How do you build a golden dataset for evaluation?
questions.simple: A golden dataset is a set of real inputs with answers that experts have confirmed. I start small with real cases, include the hard and awkward ones, and grow it every time production shows a new failure.

answer.label: Cover the edges
answer.text: Include ambiguous, missing and adversarial cases, not only the clean ones.

questions.question: What are guardrails in AI applications and why do we need them?
questions.simple: Guardrails are checks and limits around a model that keep it inside safe behaviour. They cover what goes in, what comes out and what the system may do. I need them because a model cannot be trusted to police itself.

answer.label: Input checks
answer.text: Treat user and document text as untrusted. Strip or flag what should not reach the model.

answer.label: Output checks
answer.text: Validate format, check citations and block content that breaks policy.

answer.label: Action limits
answer.text: Tools get least-privilege permissions. Risky actions need a person.

answer.label: Enforce in code
answer.text: A guardrail in a prompt is a request. A guardrail in code is a rule.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: Fresh Tracks: Guardrails AI checked every customer and sales mail, and PreToolUse hooks block the coding agent from running pytest, because the containers point at dev RDS, and from mutating data under the staging profile. questions.question: What is prompt injection and how do you prevent it?
questions.simple: Prompt injection is text that tries to override the model's instructions. It can come from a user, or from a document the model reads, which is called indirect injection. You cannot filter it away completely, so you limit what a hijacked model can do.

answer.label: Two routes
answer.text: Direct: a user types the attack. Indirect: a document, web page or email carries it.

answer.label: Separate data from instructions
answer.text: Mark untrusted text clearly and tell the model to treat it as data.

answer.label: Limit the blast radius
answer.text: Give tools the least privilege. Do not let one model hold both untrusted input and dangerous tools.

answer.label: Confirm risky actions
answer.text: A person approves anything that writes, sends or spends.

answer.label: Check outputs
answer.text: Validate before acting. Do not trust the model's own say-so.

answer.label: Where I've used it

answer.label: Grounding

questions.question: How do you handle PII in LLM inputs and outputs?

answer.label: Reversible tokens

answer.label: Provider terms

answer.label: Logs and traces

questions.question: How do you make an AI system explainable and auditable for a regulator?

answer.label: Keep people accountable

questions.question: What is LLM memory, and what's the difference between short-term and long-term memory?
questions.simple: A model has no memory of its own. Short-term memory is what I put in the current context: the conversation and the working state. Long-term memory is anything I store outside and bring back on demand, such as notes, summaries or a knowledge base.

answer.label: Short-term
answer.text: The current context window plus the agent's state for this run. It disappears when the run ends unless I save it.

answer.label: Long-term
answer.text: Stored in a database, files or a vector index. I retrieve it when it is relevant.

answer.label: Checkpoints are not long-term memory
answer.text: A checkpoint saves a run so it can resume. Long-term memory carries knowledge across runs.

answer.label: Governance
answer.text: Anything stored needs a source, an owner and a way to correct it. Unsourced memory becomes confident nonsense.

followUps.question: What does attention do?
followUps.answer: It lets every token weigh every other token. Weights come from query and key similarity, and values are mixed by those weights.
followUps.remember: Weighted mixing by relevance.

followUps.question: Why does context length cost so much?
followUps.answer: Attention work grows with the square of the length, and the memory for cached keys and values grows with it too.
followUps.remember: Cost grows faster than length.

questions.question: How does a transformer model work at a high level?
questions.simple: A transformer turns text into tokens, then into vectors. Layers of attention let each token look at every other token and decide which ones matter. The final layer predicts the next token, and the model repeats that to write text.

answer.label: Tokens to vectors
answer.text: Text is split into tokens. Each token becomes a vector, with position information added.

answer.label: Attention
answer.text: For each token, the model scores how relevant every other token is, then mixes their information by those scores. This is how it links a pronoun to its noun far away.

answer.label: Many layers
answer.text: Attention plus a small network, stacked many times. Each layer refines the representation.

answer.label: Next-token prediction
answer.text: The output is a probability for each possible next token. Sampling picks one, and the loop repeats.

answer.label: Cost
answer.text: Attention compares every token with every other, so the cost grows fast with length. That is why long contexts are expensive.

questions.question: How does tokenization work?
questions.simple: A tokenizer splits text into pieces from a fixed vocabulary, often parts of words. Each piece has an id the model understands. Common words are one token and rare words split into several. Cost and limits are counted in tokens, not words.

answer.label: Subwords
answer.text: Most tokenizers use byte-pair encoding or similar. They merge frequent character sequences into tokens.

answer.label: Vocabulary
answer.text: The vocabulary is fixed when the model is built. Text outside it breaks into smaller pieces.

answer.label: Why it matters
answer.text: Pricing, context limits and latency are all counted in tokens. Numbers, code and non-English text often take more tokens per word.

answer.label: Surprises
answer.text: Models see tokens, not letters. That explains odd failures such as counting letters or exact digits.

followUps.question: Why cosine similarity?
followUps.answer: It compares direction, not length. Embedding length rarely carries meaning, so direction is what matters.

questions.question: What are embeddings and how do they work?
questions.simple: An embedding is a list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text. Texts with similar meaning get vectors that sit close together. That lets me search by meaning, using a distance measure such as cosine similarity.

answer.label: What they are
answer.text: A fixed-length vector from an embedding model. Typically hundreds to a few thousand numbers.

answer.label: How they work
answer.text: The model is trained so related texts land near each other in the vector space.

answer.label: How I use them
answer.text: Embed the chunks once, embed the query at search time, and find the nearest vectors with cosine similarity.

answer.label: Limits
answer.text: They blur exact terms such as codes and names, which is why I pair them with keyword search. Changing the embedding model means re-embedding everything.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: AML SoftServe. OpenAI embeddings of the AUSTRAC documents sat in pgvector on Supabase, and an o4-mini LLM reranker sorted the shortlist. I do not have the embedding model name or the dimensions written down. sandvick-agents lists pgvector too, but that is a design with no code.

questions.remember: Meaning as a vector. Near in space means near in meaning.

questions.question: What is a context window, and how does it differ from a prompt?

answer.label: The difference
answer.text: The prompt is what I send to the model. The context window is the model's total limit. It holds the system prompt, any documents I add, the conversation history and the output the model writes.

answer.label: What follows
answer.text: So the prompt is only one part of what fills the window. Quality tends to fall as the window fills.

answer.label: Then how I manage it
answer.text: Only after that do I talk about managing it. In my delivery work I keep context files short and verified, so the agent starts from facts and not from a full window.

questions.question: What is fine-tuning, and what is LoRA?
questions.simple: Fine-tuning trains a pre-trained model further on your own examples, so its behaviour shifts. LoRA does this by training small add-on matrices while the original weights stay frozen. It costs far less than updating every weight.

answer.label: What fine-tuning is
answer.text: Fine-tuning takes a pre-trained model and trains it further on examples from my task. The weights shift. The model picks up a style, a format or a narrow skill. It changes behaviour more reliably than it adds facts.

answer.label: Full versus parameter-efficient
answer.text: Full fine-tuning updates every weight. It needs a lot of GPU memory and a separate copy of the model per task. Parameter-efficient methods update a small fraction of the parameters instead.

answer.label: LoRA
answer.text: LoRA freezes the base weights. For chosen layers it learns two small low-rank matrices, and their product is added to the layer output. Only those matrices train. I can swap them per task. QLoRA does the same on a quantised base model, which cuts memory again.

answer.label: Risks
answer.text: Catastrophic forgetting, overfitting on a small set, and a training set that bakes in its own mistakes. I would compare against a held-out set before and after.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: No evidence yet. I have not fine-tuned a model in any engagement. I would say so plainly. At MITCON the reliability problem was solved with a prompt contract and validation, not training.

questions.remember: Fine-tuning changes behaviour. LoRA trains small adapters on a frozen base.
questions.steer: Move to what I can prove: the grounding contract made extraction reliable without any training.
questions.trap: Do not imply you have fine-tuned a model. Do not say fine-tuning is a good way to teach a model new facts.

followUps.question: What is catastrophic forgetting?
followUps.answer: Training on a narrow set can overwrite what the model knew before. It loses general ability. Mixing in general data, a low learning rate and adapter methods like LoRA all reduce it.
followUps.remember: Narrow training overwrites broad ability.

followUps.question: What does the rank in LoRA control?
followUps.answer: Rank sets the size of the two small matrices, so it sets how much the adapter can change. A low rank is cheap and often enough for style or format. A higher rank gives more capacity and costs more memory.
followUps.remember: Rank is adapter capacity.

questions.question: If you had to fine-tune a model, how would you approach it?
questions.simple: I would start by proving that prompting and retrieval cannot solve the problem. Then I would build a clean dataset, train a LoRA adapter and compare it with the prompted baseline on a held-out set.

answer.label: First, rule out the cheap options
answer.text: I would write down the failure first. Then I would try a better prompt, few-shot examples, structured output and retrieval. Fine-tuning is the last step, not the first.

answer.label: Build the dataset
answer.text: I would collect real inputs with correct outputs, reviewed by a domain expert. A few hundred clean examples beat thousands of noisy ones. I would split off a held-out set before training and never touch it.

answer.label: Train small
answer.text: I would start with a LoRA or QLoRA run on an open model of a size that fits the hardware. I would log the loss and run a held-out evaluation at each checkpoint.

answer.label: Compare with the baseline
answer.text: The tuned model has to beat the prompted baseline on the held-out set, at lower cost or latency. If it does not, I would drop it.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: No evidence yet for fine-tuning. This is how I would do it, not something I have done. My evaluation habits are first-hand: DeepEval scoring and LangSmith tracing on the Fresh Tracks payment agents, DeepEval on the AML SoftServe RAG, and golden-set evals at MITCON. Those carry over.

questions.trap: Do not describe a fine-tuning project. Do not promise the tuned model will beat a well-prompted frontier model.

followUps.question: How many examples do you need?
followUps.answer: It depends on the task. For a format or style change, a few hundred good examples can be enough. For a new skill it needs more. Quality and coverage of the edge cases matter more than count.
followUps.remember: Clean and covering beats large.

followUps.question: How would you know it worked?
followUps.answer: It beats the prompted baseline on a held-out set the training never saw, and it does not regress on a general set. I would also read failures by hand.
followUps.remember: Held-out set against baseline.

questions.question: How do you handle long-running LLM requests in a web API?
questions.simple: A web request should not wait for a slow model call. The API accepts the job, returns an id at once, and a worker does the call. The client polls, subscribes to a stream or gets a callback.

answer.label: Accept, queue, return
answer.text: The endpoint validates the input, stores a job row and puts a message on a queue. It returns 202 with a job id in milliseconds. A worker does the slow call.

answer.label: Tell the client how to follow
answer.text: For a simple client I expose a status endpoint to poll. For a live feel I stream progress over server-sent events. For system-to-system calls I send a webhook when the job completes.

answer.label: Make the job safe to retry
answer.text: Workers die and models time out. So each job has a state, a retry limit and an idempotent write. A retried job must not double-write.

answer.label: Bound the cost
answer.text: I set a timeout on the model call, a cap on retries and a per-job budget. A stuck job fails visibly instead of running for ever.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: MITCON runs on Django, DRF and Celery with Redis, and the work is document extraction and report drafting. techcirkle-agents streams agent output over SSE. I would confirm which MITCON steps run as Celery tasks before I say more.

questions.remember: 202 and a job id, a worker does the call, the client polls or streams.
questions.steer: Use MITCON: long document work sits behind a queue, and experts review at checkpoints.
questions.trap: Do not hold an HTTP connection open for a minute and call it a design. Do not claim every MITCON step is a Celery task until you have checked.

followUps.question: Polling or streaming, which do you pick?
followUps.answer: Polling is simplest and works through any proxy. I use streaming when the user watches progress, such as an agent working through steps. SSE is enough for one-way progress.
followUps.remember: Poll for simple, stream for live progress.

followUps.question: What happens if the worker crashes mid-job?
followUps.answer: The job stays in a non-terminal state. The broker redelivers or a sweeper requeues it. The write is idempotent, so the retry is safe.
followUps.remember: Redeliver and make writes idempotent.

questions.question: When would you use Celery vs FastAPI BackgroundTasks?
questions.simple: BackgroundTasks runs a small job in the same process after the response is sent. Celery runs jobs in separate workers with a broker, retries and scheduling. Use BackgroundTasks for light, loss-tolerant work and Celery for anything that must survive a restart.

answer.label: BackgroundTasks
answer.text: It runs after the response, inside the same process. There is no broker, no retry and no record. If the process restarts, the task is gone. It suits sending a log line or a cache warm.

answer.label: Celery
answer.text: Celery puts jobs on a broker such as Redis. Separate workers consume them. I get retries, rate limits, scheduling, routing and a place to scale workers independently of the API.

answer.label: How I decide
answer.text: If losing the task would hurt, or it takes more than a few seconds, or I need retries or visibility, I use Celery. If it is quick and loss is harmless, BackgroundTasks is fine.

answer.label: The cost of Celery
answer.text: It adds a broker, workers and deployment. For a small service that is real overhead, so I do not reach for it by default.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: I used Celery with Redis in the Django stack at MITCON, and at Ernst & Young and Spotmentor. MITCON began as a FastAPI monolith before I re-cut it to Django. I have not recorded a specific BackgroundTasks use.

questions.remember: BackgroundTasks for loss-tolerant and quick. Celery when it must survive and be seen.
questions.steer: Mention that the same stack ran at EY and at MITCON, which shows the choice was repeated, not one-off.
questions.trap: Do not claim production BackgroundTasks experience. Do not say Celery is always better.

followUps.question: Why not just use threads?
followUps.answer: Threads share the API process and its memory, and they die with it. Workers isolate the load, scale separately and can be restarted without dropping web traffic.
followUps.remember: Isolation and independent scaling.

followUps.question: What would you use instead of Celery today?
followUps.answer: For a small async service I might use a lighter queue like RQ or a managed queue like SQS with a consumer. For workflows with many steps, a workflow engine. I would pick by the failure behaviour I need.
followUps.remember: Pick by failure behaviour.

questions.question: How do you design an API for an AI-powered service?
questions.simple: An AI endpoint is an ordinary API with three extra concerns: slow calls, uncertain output and cost. I treat the schema as the contract, make results typed and traceable, and treat the model as a dependency that can fail.

answer.label: Typed contract
answer.text: The API is described by an OpenAPI schema. Consumers generate a typed client from it. A change to the contract then breaks the build, not production.

answer.label: Slow work is a job
answer.text: Anything that calls a model is asynchronous. The API returns a job id and a status resource. Progress can stream.

answer.label: Typed, traceable results
answer.text: Every AI result carries its source, its confidence or status, and an id I can trace back to the prompt and model version. Failures return a clear error shape, not a half answer.

answer.label: Guard the edges
answer.text: Inputs are validated and size-capped. Outputs are validated before they are stored. Each tenant gets a rate limit and a budget.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: The MITCON and fde-os stack is Django and DRF with an openapi.json and a React front end that uses a generated API client. I would say whether the schema was written first or generated from the code only after I have checked.

questions.remember: Typed contract, slow work as jobs, typed traceable results, guarded edges.
questions.steer: Say the generated client: it removes a class of drift between front end and back end.
questions.trap: Do not describe the AI layer as the API. The API is the contract around it.

followUps.question: How do you version an AI endpoint?
followUps.answer: I version the contract as usual. I also record the prompt and model version in each result, because behaviour can change without the schema changing.
followUps.remember: Version the contract and the model.

followUps.question: How do you return a partial or uncertain answer?
followUps.answer: I return a status field and the evidence. A missing field is explicit and a conflicting one carries both readings. I never fill a gap with a guess.
followUps.remember: Gap on screen beats a guess.
