questions.question: How do you stream agent output to a client?
questions.simple: Agents work in steps, so the useful stream is events, not just tokens. I send each step, tool call and result as a server-sent event. The client renders progress and can pause at an interrupt.

answer.label: Choose the transport
answer.text: Server-sent events fit one-way progress. They run over plain HTTP, reconnect on their own and pass through most proxies. I would use WebSockets only if the client must send messages mid-stream.

answer.label: Stream events, not text
answer.text: I emit typed events: step started, tool called, tool result, token chunk, interrupt, done, error. The client decides how to show each.

answer.label: Handle interrupts
answer.text: When the graph reaches a human-in-the-loop interrupt, the stream sends an interrupt event with the pending question. The run is checkpointed. A later request resumes it.

answer.label: Handle failure
answer.text: Events carry ids, so a reconnecting client can resume. Errors arrive as events, and the stream always ends with a terminal event.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: techcirkle-agents is a LangGraph service that exposes agents over SSE, with human-in-the-loop interrupts and Postgres checkpointing. It is a working prototype, deployed on Railway.

questions.remember: SSE, typed events, checkpointed interrupts, always a terminal event.
questions.steer: Point at techcirkle-agents as the concrete build, and say it is a prototype.
questions.trap: Do not call it a production product. Do not stream raw model tokens only and call that agent streaming.

followUps.question: What if the client disconnects mid-run?
followUps.answer: The run is checkpointed in Postgres, so it keeps its state. The client reconnects with the last event id and resumes the stream or fetches the current state.
followUps.remember: State lives in the checkpoint, not the connection.

followUps.question: SSE versus WebSockets?
followUps.answer: SSE is simpler and enough for server-to-client progress. WebSockets add two-way traffic and more operational cost. I pick SSE unless I need the second direction.
followUps.remember: SSE until you need two-way.

questions.question: How do you handle rate limits and cost budgets with LLM providers?
questions.simple: Rate limits are handled with retries, backoff and queues. Cost is handled by budgets that are checked before each call, per tenant, with cheaper models used wherever they are good enough.

answer.label: Rate limits
answer.text: On a 429 I retry with exponential backoff and jitter, honour any retry-after header, and cap the attempts. Bulk work goes through a queue with limited concurrency so I do not create the burst myself.

answer.label: Budgets
answer.text: Each tenant or cohort has a spend budget. The call checks the remaining budget before it runs and records the actual cost after. When the budget is gone, the call is refused with a clear message.

answer.label: Model choice as a cost lever
answer.text: I use the cheapest model that passes the evaluation for the task, and a stronger one only where it matters. Prompt size matters as much as model price.

answer.label: Visibility
answer.text: I log tokens and cost per call, tagged by tenant and feature. A cost jump should show up on a dashboard before it shows up on an invoice.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: ai-gym runs Claude through OpenRouter under per-cohort cost budgets, and I built that. At MITCON, OpenRouter is the only model gateway and a lightweight decision model narrows each document before Gemini Flash-Lite extracts. The extra call added no net cost per file. I chose Gemini for accuracy: on the same first stage its wrong values were 11.1% against 24.0% for gpt-4o-mini. I have not recorded a retry-and-backoff story, so I would describe that part as my standard practice.

questions.remember: Backoff for limits, budgets for cost, cheapest model that passes.
questions.steer: Lead with ai-gym budgets. They are the concrete cost-control build.
questions.trap: Do not say ai-gym is in production. Its production status is not stated anywhere. Do not invent a rate-limit incident.

followUps.question: Where do you enforce the budget, client or server?
followUps.answer: Always on the server, before the provider call. A client-side check can be skipped. The server holds the counter and refuses the call.
followUps.remember: Enforce server-side, before the call.

followUps.question: How do you avoid a retry storm?
followUps.answer: Backoff with jitter, a retry cap, and a circuit breaker that stops calls for a short time after repeated failures. Queue concurrency stops my own burst.
followUps.remember: Jitter, caps and a breaker.

questions.question: When would you use JSONB vs normalised tables?
questions.simple: Use normalised tables for data with a stable shape that you query, join and constrain. Use JSONB for payloads whose shape varies or that you mostly store and read whole. Often the answer is both: columns for what you filter on, JSONB for the rest.

answer.label: Normalised tables
answer.text: They give me constraints, foreign keys, clear types and fast joins. I use them for the core entities that the business reasons about and that I filter or aggregate on.

answer.label: JSONB
answer.text: It suits payloads that vary by source, third-party responses I want to keep as received, and settings that change shape. Postgres can index it with GIN and query inside it.

answer.label: The trade-off
answer.text: JSONB moves validation from the database into the application. Queries inside it are harder to plan, and updates rewrite the whole value. Reporting gets messy.

answer.label: The hybrid
answer.text: I promote any field I filter on often into a real column and keep the raw payload in JSONB. That also preserves the original for audit.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: No evidence yet for JSONB specifically. I have used Postgres in every engagement since 2025, and the AML SoftServe questionnaire snapshot is a frozen record. I do not know whether it is stored as JSONB, so I would not claim it.

questions.remember: Columns for what you query, JSONB for what varies.
questions.steer: Tie it to the snapshot idea: freeze the shape you scored, keep it immutable.
questions.trap: Do not say JSONB replaces schema design. Do not claim a JSONB design you cannot recall.

followUps.question: How do you index JSONB?
followUps.answer: A GIN index for containment and key-existence queries, or an expression index on one extracted key. I index only what I query.
followUps.remember: GIN, or an expression index.

followUps.question: Why keep the raw supplier payload?
followUps.answer: It lets me replay parsing after a bug and it is evidence of what the supplier actually sent. I would keep it next to the parsed columns.
followUps.remember: Keep the raw, query the parsed.

questions.question: How do vector databases work? What indexing strategies exist?
questions.simple: A vector database stores embeddings and finds the nearest ones to a query vector. Exact search compares against everything. Approximate indexes such as HNSW and IVF trade a little recall for much more speed.

answer.label: What it stores
answer.text: It stores a vector per chunk, plus metadata. A query is embedded the same way and the store returns the nearest vectors by cosine similarity or dot product.

answer.label: Exact versus approximate
answer.text: A flat scan is exact and slow at scale. Approximate nearest neighbour indexes give most of the accuracy at a fraction of the cost.

answer.label: HNSW and IVF
answer.text: HNSW builds a layered graph and walks it towards the query. It is fast and accurate and uses more memory. IVF clusters the vectors and searches only the nearest clusters. It is lighter and needs tuning of the cluster count.

answer.label: Practical choices
answer.text: I filter by metadata, such as tenant, before or during the search. I choose pgvector when I already run Postgres and the corpus is modest, and a dedicated store when scale or latency demands it.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: I built this at AML SoftServe. Chunks sat in pgvector on Supabase with OpenAI embeddings, behind an agent that retrieved, reranked with an in-house o4-mini reranker and checked grounding. I did not run an ANN tuning study, so I would not quote index parameters. I also designed pgvector for the sandvick-agents SharePoint RAG assistant, which is a design with no code.

questions.remember: Embed, index approximately, filter by metadata. pgvector first, dedicated store at scale.
questions.steer: Say the AML SoftServe build first: pgvector inside the Postgres already running the tenant boundary, then an LLM reranker on top. Mention sandvick-agents only as a second design.
questions.trap: Do not quote HNSW or IVF settings from AML SoftServe. They are not recorded. Do not call sandvick-agents built, it has no code.

followUps.question: Why pgvector rather than a dedicated store?
followUps.answer: For a modest corpus it keeps one system to run and lets me join vectors with relational data and tenant filters. I would move to a dedicated store when scale or latency forced it.
followUps.remember: One system until scale forces two.

followUps.question: What does recall mean for an ANN index?
followUps.answer: It is the share of the true nearest neighbours the index actually returns. Index parameters trade recall against speed and memory, so I measure it on my own data.
followUps.remember: Recall is what approximate search gives up.

questions.question: How do you optimise SQL queries in a data-heavy application?
questions.simple: I measure first. I read the query plan, fix the worst query, and only then change indexes, queries or caching. Most wins come from removing repeated queries and adding the right index.

answer.label: Measure
answer.text: I find the slow queries from real traffic or logs. I run EXPLAIN ANALYZE and read the plan for sequential scans, bad row estimates and sorts that spill.

answer.label: Fix the shape
answer.text: I remove N+1 patterns with joins or prefetching, select only the columns I need, and paginate. These changes often beat any index.

answer.label: Index with care
answer.text: I add the index that matches the filter and sort, and check the planner uses it. Every index slows writes, so I do not add them blindly.

answer.label: Cache last
answer.text: If a result is expensive and slow to change, I cache it with a clear invalidation rule. Caching hides problems, so I do it after the query is sound.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: At Ernst & Young I improved API performance by 50% through query tuning and caching. That is the CV figure. I can walk through the approach but I would check the specifics before I give examples.

questions.remember: Measure, fix the shape, index with care, cache last.
questions.steer: Lead with the 50% API improvement, then the method behind it.
questions.trap: Do not invent the queries behind the 50%. Do not say you add indexes first.

followUps.question: How do you spot an N+1 problem?
followUps.answer: The query count per request grows with the number of rows returned. A query log or an ORM debug tool shows it. The fix is a join or a prefetch.
followUps.remember: Query count scales with rows.

followUps.question: When does an index not help?
followUps.answer: Low-selectivity columns, small tables, queries that wrap the column in a function, and write-heavy tables. The planner may ignore it, and it still costs on writes.
followUps.remember: Check the planner uses it.

questions.question: How do you handle schema evolution in a production database?
questions.simple: Change the schema in small, reversible steps that old and new code can both live with. Add first, move data, switch readers, then remove. Never rename or drop in one step while code still reads the old shape.

answer.label: Expand and contract
answer.text: I add the new column or table first, keeping the old one. I backfill, switch the code to the new shape, and drop the old one in a later release.

answer.label: Migrations as code
answer.text: Every change is a versioned migration in the repo, reviewed like code and run in CI against a copy of the schema.

answer.label: Make it safe to deploy
answer.text: Migrations must work while the old code is still running. I avoid long locks, add indexes concurrently where the database allows it, and backfill in batches.

answer.label: Plan the rollback
answer.text: Each migration either reverses cleanly or is paired with a forward fix. For risky ones I rehearse on a production-sized copy.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: AML SoftServe has 111 migrations across 22 domain modules, using Supabase and Drizzle, and I was the top contributor. The Fresh Tracks stack also has Django services across several repos. The AML SoftServe migrations are the part I can speak to first-hand.

questions.remember: Expand, backfill, switch, contract. Always compatible with the running code.
questions.steer: Use the 111 migrations as proof of sustained schema change under a live product.
questions.trap: Do not claim zero-downtime migrations unless you can name one. Do not say 111 migrations are all yours.

followUps.question: How do you rename a column safely?
followUps.answer: I add the new column, write to both, backfill, move readers, then drop the old one in a later release. A direct rename breaks the running code.
followUps.remember: Never rename in one step.

followUps.question: How do you backfill a large table?
followUps.answer: In small batches, with a pause between them, outside peak hours. I make the job resumable and watch locks and replication lag.
followUps.remember: Batch, resume, watch the locks.

questions.question: When would you use Elasticsearch, DuckDB or Postgres for retrieval and analytics?
questions.simple: Postgres is the default for transactional data and modest search. Elasticsearch is for heavy full-text search and relevance tuning. DuckDB is for fast analytical queries over files or tables in a single process, with no server.

answer.label: Postgres first
answer.text: It holds the system of record, supports transactions and constraints, and handles full-text search and vectors through extensions. For a modest corpus it is enough.

answer.label: Elasticsearch
answer.text: I reach for it when search is a product feature: relevance scoring, fuzzy matching, facets and a large corpus. It is a second system to run and keep in sync.

answer.label: DuckDB
answer.text: It is a columnar, in-process engine. It is good for aggregates over large tables, CSV or Parquet files, without standing up a warehouse. It is not a transactional store.

answer.label: How I choose
answer.text: I ask what the query looks like. Lookup and write by key: Postgres. Ranked text search over a lot of text: Elasticsearch. Heavy aggregation over a snapshot: DuckDB.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: Elasticsearch is in the Fresh Tracks stack and in the Spotmentor and EY stack. Postgres is in every engagement since 2025. The AML SoftServe retrieval ran on pgvector inside Postgres on Supabase, which is the Postgres-first answer. I have no recorded DuckDB use, so I would not claim it.

questions.remember: Postgres by default, Elasticsearch for ranked text, DuckDB for in-process analytics.
questions.steer: Say the rule of thumb: add a second system only when Postgres cannot do the job. AML SoftServe kept vectors in Postgres for that reason.
questions.trap: Do not claim Elasticsearch or DuckDB at AML SoftServe. The retrieval stack was pgvector. Do not call DuckDB a database server.

followUps.question: How do you keep Elasticsearch in sync with Postgres?
followUps.answer: Postgres stays the source of truth. I index through events or a change feed, make the indexing idempotent, and keep a way to rebuild the index from scratch.
followUps.remember: Postgres is truth, the index is rebuildable.

followUps.question: Why DuckDB for analytics?
followUps.answer: It runs queries over columnar data in-process, so there is no cluster to run. For a snapshot analysis it is quick to set up and quick to query.
followUps.remember: Warehouse speed with no warehouse.

checks: The old CV line put Elasticsearch and DuckDB in the AML SoftServe retrieval. The locked resume does not. Keep AML at pgvector, and add DuckDB only if you can name where you used it.

questions.question: How does Celery work? Explain the architecture.
questions.simple: Your app publishes a task message to a broker. Workers pull messages, run the task and optionally write a result to a backend. Celery beat adds scheduled tasks.

answer.label: The parts
answer.text: There is a producer, which is my app. There is a broker, such as Redis or RabbitMQ, that holds the queue. Workers consume tasks. An optional result backend stores outcomes.

answer.label: The flow
answer.text: The app calls delay or apply_async. Celery serialises the task name and arguments into a message. A worker picks it up, runs the function and acknowledges it.

answer.label: Reliability settings
answer.text: Acknowledging late means a crashed worker lets the broker redeliver the message. That makes at-least-once delivery, so tasks must be idempotent. Visibility timeouts and prefetch settings matter for long tasks.

answer.label: Operating it
answer.text: I run queues per workload, set concurrency per worker, watch queue depth and retry counts, and use Celery beat or a scheduler for periodic jobs.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: Celery with Redis is in the MITCON stack, which I built. It was also in the Spotmentor and Ernst & Young stack. I would check which MITCON steps run on it before I give task-level detail.

questions.remember: Producer, broker, workers, result backend. At-least-once, so be idempotent.
questions.steer: Move quickly to idempotency and queue depth. That shows you have run it.
questions.trap: Do not describe Celery as exactly-once. Do not recite task details for MITCON you have not checked.

followUps.question: What does late acknowledgement change?
followUps.answer: The worker acknowledges after the task finishes, not before. If it dies mid-task, the broker redelivers. You gain safety and you must handle duplicates.
followUps.remember: Safer delivery, duplicate work.

followUps.question: How do you handle one very slow task blocking others?
followUps.answer: Separate queues per workload, a lower prefetch for long tasks, and time limits. Slow tasks go to their own workers.
followUps.remember: Isolate slow tasks on their own queue.

checks: Confirm which MITCON steps run as Celery tasks before you give task-level examples.

questions.question: How do you handle task failures, retries and idempotency in a distributed system?
questions.simple: Assume messages can arrive twice and tasks can fail halfway. Retry transient failures with backoff, send repeat failures to a dead-letter queue, and design each task so running it twice gives the same result.

answer.label: Classify the failure
answer.text: A timeout or a 503 is transient and worth a retry. A validation error will fail every time, so it should not retry. I mark each error type.

answer.label: Retry with discipline
answer.text: Exponential backoff with jitter, a retry cap, and a visible failure state at the end. Silent infinite retry is a bug.

answer.label: Idempotency
answer.text: Each task has a natural or generated key. The write is an upsert or checks the key first. Running it twice leaves the same final state.

answer.label: Dead letters and visibility
answer.text: After the cap, the message goes to a dead-letter queue with its error, and an operator can see and replay it. Each run is logged with a verdict.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: At Fresh Tracks the availability pipeline ran scrapes through SQS into a consumer that wrote run logs. A run passed only if every valid config passed. The payment agents also ran on schedules, with a 9 am payment request and a nightly reconciliation that starts refunds, so a repeat run must not pay out twice. I would confirm the consumer's idempotency mechanism and the refund de-duplication before I describe either.

questions.remember: Classify the error, back off, cap, dead-letter, make writes idempotent.
questions.steer: Use the ScrapeRun semantics: a run passes only if every valid config passes.
questions.trap: Do not promise exactly-once delivery. Do not claim a dead-letter queue at Fresh Tracks without checking that it existed.

followUps.question: How do you make a payment-style write idempotent?
followUps.answer: The caller sends an idempotency key. The server stores the key with the result and returns the stored result on a repeat. The key is unique in the database.
followUps.remember: One key, one result.

followUps.question: What goes in a dead-letter queue?
followUps.answer: Messages that exhausted their retries, with the error and enough context to replay them. Someone has to watch it, or it is a graveyard.
followUps.remember: A dead-letter queue needs an owner.

checks: Confirm how the Fresh Tracks PMS consumer and the nightly refund run handled duplicates, and whether a dead-letter queue was configured. Neither is stated in the profile. Tagged ours until you confirm.

questions.question: When would you use Kafka, SQS or a Redis broker?
questions.simple: A Redis broker is the light option for background jobs. SQS is a managed queue for decoupling services without running anything. Kafka is a durable, replayable event log for high-volume streams that several consumers read.

answer.label: Redis as a broker
answer.text: It is quick to run and fits Celery job queues. Durability is weaker, so I use it for work I can regenerate or retry. I keep an eye on memory.

answer.label: SQS
answer.text: It is managed, durable and simple. A producer sends, a consumer receives and deletes. It scales without operations work, and I add a dead-letter queue for poison messages. It has no replay once messages are deleted.

answer.label: Kafka
answer.text: It is a partitioned log. Consumers pull from the broker and track their own offsets, so many consumers can read the same stream and I can replay history. It costs more to run and to understand.

answer.label: How I choose
answer.text: Jobs for one worker pool: Redis. Cross-service handoff with minimal ops: SQS. A stream several systems need, with replay: Kafka.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: Fresh Tracks used all three families. Kafka with Faust is in the stack, the availability scrapes feed a consumer through SQS, and Redis sits alongside Celery at MITCON. I would be careful to describe the Kafka work only as far as I remember it.

questions.remember: Redis for jobs, SQS for handoff, Kafka for replayable streams.
questions.steer: Use the availability pipeline: SQS decouples a slow scrape from a fast read.
questions.trap: Do not claim deep Kafka operations. Do not call SQS and Kafka interchangeable. Don't call Kafka "a subscriber model". Consumers pull. Don't tie push and pull to strong and eventual consistency.

followUps.question: Why did the scrape results go through SQS?
followUps.answer: The scrape runs on Fargate and the consumer lives in the PMS service. A managed queue decouples them, so a slow or failed scrape never blocks the read path.
followUps.remember: Decouple slow producers from fast readers.

followUps.question: What is a consumer group in Kafka?
followUps.answer: A set of consumers that share a topic's partitions, each partition read by one member. It lets me scale a reader and still keep order within a partition.
followUps.remember: Partitions are the unit of parallelism.

followUps.question: Is Kafka push or pull?
followUps.answer: Pull. Consumers fetch records from the broker at their own pace and track their own offsets.
followUps.remember: Kafka consumers pull.
followUps.trap: Don't say it's a subscriber model.

checks: The portfolio lists Kafka and Faust in the Fresh Tracks stack but does not describe what ran on them. Confirm what you built on Kafka before you describe it.
The reason the scrape results went through SQS is our inference from the architecture. The portfolio does not record the decision. Say "I would" unless you remember the reason.

questions.question: What is the difference between push and pull queues? Give a use case for each.

answer.label: Push
answer.text: The sender delivers each message to the receiver as it arrives. That gives low latency. It suits a receiver that can always keep up.

answer.label: Pull
answer.text: The consumer asks for messages when it is ready, so it controls its own pace. That suits workers draining a backlog, because a slow worker is never flooded.

answer.label: My own example
answer.text: My payment queue is a pull case. The 9 o'clock cron puts a burst of due instalments on Kafka, and the consumers work through them at their own pace. Kafka consumers pull from the broker.

questions.remember: Push: low latency, the receiver keeps up. Pull: the consumer sets the pace, like a worker draining a backlog.
questions.steer: Finish on the payment queue. It is my own pull example.
questions.trap: Don't tie push and pull to strong and eventual consistency. They describe who starts delivery. Don't call Kafka a subscriber model.

followUps.question: Is Kafka push or pull?
followUps.answer: Pull. Consumers fetch records from the broker and track their own offsets.
followUps.remember: Kafka consumers pull.

checks: The payment queue on Kafka is from your account on the 3 November call. The portfolio doesn't record it. Confirm before you use it as your pull example.

questions.question: How do you monitor an LLM pipeline in production?
questions.simple: I watch four things: errors, latency, cost and quality. Tracing shows each step of a run. Quality needs sampled review or automated evaluation, because a model can fail without raising an error.

answer.label: Trace every run
answer.text: I record each step: the prompt, the model and version, the tool calls, the output and the timing. When something goes wrong I can replay the exact run.

answer.label: Operational metrics
answer.text: Error rate, latency by step, token use and cost per request, and queue depth. These go on a dashboard with alerts on thresholds.

answer.label: Quality signals
answer.text: A model can return a 200 and a wrong answer. So I sample outputs for review, run automated checks on a fixed set, and watch the rate of gaps, refusals and user corrections.

answer.label: Product signals
answer.text: Feature flags and product analytics tell me whether the feature is used and whether people work around it.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: At Fresh Tracks the payment agents were traced end to end in LangSmith, with mails checked by Guardrails AI and scored with DeepEval. At AML SoftServe DeepEval scored retrieval and faithfulness on each change, and Braintrust was used outside evals. Sentry and PostHog are in both stacks. At MITCON I log token counts and provider per job in SweepRun and StepRun tables. At Fresh Tracks I also built a scrape-run dashboard with per-config verdicts.

questions.remember: Trace, measure cost and latency, sample quality, watch for silent failure.
questions.steer: Lead with the Fresh Tracks agents: traced in LangSmith, guarded and scored on every mail. Then the operator dashboard: a run that cannot be seen cannot be trusted.
questions.trap: Do not call Braintrust an eval tool or say it did tracing. That reading is unconfirmed. Do not treat HTTP 200 as success. MITCON has no LangSmith or Langfuse, so do not claim it.

followUps.question: How do you detect a silent quality regression?
followUps.answer: I run a fixed evaluation set on a schedule and after each change, and I compare the scores with the last good baseline. A drop triggers an alert.
followUps.remember: Fixed set, baseline, alert on a drop.

followUps.question: What would you log for privacy?
followUps.answer: I would redact personal data before it reaches the trace store, set a retention limit and restrict access. The trace is useful and sensitive at the same time.
followUps.remember: Redact before you store.

checks: Braintrust at AML SoftServe was used outside evals. Tracing is our reading and is not confirmed. Say "I used Braintrust" and confirm its role before you say more.

questions.question: How do you track and reduce LLM costs?
questions.simple: First I measure cost per call, by feature and tenant. Then I cut the biggest lines. I use a cheaper model where it passes the evaluation, shorten prompts and cache repeated work. I also skip the model when code can do the job.

answer.label: Measure
answer.text: I log input and output tokens and cost on every call, tagged by tenant, feature and model. I look at the top few lines, not the average.

answer.label: Right-size the model
answer.text: I evaluate a smaller model against the task. If it passes, I use it. I keep the stronger model for the hard cases.

answer.label: Shrink the work
answer.text: I trim the prompt, send only the relevant chunks and cache stable prefixes or repeated results. I also avoid the model altogether where a rule or a parser is enough.

answer.label: Cap it
answer.text: Budgets per tenant and per job stop a runaway loop from becoming a bill.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: At MITCON I route in two stages through OpenRouter. A lightweight decision model drops fields below a 0.3 score before the extraction model sees the text, and that extra call added no net cost per file. I chose Gemini Flash-Lite plus the narrowing step for accuracy at no extra cost. On the same first stage, Gemini's wrong values were 11.1% against 24.0% for gpt-4o-mini. ai-gym applies per-cohort cost budgets on Claude calls.

questions.remember: Measure by feature, right-size the model, shrink the prompt, cap the spend.
questions.steer: Say budgets first. They make cost a design property, not a monthly surprise.
questions.trap: Do not quote a percentage saving or call the narrowing figures production results. They are spike numbers. Say the route was chosen for cost and accuracy. Do not say cost alone or accuracy alone.

followUps.question: Does prompt caching change your design?
followUps.answer: Yes. I keep the stable part of the prompt first and the variable part last, so repeated calls reuse the cached prefix.
followUps.remember: Stable first, variable last.

followUps.question: When is the cheaper model the wrong call?
followUps.answer: When it fails the evaluation on the hard cases, or when a wrong answer costs more than the saving. In a regulated document I would not trade accuracy for tokens.
followUps.remember: Cost is a constraint, not the goal.

checks: ai-gym production status is unclear. Describe the budgets as built, not as live.
No cost saving is quotable. The narrowing route added no net cost per file, and $4.00 to $3.34 leaves out the decision model's own call. Do not quote a saving.

questions.question: How do you handle model version changes in production?
questions.simple: I pin the model version, run my evaluation set against any candidate and roll out behind a flag. A model change is a release, and it needs the same gates as code.

answer.label: Pin versions
answer.text: I use a dated model id, not a floating alias. Behaviour should not change under me without a decision.

answer.label: Evaluate before switching
answer.text: I run the candidate on a fixed set and compare scores and failure types with the current model. Prompts often need small changes.

answer.label: Roll out gradually
answer.text: I put the change behind a flag or a canary and keep the old model one switch away. I watch cost, latency and quality.

answer.label: Plan for deprecation
answer.text: Providers retire models. I keep the model id in config, not in code, and keep the evaluation set current so a forced move is routine.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: At MITCON I changed provider twice, each time for a recorded reason. I moved off Anthropic because its document block accepted only PDF among binary files, so workbooks failed with a 400 before reaching the model. Later a golden-set comparison on the same first stage showed Gemini beat gpt-4o-mini for extraction: wrong values 11.1% against 24.0%, recall 57.3% against 36.1%. I chose Gemini Flash-Lite plus the narrowing step, and the extra call added no net cost per file. Model names live in per-task config files, never in Python.

questions.remember: Pin it, evaluate it, flag it, keep the old one one switch away.
questions.steer: Tell both stories. The Anthropic move was a hard constraint. The Gemini move was a measured decision against a golden set.
questions.trap: Do not say the Anthropic move was about quality or price. It was a document-format constraint. Do say the Gemini move was driven by the spike numbers.

followUps.question: What did you do to confirm the model choices were right?
followUps.answer: For the Anthropic move I reproduced the failure with a workbook and filed the reproduction. For Gemini I scored both models on golden answer keys and compared wrong-value rate, recall and repeatability. I would not claim a wider model comparison.
followUps.remember: Reproduce, or score on a golden set.

followUps.question: How do you handle a forced deprecation date?
followUps.answer: The model id sits in config. I'd keep an evaluation set ready, so I can run the candidate early, fix the prompts and flag the rollout well before the date.
followUps.remember: Config plus a live evaluation set.

checks: The Anthropic move is recorded as a constraint with a filed reproduction. The Gemini move rests on the 110-upload spike. Do not claim any other side-by-side comparison.
MITCON has golden answer keys and spike scorers, so the evaluation habit is first-hand there. There is no CI gate on them recorded. Say "I'd gate on it" for the CI part.

questions.question: How do you deploy an LLM-powered application and roll it back safely?
questions.simple: Ship the model, prompt and config as versioned parts of a release. Gate the release on an evaluation run. Roll out behind a flag or a blue-green switch, so going back is one switch, not a rebuild.

answer.label: Version everything
answer.text: The code, the prompts, the model id and the config are all versioned. A release names all four, so I can reproduce it.

answer.label: Gate on evaluation
answer.text: A change to a prompt or model runs against the fixed evaluation set in CI. A drop below the baseline blocks the release.

answer.label: Roll out reversibly
answer.text: I use blue-green deploys for the service and feature flags for behaviour. The old path stays warm until the new one proves itself.

answer.label: Keep a business fallback
answer.text: Where a model or a data source can fail, I keep a non-AI path an operator can switch to. A fallback is a decision someone can make in a minute.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: At Ernst & Young I ran Kubernetes blue-green deploys with 99.9%+ uptime. At Fresh Tracks I shipped a PostHog per-supplier flag that swapped a lookup for an Excel link when the client's data slipped. Fresh Tracks ran on AWS Fargate, and AML SoftServe on Railway.

questions.remember: Version the lot, gate on evaluation, roll out by flag, keep a fallback.
questions.steer: Use the PostHog flag: a reversible business fallback beats a code fork.
questions.trap: Do not claim an LLM-specific canary pipeline you did not build. The blue-green work at EY was not an LLM service.

followUps.question: Blue-green or canary for an LLM change?
followUps.answer: Blue-green for the service. A flag or a percentage rollout for behaviour, because I want to compare quality on live traffic before I commit.
followUps.remember: Blue-green for infrastructure, flags for behaviour.

followUps.question: What do you roll back, the model or the prompt?
followUps.answer: Whichever changed. That is why both are versioned in the release. I should be able to revert one without the other.
followUps.remember: Revert the part that changed.

checks: The EY blue-green work was on the learning platform, not an LLM service. Keep the two separate when you speak.

AML SoftServe ran on Railway and Fresh Tracks on AWS (Fargate, EventBridge, SQS, Bedrock). Keep the two hosts apart. The old CV wording put AWS at AML SoftServe, so be ready if an interviewer has seen it.

questions.question: How do you isolate tenants in a multi-tenant AI SaaS?
questions.simple: I enforce isolation in the database, not only in application code. Every row carries a tenant id and row-level security policies refuse any query that crosses tenants. AI calls, caches and logs are tenant-scoped too.

answer.label: Pick the model
answer.text: Shared tables with a tenant id on every row is the usual start. Separate schemas or databases cost more and suit stricter isolation needs.

answer.label: Enforce it at the database
answer.text: Row-level security policies tie each query to the caller's tenant. A bug in the application code then cannot leak another tenant's rows.

answer.label: Cover the AI paths
answer.text: Retrieval filters on tenant. Prompts never include another tenant's data. Caches, traces and embeddings are keyed by tenant. Budgets are per tenant.

answer.label: Test it
answer.text: I write policy tests that act as tenant A and try to read tenant B. See the next question.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: At AML SoftServe, Supabase row-level security is the security boundary, and I was the top contributor with 327 of 986 commits. ai-gym uses an RLS boundary with psql policy tests. Spotmentor was a multi-tenant platform whose engineering I led as CTO.

questions.remember: Tenant id on every row, enforce in the database, scope the AI paths too.
questions.steer: Say "the database is the boundary". It shows the design is defensive.
questions.trap: Do not claim a formal isolation audit. Do not say the CV's AUSTRAC readiness means a regulator certified it.

followUps.question: Why not just filter by tenant in the application?
followUps.answer: One missed filter leaks data. A database policy applies to every query, including ones written later. It is a second, independent line of defence.
followUps.remember: Defence in depth at the database.

followUps.question: How do you isolate a RAG index per tenant?
followUps.answer: I filter by tenant id in the search itself, not after it. For stricter needs I keep a separate index per tenant. I also check that cached answers are keyed by tenant.
followUps.remember: Filter inside the search, not after.

checks: The default resume says multi-tenant and traceable. "Governance-grade" and "AUSTRAC-reporting-ready" came from the retired CV. Describe the isolation design, not a label.

questions.question: How do you test that your authorisation rules actually hold?
questions.simple: I test the denials, not just the grants. For each role I write tests that attempt forbidden reads and writes against the real database policies and expect them to fail.

answer.label: Test at the policy layer
answer.text: I run tests directly in the database, such as psql scripts, acting as each role and tenant. They exercise the real policies, not a mock.

answer.label: Negative cases first
answer.text: Tenant A tries to read, update and delete tenant B's rows. An anonymous caller tries everything. Each must fail.

answer.label: Cover each role
answer.text: For every role I list what it may and may not do and turn the list into cases. A new table without a policy test is a gap I can find.

answer.label: Run them in CI
answer.text: The tests run on every migration, since a migration is the usual way a policy breaks.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: ai-gym has an RLS boundary with psql policy tests, and I built it. At AML SoftServe RLS is the security boundary across a schema with 111 migrations. It was the tested boundary there too, and I'd confirm how before going into detail.

questions.remember: Test the denials, at the database, for every role, on every migration.
questions.steer: Name the psql policy tests in ai-gym. They are concrete and rare.
questions.trap: Do not describe a policy test suite at AML SoftServe. The portfolio says tested, and only ai-gym records psql policy tests.

followUps.question: How do you simulate a user in a Postgres test?
followUps.answer: I set the role and the claims for the session, run the statement and assert on the rows or the error. Then I reset. Each test starts from a clean state.
followUps.remember: Set the role, run, assert, reset.

followUps.question: What breaks policies silently?
followUps.answer: A new table with RLS off, a view that runs as its owner, or a function with elevated rights. I test for each of those.
followUps.remember: Views and functions bypass policies.

checks: The portfolio lists RLS as tested on softserve360 and ai-gym, but only ai-gym records psql policy tests. Confirm how AML SoftServe was tested before you describe it.

questions.question: How do you share authentication across many services?
questions.simple: One service issues a signed token, and the others verify it with a shared key or a public key. A cookie scoped to the parent domain carries the token to every service. Authorisation stays local to each service.

answer.label: One issuer
answer.text: A single identity service signs a JWT after login. It carries the user id, the tenant and the roles, and it expires quickly.

answer.label: Many verifiers
answer.text: Each service validates the signature and the expiry itself, with no call back to the issuer. Public-key signing means services never hold the signing secret.

answer.label: Carry it with a cookie
answer.text: For browser clients I use an HTTP-only cookie scoped to the parent domain, so every service under it receives the token. That also keeps the token out of JavaScript.

answer.label: Keep authorisation local
answer.text: The token says who the caller is. Each service decides what that caller may do. I plan for key rotation and revocation, since a signed token is valid until it expires.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: The Fresh Tracks platform used shared-cookie JWT identity and access management across its services behind an nginx gateway. I would confirm the service count and the signing method before I quote them.

questions.remember: One signer, many verifiers, cookie scoped to the parent domain, local authorisation.
questions.steer: Say it was across a multi-repo platform behind a gateway. That is the realistic case.
questions.trap: Do not quote a service count. The portfolio gives none in the quotable table. Do not claim a vendor SSO integration.

followUps.question: How do you revoke a JWT?
followUps.answer: Short expiry plus a refresh token I can revoke. For urgent cases a small deny list that services check. Pure stateless tokens cannot be revoked before they expire.
followUps.remember: Short expiry and revocable refresh.

followUps.question: Cookie or authorisation header?
followUps.answer: An HTTP-only cookie for browsers, since scripts cannot read it, with CSRF protection. A bearer header for service-to-service and mobile clients.
followUps.remember: Cookie for browsers, header for services.

checks: The portfolio notes shared-cookie JWT IAM across several Fresh Tracks services but gives no count in the quotable table. Confirm the details before you quote them.
The portfolio does not say who built the shared-cookie JWT work. Confirm your part before you say "I built" it.

categories.title: Tool use, MCP and AI-assisted delivery

questions.question: What is function calling, and how do you design tools for an agent?
questions.simple: Function calling lets a model request a named function with arguments that match a schema. My code runs the function and returns the result. Good tools are narrow, well described and safe to call.

answer.label: The mechanism
answer.text: I give the model a list of tools, each with a name, a description and a JSON schema. The model returns a call with arguments. My code validates them, runs the tool and feeds back the result.

answer.label: Design narrow tools
answer.text: One tool does one thing. The name and description say when to use it. The parameters are typed and constrained, with enums where possible.

answer.label: Return useful errors
answer.text: When a call fails, the error says what was wrong and how to fix it, so the agent can correct itself. Results are small and structured.

answer.label: Guard the dangerous ones
answer.text: Read tools are free. Write tools sit behind validation, permissions and often a human approval step. The model never gets more rights than the user.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: At Fresh Tracks the payment agents on LangGraph and AWS Bedrock read each itinerary's payment history and chose the next action, while deterministic code computed every amount, so no LLM ever computed money. That split is my main tool-design rule. techcirkle-agents exposes the delivery lifecycle as callable LangGraph agents with human-in-the-loop interrupts. On MITCON the pipeline runs code tool steps that read uploaded AutoCAD and Excel files, convert AutoCAD drawings to KML and query the database over SQL. The workflow calls them in code and the model does not choose them. I also wrote PreToolUse hooks that block a coding agent from dangerous commands.

questions.remember: Typed schema, narrow tool, helpful errors, guard the writes.
questions.steer: Lead with the split: deterministic code for money, the agent for the next action. Then the hooks that block the coding agent.
questions.trap: Never say the model chooses the tools on MITCON: the workflow calls its code tool steps. The Fresh Tracks tools you may name are payment requests, mails, refunds and payment-term changes. Don't claim more tools than those.

followUps.question: How many tools can an agent handle?
followUps.answer: Fewer is better. As the list grows, the model picks the wrong one more often. I group tools, keep descriptions sharp and split agents by role before I add tools.
followUps.remember: Fewer, sharper tools.

followUps.question: How do you stop a tool being misused through prompt injection?
followUps.answer: I treat tool arguments as untrusted input. I validate against the schema, check permissions on the server and require approval for writes with side effects.
followUps.remember: Validate and authorise on the server.

questions.question: What is MCP, and when would you build an MCP server?
questions.simple: MCP is an open protocol that lets an AI client discover and call tools, read resources and use prompts from any server that speaks it. You build an MCP server when many clients need the same capability and you want one integration instead of many.

answer.label: What it is
answer.text: A client such as an assistant or an IDE connects to an MCP server over a standard transport. The server lists its tools, resources and prompts, and the client calls them. It replaces bespoke glue for each tool and each client.

answer.label: When I would build one
answer.text: When several agents or tools need the same data or action, such as a governed knowledge base. One server, many clients. I would not build one for a single script.

answer.label: Design care
answer.text: The same rules as any tool surface apply: narrow tools, typed inputs, clear errors, authentication and least privilege. A server is a new attack surface.

answer.label: Honest limits
answer.text: The protocol standardises the connection. It does not make a tool safe or a model correct.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: In my own Claude delivery workflow I use MCP connectors for Jira, Linear, Outlook and Google Drive. That is the delivery process, not a shipped product. I also wrote the org-memory spec, where coding-agent sessions become a governed knowledge base recalled over MCP. The spec is locked and there is no code. No deployed system of mine has an MCP connector and I have not built an MCP server.

questions.remember: One standard way to expose tools and context. Build a server when many clients need it.
questions.steer: Describe the org-memory spec as a design, then say what the recall interface would look like.
questions.trap: Do not say you have built or deployed an MCP server, or that a deployed system has an MCP connector. org-memory has no code. Your MCP use is connectors in your own delivery workflow.

followUps.question: Tools, resources and prompts: what is the difference?
followUps.answer: Tools are actions the model can call. Resources are data the client can read. Prompts are reusable templates the user can pick. I use tools for actions and resources for context.
followUps.remember: Act, read, template.

followUps.question: What are the security concerns?
followUps.answer: Untrusted servers can inject instructions through tool results, and over-broad tools can do damage. I would authenticate, scope each tool to least privilege and log every call.
followUps.remember: Treat every tool result as untrusted.

checks: org-memory is a spec with no code. Always say "I specified" or "I designed" and never "I built".

questions.question: How do you use coding agents on a team without losing control of quality or safety?
questions.simple: I give the agent written context, narrow skills for repeatable steps and hard blocks for dangerous actions. Humans review every change, and the process produces a record.

answer.label: If asked which tools
answer.text: Name the tools first, then the method. I use Claude Code daily, with Cursor and Codex at times. My team skill library, tc-skills, has 16 SDLC and 8 productivity skills and works in Claude and Cursor. PreToolUse hooks block the agent from unsafe commands. I work with People Equation's fde plugin, which carries the method across engagements. The method is: context in files, steps as skills, hooks as hard blocks and a person in review.

answer.label: Write the context down
answer.text: A root CLAUDE.md holds a verified map of the services and the rules. A router file maps ticket keywords to starting files. The agent starts from facts, not guesses.

answer.label: Package the steps as skills
answer.text: Repeatable steps, such as start a ticket, sync a session or prepare a pull request, are skills the whole team shares and versions.

answer.label: Block what must not happen
answer.text: Hooks stop the agent before it runs a dangerous command. At Fresh Tracks they blocked running tests against a shared dev database and mutating staging data.

answer.label: Keep humans in review
answer.text: Every change goes through a pull request and a person. The agent speeds the draft. It does not own the decision.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: I authored this tooling at Fresh Tracks: Claude Code skills with pre-execution guardrails for the engineering team across a 10-repo platform. I also built tc-skills as a shared library for Claude and Cursor. At TekMindz I introduced an AI-enabled delivery method and an LLM-maintained project wiki on every project. Sprint velocity rose 40 to 50% on the pilot project. People Equation's fde plugin pins skill versions per engagement.

questions.trap: Do not generalise the 40 to 50% beyond the TekMindz pilot project. Do not call the project wiki "Memory Bank" or an organisation brain. Do not say the agent replaces review. Never say "instead of talking about tools". Answer the tools question as asked.

followUps.question: What do you do when the agent is confidently wrong?
followUps.answer: I rely on tests, review and the hooks. I also write the rule down in the context file after a miss, so the next run starts better.
followUps.remember: Fix the context, not just the output.
