tabs.title: Scenarios
tabs.purpose: Things that go wrong in production, and how you would diagnose them.

questions.question: Your RAG system returns confident but wrong answers. Retrieval scores look fine. What is happening?
questions.simple: A high similarity score means the passage looks like the question. It does not mean the passage answers it. The usual causes are wrong chunks, stale content, a model that ignores the context, and no instruction to abstain.

answer.label: 1. The right passage is not in the top results
answer.text: Similarity measures topic closeness, not correctness. A near-duplicate, an outdated version or a chunk cut mid-table can score well and mislead. Check: read the retrieved chunks for ten failing queries by hand.

answer.label: 2. Chunking lost the context
answer.text: A figure without its heading or unit is dangerous. Check: look for chunks that split a table, a clause or a caveat. Fix: chunk by structure and keep headings and metadata with each chunk.

answer.label: 3. The model ignores or over-reads the context
answer.text: It fills gaps from its own memory, or blends two passages. Check: ask the same question with the right passage supplied directly. Fix: require a quoted citation for each claim.

answer.label: 4. Nothing tells the model to say "I do not know"
answer.text: Without an abstain path it answers anyway. Fix: allow and reward abstention, and show the gap to the user.

answer.label: 5. Stale or conflicting sources
answer.text: Two versions of a policy both match. Check: look at document dates and duplicates. Fix: version the corpus and filter to the current one.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: At AML SoftServe the agentic RAG over 800+ AUSTRAC documents had zero tolerance for an ungrounded finding. Every finding cited its source clause, Guardrails AI blocked ungrounded output, and DeepEval scored retrieval and faithfulness separately on each change. The MITCON grounding contract works the same way: propose a value only if the document states it, quote the fragment, omit the rest. I have no recorded incident of this exact kind, so the diagnosis is how I would work.

questions.remember: Similar is not correct. Read the chunks, force citations, allow "I do not know".
questions.steer: Move to the grounding contract: quote the source or leave the field empty.
questions.trap: Do not blame the model first. Do not say you fixed this exact incident at AML SoftServe. Do not name the agent framework there, you do not remember it.

followUps.question: How would you measure this going forward?
followUps.answer: I would score faithfulness (is the answer supported by the passage) separately from retrieval relevance, on a fixed set. A faithfulness drop with steady retrieval points at generation.
followUps.remember: Measure faithfulness apart from retrieval.

checks: Be ready for why an in-house LLM reranker. The reason is cost: a managed one charged a platform fee on top of LLM cost, and the harness let the team switch models (stated 2026-10-22). Expect questions on latency and cost per event.
questions.scenario: Your RAG system returns confident but wrong answers. Retrieval scores look fine. What is happening?
questions.testing: Whether you separate retrieval quality from generation quality, and whether you know that a good similarity score does not mean the right passage.
questions.structure: Say the likely causes in order. Name the one check that confirms each. Finish with the fix and how you would prevent a repeat.

questions.question: Your LangGraph agent enters an infinite loop: it keeps calling the same tool with slightly different parameters. How do you fix it?
questions.simple: Stop the loop with a hard limit. Read the trace to see why the tool result did not satisfy the agent, and fix that cause. Then add a repeat-call check so it cannot happen silently again.

answer.label: Contain it
answer.text: Set a recursion or step limit on the graph and a time limit on the run. The run ends with a clear failure state and goes to a human, not into a retry spiral.

answer.label: Read the trace
answer.text: Look at the tool calls and results in order. The usual cause is a result the agent cannot use: an empty list, an error string, or an unhelpful format. It then retries with small variations.

answer.label: Fix the cause
answer.text: Improve the tool: return a clear result for "nothing found" and a useful error that says what to change. Tighten the schema so the parameters cannot drift.

answer.label: Add loop detection
answer.text: Track the calls in graph state. If the same tool repeats with similar arguments, route to a different node: ask the user, escalate or stop.

answer.label: Test it
answer.text: Add the failing run to my regression set so a change cannot bring it back.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: techcirkle-agents is a LangGraph service with human-in-the-loop interrupts and Postgres checkpointing, which gives the interrupt route for a stuck run. The Fresh Tracks payment agents also ran on LangGraph, with every amount computed by deterministic code, so a looping agent could not change money. I have no recorded loop incident.

questions.remember: Limit the run, read the trace, fix the tool result, detect repeats, send to a human.
questions.steer: Say the human interrupt: a stuck agent should ask, not spin.
questions.trap: Do not fix it by only adding "do not loop" to the prompt. Do not claim you hit this in production.

followUps.question: Why not just lower the step limit?
followUps.answer: A lower limit contains the cost but hides the cause. The agent still cannot finish. I want the limit as a safety net and the tool fix as the real change.
followUps.remember: A limit contains. A fix cures.

questions.scenario: Your LangGraph agent enters an infinite loop. It keeps calling the same tool with slightly different parameters. How do you fix it?
questions.testing: Whether you stop the damage first and then find why the agent cannot make progress. Also whether you put limits in the graph rather than in the prompt alone.
questions.structure: Contain, diagnose from the trace, fix the cause, add a limit, add a test case.

questions.question: After a deployment, your LLM token costs jumped 5x. Nothing else changed. Diagnose.
questions.simple: Something did change. I would break the cost down by feature, model and tenant, and compare it with the last good deploy. Then I would look for a longer prompt, a loop, a model switch or a retry storm.

answer.label: Locate the spend
answer.text: Split the cost by feature, model, tenant and call type. A 5x jump is usually one or two lines, not everywhere.

answer.label: Diff the deploy
answer.text: Compare prompts, model ids, config and retrieval settings with the last good release. A pasted document in the system prompt, a larger top-k or a switch to a bigger model are the common ones.

answer.label: Check for loops and retries
answer.text: Count calls per request. An agent loop, a retry without a cap or a queue redelivering a message creates calls rather than longer ones.

answer.label: Check the inputs
answer.text: One tenant sending very large documents, or a cache that stopped hitting, gives the same pattern.

answer.label: Fix and guard
answer.text: Roll back the change or fix the cause. Then set per-tenant budgets and an alert on cost per request, so the next jump shows up in minutes.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: ai-gym applies per-cohort cost budgets on Claude calls, which is the guard. At MITCON I measured cost per 1,000 files in the narrowing spike and confirmed the extra call added no net cost, so I log cost per unit of work. I have no recorded cost incident.

questions.remember: Split by feature and model, diff the deploy, count calls, cap the spend.
questions.steer: Mention budgets per tenant. They turn an incident into a refused call.
questions.trap: Do not say "nothing changed". Do not guess before you look at per-call logs.

followUps.question: How do you tell more calls from longer calls?
followUps.answer: I compare calls per request and tokens per call before and after. More calls points at loops or retries. Longer calls points at prompts, context size or retrieval.
followUps.remember: Calls per request versus tokens per call.

checks: ai-gym production status is unclear. Describe the budgets as built.
questions.scenario: After a deployment, your LLM token costs jumped 5x. Nothing else changed. Diagnose.
questions.testing: Whether you know that something did change, and whether you use per-call cost logs to find it rather than guessing.
questions.structure: Say "something changed". Check the cost logs by feature and tenant. List the likely causes by probability. Then fix and add an alert.

questions.question: Your search works for most queries but fails for a new document type, such as spreadsheets or financial tables. Why?
questions.simple: The pipeline was built for prose. A parser flattens a table into noise, a chunker cuts through rows, and embeddings of numbers match poorly. The fix is to treat structured data as structured.

answer.label: Parsing
answer.text: A prose parser turns a sheet into a stream of cells with no row or column meaning. Check: print what the parser produced for one workbook. The first failure is often here, or the file does not load at all.

answer.label: Chunking
answer.text: Fixed-size chunks cut a table through the middle and drop the header row. Fix: chunk by row groups or by sheet, and repeat the headers and units with each chunk.

answer.label: Embedding
answer.text: Embeddings represent numbers and codes weakly. A query for an exact figure needs lexical match. Fix: hybrid search with keyword matching, and metadata filters on sheet and column.

answer.label: Use the right tool
answer.text: For aggregates and look-ups, query the table directly with SQL or a dataframe. Do not ask retrieval to do arithmetic.

answer.label: Keep the address
answer.text: Store sheet and cell references with every value, so an answer can cite the exact source.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: At MITCON, Anthropic's document block accepted only PDF among binary files, so workbooks failed with a 400 before reaching the model. I moved to OpenAI, and the extractor cites the sheet and cell for spreadsheet values. That was an extraction path rather than search, and the ingestion lesson is the same: check what actually reaches the model.

questions.remember: Check the parser first, chunk by structure, add keyword match, cite sheet and cell.
questions.steer: Tell the workbook 400 story. It is a real failure at the ingestion boundary.
questions.trap: Do not say the MITCON failure was a search failure. It was an extraction input failure.

followUps.question: Why not embed the whole sheet as text?
followUps.answer: The meaning lives in the row and column relationships, and long sheets overflow the context. Row-aware chunks with headers keep the meaning and the size under control.
followUps.remember: Keep the structure, repeat the headers.

questions.scenario: Your search works for most queries but fails for a new document type, such as spreadsheets or financial tables. Why?
questions.testing: Whether you know that ingestion is usually the fault: prose parsers and chunkers break structured data.
questions.structure: Name the ingestion cause first. Then chunking, then embeddings, then the query side. Give the structure-aware fix.

questions.question: Celery workers are consuming messages but tasks are not completing. The queue is growing. What do you check?
questions.simple: Workers that take messages but finish nothing are usually blocked. The cause is a slow external call, a deadlock, a prefetch hoarding messages, or a task that hits its time limit and restarts.

answer.label: 1. What are the workers doing?
answer.text: Inspect active and reserved tasks. If the same tasks run for a very long time, they are stuck. Check the worker logs for time-limit kills and restarts.

answer.label: 2. Is a dependency blocking them?
answer.text: An LLM provider timeout, a slow database query or a lock on a table can hold every worker slot. Check the external call latency and set client timeouts.

answer.label: 3. Prefetch and acknowledgement
answer.text: With a high prefetch, one worker holds a batch of messages while it grinds on a slow one. With late acknowledgement, a crashing task keeps getting redelivered. Check both settings.

answer.label: 4. Is it a poison message?
answer.text: One task that always fails and always retries can fill the pool. Check retry counts and send repeat failures to a dead-letter path.

answer.label: 5. Broker health
answer.text: Check Redis memory, connections and the visibility timeout. A task longer than the visibility timeout gets delivered again while it is still running.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: Celery with Redis is in the MITCON stack, and in the Spotmentor and Ernst & Young stack. I have no recorded Celery incident like this.

questions.remember: Inspect active tasks, find the blocked dependency, check prefetch, kill the poison message.
questions.steer: Mention the visibility timeout. It is a detail people miss.
questions.trap: Do not restart the workers first. That destroys the evidence and the stuck tasks come back.

followUps.question: How do you stop it recurring?
followUps.answer: Client timeouts on every external call and task time limits. A retry cap with a dead-letter path. Separate queues for slow work, and an alert on queue depth and age.
followUps.remember: Timeouts, caps, separate queues, alerts.

checks: Confirm which MITCON steps run on Celery before you tie this to MITCON.
questions.scenario: Celery workers are consuming messages but tasks are not completing. The queue is growing. What do you check?
questions.testing: Whether you have a systematic order of checks and whether you know the failure modes specific to Celery.
questions.structure: Start with the worker and task state, then the broker, then the external dependency, then fix and prevent.

questions.question: Your LLM structured extraction returns malformed JSON about 15% of the time. How do you fix it?
questions.simple: Stop asking for JSON in free text. Use the provider's structured-output feature with a schema, validate every response, retry once with the validation error, and track the failure rate by cause.

answer.label: Constrain the output
answer.text: Use native structured output or function calling with a JSON schema, so the decoder is held to the shape. Keep the schema small and the field descriptions clear.

answer.label: Validate every response
answer.text: Parse with a strict schema validator. Check types, enums, ranges and required fields. Never pass an unvalidated response downstream.

answer.label: Retry with feedback
answer.text: On failure, send the validation error back to the model once or twice. If it still fails, mark the item for review rather than guess.

answer.label: Look at the failure causes
answer.text: Truncation at the token limit, unescaped quotes in long text and a schema that is too wide are the usual ones. Raise the limit or split the task.

answer.label: Check the semantics too
answer.text: Valid JSON can still hold an invented value. The grounding rule matters more than the syntax: each value must come with a quote from the source, or be left out.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: The MITCON extractor works under a contract, with Gemini Flash-Lite as the extraction model. It proposes a value only when the document states it and quotes the exact fragment. It offers both readings when ambiguous and omits what cannot be grounded. Hand-written gates reject an unknown path, a blank value, an uncited value and an invented citation, meaning one not found in the evidence text. I built it. I have no record of a 15% malformed rate.

questions.remember: Schema-constrained output, strict validation, one retry with the error, then a human.
questions.steer: Move from syntax to semantics: a valid number can still be an invented number.
questions.trap: Do not quote the 15% as something you saw. Do not rely on "respond only in JSON" in the prompt.

followUps.question: Do you parse leniently or strictly?
followUps.answer: Strictly. A lenient parser that fixes things silently can hide a real drop in quality. I would repair only in a known, logged way.
followUps.remember: Strict parse, logged repair.

checks: "Pydantic" is a tooling suggestion tagged ours. The portfolio does not name the validation library used at MITCON.
questions.scenario: Your LLM structured extraction returns malformed JSON about 15% of the time. How do you fix it?
questions.testing: Whether you know the layered fixes: constrain the output, validate it, repair or retry with the error, and measure.
questions.structure: Constrain first, then validate, then retry with feedback, then measure what is left. Mention the failures that are not syntax.

questions.question: Redis memory usage is growing unbounded in your production system. It started at 2GB and is now at 12GB after a week.
questions.simple: Redis grows when keys are written without an expiry or when a queue is not drained. I would find the biggest key patterns, find the code that writes them, add expiry or eviction, and alert on memory.

answer.label: 1. Look inside
answer.text: Check memory stats and sample the keys by prefix and size. Find the few patterns that account for most of the memory.

answer.label: 2. Result backend and queues
answer.text: In a Celery setup, stored task results with no expiry are a classic cause. A queue that workers are not draining is another. Check result expiry and queue length.

answer.label: 3. Caches without a time limit
answer.text: Cache keys written with no time-to-live grow for ever. Check the writers and add expiry.

answer.label: 4. Big values and fragmentation
answer.text: A few huge values, such as whole documents, can dominate. Check the largest keys and the fragmentation ratio.

answer.label: 5. Set policy
answer.text: Choose an eviction policy that fits the role. A cache can evict the least recently used. A broker must not evict job data. Split roles into separate instances if both are present.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: Redis is in the MITCON stack with Celery, in the Fresh Tracks stack, and in the Spotmentor and Ernst & Young stack. I have no recorded Redis memory incident.

questions.remember: Find the big key patterns, expire results and caches, drain queues, separate cache from broker.
questions.steer: Say "separate the cache from the broker". It shows you know why one policy cannot serve both.
questions.trap: Do not just raise the memory limit. Do not flush production Redis to fix it.

followUps.question: How do you stop it recurring?
followUps.answer: An alert on memory and key count. A default expiry on every cache write, and result expiry in Celery. A review of any new key pattern in code review.
followUps.remember: Expiry by default, alert on growth.

questions.scenario: Redis memory usage is growing unbounded in your production system. It started at 2GB and is now at 12GB after a week.
questions.testing: Whether you can find what is in memory, separate caches from queues from results, and apply eviction and expiry policy.
questions.structure: Find what is using the memory, find who writes it and why it does not expire, fix expiry and eviction, add monitoring.

questions.question: You are getting different quality scores from the same LLM evaluation pipeline when you run it twice on the same data. The variance is significant.
questions.simple: Two runs differ because the judge model, the system under test or the sample is not deterministic. I would pin temperature and versions, score with a rubric, run each case several times and compare averages with a margin.

answer.label: 1. The judge is random
answer.text: A judge at a high temperature gives different scores for the same output. Set temperature to zero where the provider allows, and pin the judge model version.

answer.label: 2. The system under test is random
answer.text: The generator has its own sampling. Run each case several times and average, or fix the seed where supported.

answer.label: 3. The rubric is loose
answer.text: A vague "rate quality 1 to 10" is noisy. Use a specific rubric with anchored levels and a binary check per criterion.

answer.label: 4. The sample is small
answer.text: On a small set, one case moves the mean. Increase the set and report an interval.

answer.label: 5. Decide with a margin
answer.text: I gate a release on a score difference larger than the observed run-to-run noise, not on any difference.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: At MITCON I scored extraction on golden answer keys and measured repeatability: 46.0% for the old pipeline against 87.2% for the rebuilt one on 110 uploads. At AML SoftServe DeepEval scored retrieval and faithfulness on each change. At Fresh Tracks DeepEval scored agent mails and LangSmith traced them. I have no recorded incident of unstable judge scores, so the fixes are how I would work.

questions.remember: Pin the judge, anchor the rubric, repeat the runs, gate on a margin larger than the noise.
questions.steer: Say "gate on a margin above the noise". It shows you have thought about release gates.
questions.trap: Do not describe a specific evaluation incident. Do not call Braintrust an eval tool, it was used outside evals. Do not claim a judge-calibration study you did not run.

followUps.question: How do you check the judge itself?
followUps.answer: I label a small set by hand and measure how often the judge agrees with the human labels. A judge that disagrees often is not ready to gate anything.
followUps.remember: Calibrate the judge against human labels.

checks: The MITCON repeatability figures come from the 110-upload spike scorers. Quote them as spike results.
Braintrust's role at AML SoftServe (tracing) is our reading and is not confirmed. Confirm before you name it.
questions.scenario: You are getting different quality scores from the same LLM evaluation pipeline when you run it twice on the same data. The variance is significant.
questions.testing: Whether you know the sources of non-determinism in an LLM judge, and how to make an evaluation stable enough to gate a release.
questions.structure: Name the sources of variance. Show how to reduce each. Explain how to decide when a change is real.

questions.question: Your scraped availability data goes stale and a sales agent quotes a train that has sold out. What do you change?
questions.simple: I make age visible, so the agent sees how old each answer is. I detect failed or late sweeps and mark the data stale automatically. The read path never blocks on a scrape, and an operator has a manual override.

answer.label: 1. Contain the quote
answer.text: Tell the agent which sources are stale. Quote only fresh data as available, and show everything else as unconfirmed with its age.

answer.label: 2. Show the age
answer.text: Every snapshot carries the time it was captured and the source. The read path shows both. A reader should never have to guess whether a number is current.

answer.label: 3. Detect staleness automatically
answer.text: The sweep records a run log with a verdict. A run passes only if every valid config passes. A missed or failed sweep marks that source stale and alerts an operator.

answer.label: 4. Keep a fallback
answer.text: A manual upload works as an override with its own flag. A feature flag per supplier can swap the lookup for a safe fallback, such as a pointer to check manually.

answer.label: 5. Find why the sweep went stale
answer.text: Use the run history and the scrape dashboard. Typical causes are a site layout change, a blocked proxy or a scheduler problem. Fix the adapter and add a check for that failure.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: This is the Fresh Tracks Trip Availability Assistant. I built four sources behind one adapter model, with a read path that never blocks on a scrape. It has a run dashboard with per-config verdicts, a manual override and a PostHog per-supplier flag. The scenario itself is hypothetical, because no stale-quote incident is recorded.

questions.remember: Show the age, detect stale runs, never block the read, keep a reversible fallback.
questions.steer: Tell the Trip Availability Assistant design. It is your strongest operable-system story.
questions.trap: Do not say a sold-out quote actually happened. Do not claim a staleness alert unless you confirm one existed.

followUps.question: Why not scrape on demand when the agent asks?
followUps.answer: The agent needs an answer during a live call, and a scrape is slow and can fail. Pre-fetching keeps the read fast, and the age tells the agent how far to trust it.
followUps.remember: Pre-fetch for speed, show the age for trust.

followUps.question: How does the client's own data slipping fit in?
followUps.answer: It is the same pattern. When the client's data slipped, I used a feature flag to swap the lookup for a link to the Excel sheet. It was a reversible business fallback, not a code change.
followUps.remember: A flag is a fallback an operator can use.

checks: Confirm whether an automatic staleness alert existed. The portfolio describes run verdicts and a dashboard, not an alert. Tagged ours until you confirm.
questions.scenario: Your scraped availability data goes stale and a sales agent quotes a train that has sold out. What do you change?
questions.testing: Whether you treat staleness as data quality in its own right, protect the read path and give operators a visible, reversible fallback.
questions.structure: Contain the wrong quote, show data age, detect staleness, keep a fallback, then fix the cause of the stale run.

tabs.title: System design
tabs.purpose: Design problems with clarifying questions, a step-by-step walkthrough and the trade-offs.

questions.question: Design a RAG-based knowledge assistant for a company with 50,000 internal documents
questions.simple: A knowledge assistant finds the right passages in company documents and answers from them with citations. The hard parts are keeping the index fresh, respecting who may see what, and proving the answers are grounded.
questions.problem: A company has 50,000 internal documents across its file stores. Staff want to ask questions in plain language and get answers with sources. Design the system.

clarifying.question: Where do the documents live, and how often do they change?
clarifying.why: It decides the ingestion method. A store with change feeds, such as SharePoint delta queries, avoids full re-indexing.

clarifying.question: Do document permissions differ by user?
clarifying.why: If they do, retrieval must filter by the user's access, or the assistant leaks documents.

clarifying.question: What formats are there: text, scanned PDFs, spreadsheets, slides?
clarifying.why: Tables and scans need different parsing from plain text, and they fail silently if treated the same.

clarifying.question: What does a wrong answer cost, and must every answer cite a source?
clarifying.why: It sets the grounding rules and whether the assistant may answer without a citation.

steps.title: Requirements
steps.text: Answers grounded in company documents with citations. Respect each user's document permissions. Fresh within a day of a document change. Users ask from the tool they already use, such as Teams.

steps.title: Architecture
steps.text: A connector pulls changes from the document store. An ingestion worker parses, chunks and embeds. Chunks and their access lists go into Postgres with pgvector, plus a keyword index. A FastAPI service with a LangGraph flow handles retrieval, answer and citation check. A Teams bot is the front end.

steps.title: Data flow
steps.text: A change event arrives, the worker re-parses only that document, replaces its chunks and updates the access list. At query time the user's identity filters the candidate chunks before ranking. The model answers only from the retrieved chunks and cites each claim.

steps.title: Key component
steps.text: Retrieval with permission filtering. I'd run hybrid search, vector and keyword, filtered by access list, then re-rank the top results. Filtering happens before ranking so a forbidden chunk never reaches the model.

steps.title: Scaling
steps.text: 50,000 documents is a modest index for pgvector with an HNSW index. The pressure is ingestion bursts and permission changes, so ingestion runs on a queue and permission updates are applied without re-embedding.

steps.title: Evaluation and where I've designed this
steps.text: Build a golden set of questions with known source passages, measure retrieval hit rate and answer faithfulness, and gate changes on it. I designed a SharePoint RAG chatbot in Teams along these lines for sandvick-agents: FastAPI and LangGraph, pgvector, the Graph API and Azure. That is a pre-sales design with no code. My production RAG is AML SoftServe: agentic RAG over 800+ AUSTRAC documents, with pgvector, an o4-mini LLM reranker, Guardrails AI for grounding and DeepEval for evals.

questions.whiteboard: On the left, the document store with a change feed. An arrow to an ingestion queue and worker that parses, chunks and embeds. The worker writes to Postgres holding chunks, embeddings, keyword index and access lists. In the middle, a FastAPI service running a LangGraph flow: retrieve with a permission filter, re-rank, answer, check citations. On the right, a Teams bot calling the service with the user's identity. Underneath, an evaluation job that replays a golden set.

tradeOffs.title: pgvector against a dedicated vector database
tradeOffs.text: At 50,000 documents pgvector keeps chunks, access lists and metadata in one transactional store. A dedicated vector database earns its place at far larger scale or with heavy query load.

tradeOffs.title: Filter before ranking against filter after
tradeOffs.text: Filtering first can starve the ranker of candidates for users with narrow access. Filtering after risks leaking content into the prompt. I filter first and raise the candidate count.

tradeOffs.title: Answer or abstain
tradeOffs.text: An assistant that says "I couldn't find this" is less impressive in a demo, but it is the one people trust. I'd make abstention the default when no chunk supports the answer.

answer.label: Opening line
answer.text: I'd start with where the documents live and who may see them, because those two decide the design.

answer.label: The decision that matters
answer.text: Permission filtering happens before ranking. A chunk the user can't open never reaches the model.

answer.label: Where I've designed this
answer.text: I designed this shape for a SharePoint chatbot in Teams, sandvick-agents. That one is design only. My built version of the hard part is AML SoftServe: agentic RAG over 800+ AUSTRAC documents.

questions.remember: Freshness, permissions, citations. Filter before you rank.
questions.steer: Bring up permission filtering early.
questions.trap: Never say you built sandvick-agents. It is a design with no code.

followUps.question: How do you keep the index fresh without re-embedding everything?
followUps.answer: Use the store's change feed. For SharePoint that's Graph delta queries, which return only what changed since the last token.
followUps.remember: Delta queries, not full re-index.

followUps.question: Have you run this in production?
followUps.answer: The sandvick design, no. My production RAG is AML SoftServe: agentic RAG over 800+ AUSTRAC documents, screening every onboarding and transaction, with an in-house o4-mini reranker and Guardrails AI for grounding. I don't remember the agent framework, so I won't name one.
followUps.remember: sandvick is a design. AML SoftServe is the production RAG.

checks: The permission-filtering and abstention details are a recommended design, not recorded parts of the sandvick-agents design. Confirm what the sandvick design actually specified before citing it in detail.

questions.question: Design a multi-agent system for automated research report generation
questions.simple: Several agents split the work: one plans, some research, one writes and one checks. A graph controls the order, saves state so a run can resume, and pauses for a human where it matters.
questions.problem: Users ask for a research report on a topic. The system should plan the report, gather sources, analyse them and write a cited draft, with a person able to review before it is final.

clarifying.question: What sources may the agents use: the open web, internal documents, or both?
clarifying.why: It sets the tools and the security boundary for each research agent.

clarifying.question: How long can a report take, and must users see progress?
clarifying.why: Long runs need a job model, saved state and streamed progress rather than one request.

clarifying.question: Where must a human approve?
clarifying.why: It decides where the graph pauses with an interrupt, such as after the outline or before final output.

clarifying.question: What is the cost budget per report?
clarifying.why: It caps the number of research steps and the model choice for each agent.

steps.title: Requirements
steps.text: A cited report from a topic. Visible progress. A human approves the outline and the final draft. Runs survive restarts. Cost per report is capped.

steps.title: Architecture
steps.text: A LangGraph state graph behind a FastAPI service. A planner node writes the outline. Research nodes run per section with search tools. A writer node drafts. A checker node verifies each claim has a source. Postgres holds checkpoints.

steps.title: Data flow
steps.text: The request starts a run with an id. The planner writes the outline, then the graph interrupts for approval. Research fans out by section and writes notes with source links into state. The writer drafts from the notes only. The checker flags unsupported claims and loops back once, then interrupts for final review.

steps.title: Key component
steps.text: State and checkpointing. Every node reads and writes typed state, and each step is checkpointed in Postgres. A human interrupt is just a paused checkpoint, and a crash resumes from the last one.

steps.title: Scaling
steps.text: Runs are independent, so they scale out across workers. Fan-out per section is bounded. Each run has a step cap and a token budget, and a loop guard stops repeated tool calls.

steps.title: Evaluation and where I've built this
steps.text: Trace every run, score a fixed set of topics for citation coverage and factual support, and compare before releasing a prompt or graph change. I built techcirkle-agents with a similar graph shape: a LangGraph service that exposes the SDLC as callable agents over SSE, with human-in-the-loop interrupts, Postgres checkpointing and LangSmith. It's a working prototype, deployed on Railway. In production, the Fresh Tracks payment agents run on LangGraph and AWS Bedrock, with traces in LangSmith and scores in DeepEval.

questions.whiteboard: A client on the left connected by server-sent events to a FastAPI service. Inside the service, a LangGraph graph: planner, then an interrupt box labelled "approve outline", then parallel research nodes with search tools, then writer, then checker with a loop arrow back to writer, then an interrupt box labelled "final review". Below the graph, Postgres holding checkpoints. To the right, LangSmith receiving traces.

tradeOffs.title: One agent with many tools against several agents
tradeOffs.text: One agent is simpler and cheaper. Several agents earn their place when sections are independent and need different tools or prompts. I'd start with fewer agents and split only where traces show confusion.

tradeOffs.title: Supervisor against a fixed graph
tradeOffs.text: A supervisor that routes freely is flexible but harder to test. A fixed graph with a few conditional edges is predictable, and that is what I'd ship first.

tradeOffs.title: Human interrupts against full automation
tradeOffs.text: Interrupts slow a run down. They also catch a bad outline before the expensive research step, which saves more than it costs.

answer.label: Opening line
answer.text: I'd model it as a state graph with checkpoints, and pause for a human after the outline and before the final draft.

answer.label: The decision that matters
answer.text: Checkpointing every step in Postgres. It makes human review and crash recovery the same mechanism.

answer.label: Where I've built this
answer.text: techcirkle-agents has a similar graph shape: LangGraph over SSE, human-in-the-loop interrupts and Postgres checkpointing. It exposes the SDLC as agents, not research reports. It's a deployed prototype, not a production product. My production multi-agent system is the Fresh Tracks payment system. Deterministic code computes every amount. The agents read payment history, decide the next action and write the mail.

questions.remember: State graph, checkpoints, two human gates, a step cap.
questions.steer: Talk about checkpointing as the thing that makes interrupts and recovery one mechanism.
questions.trap: Don't call techcirkle-agents production. For production, use the Fresh Tracks payment system, and say that deterministic code computed every amount.

followUps.question: How do you stop the agents looping?
followUps.answer: A step cap per run, a budget per run, and a guard that stops the same tool call with near-identical arguments. The checker loops back to the writer once, not forever.
followUps.remember: Step cap, budget, repeat guard.

followUps.question: How do you stream progress?
followUps.answer: Server-sent events from the service. techcirkle-agents exposes its agents over SSE.
followUps.remember: SSE for progress.

checks: The portfolio lists techcirkle-agents but does not say who wrote it. Confirm you built it before you say "I built", and keep to "a similar graph shape".

questions.question: Design an AI-powered pipeline that extracts structured data from PDFs and spreadsheets, where a wrong number has legal consequences
questions.simple: The pipeline reads PDFs and spreadsheets, asks a model to propose field values, and shows each value with the exact place it came from. An expert approves before anything goes into a signed document. Where the source is silent, the field stays empty.
questions.problem: A consultancy prepares statutory documents from client PDFs and spreadsheets. Values extracted from them end up in signed filings. A wrong number has legal consequences. Design the extraction pipeline.

clarifying.question: Who signs the output, and what do they need to see to sign it?
clarifying.why: It sets the review screen: each value with its source quote, sheet and cell.

clarifying.question: What source formats arrive: native PDFs, scans, Excel workbooks, Word files?
clarifying.why: Each needs its own parser, and some model APIs accept only certain file types.

clarifying.question: What should happen when a value is ambiguous or missing?
clarifying.why: It decides whether the model may pick, must show both readings, or must leave a gap.

clarifying.question: How many documents per case, and how fast must it turn round?
clarifying.why: It sizes the worker pool and whether extraction runs as background jobs.

steps.title: Requirements
steps.text: Every value traceable to a quoted source fragment. No invented values. Ambiguity shown, not resolved by the model. An expert approves before output. Output fills a fixed structure such as a consolidated statement.

steps.title: Architecture
steps.text: Django and DRF for the API, Celery workers on Redis for extraction, Postgres for cases, values and citations. The stack also includes python-docx, openpyxl and pypdfium2. A React review screen using a generated API client.

steps.title: Data flow
steps.text: Upload creates a case. A Celery task parses each file into text and cell references. The model receives the fields and the source, and returns proposed values with a quoted fragment for each. The values land as proposals. The expert approves, edits or rejects each one, and only approved values fill the output.

steps.title: Key component
steps.text: The grounding contract. The model may propose a value only when the document states it, must quote the exact fragment with sheet and cell, must propose both readings when ambiguous, and must omit any field it cannot ground. A gap on screen is recoverable. An invented number in a signed document is not.

steps.title: Scaling
steps.text: Extraction runs per file as background jobs, so cases scale with workers. A two-stage route through OpenRouter adds no net cost per file: a lightweight decision model narrows each document, then Gemini Flash-Lite extracts from it.

steps.title: Evaluation and where I've built this
steps.text: Keep a set of real source files with expert-approved values. Measure how often a proposal is correct, how often it is wrongly filled, and how often it is left empty. Track the wrong-fill rate hardest. I built this at MITCON for environmental-clearance filings. On a 110-upload golden set, the rebuilt pipeline raised recall from 28% to 62% and cut wrong values from 27% to 11%, against the old pipeline on gpt-4o-mini. The 97-row consolidated statement fills automatically under this contract, with expert checkpoints.

questions.whiteboard: Upload on the left into a Django API. An arrow to a Celery queue on Redis. Workers parse PDFs, workbooks and Word files, then call the model with the grounding contract. Proposals with quotes and cell references land in Postgres. On the right, a React review screen shows each value beside its source quote, with approve and reject. Approved values flow down into the output document builder.

tradeOffs.title: Let the model choose against showing both readings
tradeOffs.text: Choosing is smoother for users. Showing both readings costs an expert a few seconds and removes the most dangerous kind of error.

tradeOffs.title: Cheap model against large model
tradeOffs.text: A tightly specified extraction task does not need the largest model. I'd move up only if evaluation shows misses the contract can't fix.

tradeOffs.title: Provider choice by file support
tradeOffs.text: At MITCON, Anthropic's document block accepted only PDF among binary files, so workbooks failed before reaching the model. File support can decide the provider before quality does.

answer.label: Opening line
answer.text: I'd start from what the signer needs to see: every value next to the exact source it came from.

answer.label: The decision that matters
answer.text: The grounding contract. The model quotes its source, shows both readings when unsure and leaves a gap when it can't ground a value.

answer.label: Where I've built this
answer.text: This is MITCON. I built it in Django and Celery with a two-stage model route, and the 97-row consolidated statement now fills automatically, with experts approving at every gate.

questions.remember: Quote it, show both, or leave a gap.
questions.steer: Quote the line "a gap on screen is recoverable and an invented number in a signed document is not." It lands well.
questions.trap: Quote only the golden-set result: the rebuilt pipeline raised recall from 28% to 62% and cut wrong values from 27% to 11%, against the old pipeline on gpt-4o-mini. It is not a model swap. Claim no production accuracy figure.

followUps.question: How do you know the quoted fragment is real?
followUps.answer: A code-level gate accepts a value only when its citation is found in the source text. An invented citation is rejected before the expert sees it. The citation also names the sheet and cell, so the expert can check it.
followUps.remember: The gate checks the quote against the source.

followUps.question: Why did you leave Anthropic, and why Gemini?
followUps.answer: Anthropic's document block took only PDFs, so workbooks returned 400 before reaching the model. I reproduced it and filed the note. Later a spike on 110 uploads showed Gemini beat gpt-4o-mini on extraction, so Gemini replaced it.
followUps.remember: File support dropped Anthropic. The spike chose Gemini.

followUps.question: Why Django over the FastAPI monolith you started with?
followUps.answer: I re-cut it five days in, when the shape stopped fitting. The result was Django and DRF with Celery, and React in its own repo.
followUps.remember: Re-cut when the shape stopped fitting.

noEvidence.note: Golden-set evals exist, but the profile records no production accuracy figure for the MITCON extractor.
prepare: Be ready to explain the golden set: how many uploads, and who approved the answer keys.
Be ready to walk through the citation gate, which rejects a value whose citation isn't found in the source text.

checks: Re-read the gate code before the interview so you can describe its other checks, such as unknown path, blank value and unit mismatch.
Confirm which role python-docx, openpyxl and pypdfium2 each play (reading input, building output, or both). The portfolio lists the stack and gives no roles.

questions.question: Design a multi-tenant compliance SaaS where every generated document must be defensible years later
questions.simple: Many firms share one system, so each must see only its own data. Every document the system generates must be reproducible later, even after questions and templates change. Isolation and frozen inputs do most of the work.
questions.problem: Regulated firms answer a risk questionnaire. The system scores their risk, generates a compliance programme document, collects e-signatures and tracks ongoing mitigation. Many firms share the platform, and any document must be defensible to a regulator years later.

clarifying.question: What must be reproducible later: the document, the score, or the reasoning behind it?
clarifying.why: If the score must reproduce, the questions, options and weights at that moment must be frozen too.

clarifying.question: How strict is tenant isolation, and who audits it?
clarifying.why: It decides whether isolation lives in the application or in the database itself.

clarifying.question: How many entity types and risk tiers, and how often do templates change?
clarifying.why: It sets how templates are versioned and selected.

clarifying.question: Which steps need a human: signature, review dates, due diligence?
clarifying.why: It places the human checkpoints and the reminders.

steps.title: Requirements
steps.text: Tenant data isolated by the database. Every generated document reproducible from frozen inputs. Versioned templates by entity type and risk tier. Mandatory review dates driven by risk. Audit trail of who did what.

steps.title: Architecture
steps.text: A layered modular monolith: API routes under app/api/v1, a framework-agnostic domain layer, and Postgres on Supabase with row-level security as the security boundary. Next.js for the app, Drizzle for schema and migrations, an e-signature service, and a KYC and KYB provider.

steps.title: Data flow
steps.text: A firm completes a questionnaire attempt. On completion, the questions and chosen options freeze into an immutable snapshot. Scoring reads the snapshot, picks the risk tier, selects the matching versioned template and generates the PDF. Signature follows. Mitigation items generate from snapshot options flagged as triggers, and the tier sets the next mandatory review date.

steps.title: Key component
steps.text: The snapshot. Scoring and document generation never read live question rows. If the questionnaire changes next year, last year's score and document still reproduce exactly.

steps.title: Scaling
steps.text: Tenants share tables and RLS keeps them apart, so adding a tenant is a row, not a deployment. Document generation runs off the request path. Migrations run through one disciplined pipeline.

steps.title: Evaluation and where I've built this
steps.text: Test the RLS policies directly in SQL, not only through the app. I have psql policy tests for that on ai-gym. Regenerate a sample of past documents from their snapshots and compare. At AML SoftServe, for AUSTRAC AML/CTF, the product has 24 versioned templates across 3 entity types and 4 risk tiers, 111 migrations and 22 domain modules, and I was top contributor with 327 of 986 commits.

questions.whiteboard: A Next.js app on top. Under it, the API routes, then a domain box with modules for questionnaire, scoring, templates, programme and due diligence. Under that, Postgres with RLS drawn as a fence around each tenant's rows. A side box labelled "snapshot" between questionnaire and scoring, with an arrow showing scoring reads only from it. Out to the right, e-signature and KYC providers. A template store with versions by entity type and tier.

tradeOffs.title: RLS in the database against checks in the app
tradeOffs.text: App checks are easy to forget in one route. RLS enforces isolation for every query, including ones written later. The cost is harder debugging and policies that need their own tests.

tradeOffs.title: Snapshot against live reads
tradeOffs.text: Snapshots duplicate data. That duplication is the point: a regulated artefact must not change when the source rows change.

tradeOffs.title: Modular monolith against services
tradeOffs.text: One deployable with clear domain modules is faster for a small team and keeps transactions simple. Services would add network boundaries the product didn't need yet.

answer.label: Opening line
answer.text: I'd make the database enforce isolation, and I'd freeze every input a document depends on.

answer.label: The decision that matters
answer.text: The snapshot-bound questionnaire. Scoring reads the frozen snapshot, never live rows, so last year's document still reproduces.

answer.label: Where I've built this
answer.text: This is AML SoftServe, for AUSTRAC AML/CTF. Row-level security was the tenant boundary, and the templates were versioned by entity type and risk tier.

questions.remember: RLS for isolation, snapshots for defensibility.
questions.steer: Lead with the snapshot. It's the decision that shows you understand regulated software.
questions.trap: Don't bring in the AML SoftServe RAG unless asked. Then say it was one component, and don't name an agent framework. It isn't remembered.

followUps.question: How do you test RLS?
followUps.answer: With SQL tests that run as different tenants and assert what each can see. I did that with psql policy tests in ai-gym. RLS was the tested boundary on softserve360 too. The psql policy tests I can show you are on ai-gym.
followUps.remember: Test policies as each tenant, in SQL.

followUps.question: Where was the AI in this product?
followUps.answer: In the agentic RAG over 800+ AUSTRAC documents. An agent screened every onboarding and transaction against policy and decided whether to flag it. Every finding cited its source clause, and Guardrails AI blocked ungrounded output. RAG was one component of the SaaS.
followUps.remember: Agentic RAG was one component of the SaaS.
followUps.trap: Don't name an agent framework, and don't say what Braintrust did beyond that it was used.

checks: Confirm that the snapshot-bound design and the layered architecture were your decisions, not only the team's.

The portfolio lists RLS as tested on softserve360 and ai-gym, but only ai-gym records the psql policy tests. Confirm how the AML SoftServe policies were tested before you describe it, and do not say you wrote them.
The tech-lead or architect reading of your AML SoftServe role is tagged ours. Confirm it before you say it.
Braintrust was used outside evals. The tracing reading is ours, so say only that it was used. The evals tool was DeepEval.

questions.question: Design an availability service over suppliers with a live API, a batch feed and no API at all
questions.simple: Sales staff need supplier availability during a live call. Each supplier offers data differently. The service puts every supplier behind one adapter model and pre-fetches the slow ones, so a read never waits.
questions.problem: Sales agents need train and hotel availability during a live client call, before an itinerary exists. One supplier has a live API, one offers a batch feed, one has no API at all, and one already syncs into the system. Design the service.

clarifying.question: How fresh must the data be for each supplier?
clarifying.why: It sets each sweep schedule and whether the screen must show the age of the data.

clarifying.question: Are we allowed to scrape the supplier with no API?
clarifying.why: It decides whether the source is possible at all, and how carefully it must be done.

clarifying.question: What happens when a source is down or late?
clarifying.why: It sets the fallback, such as a manual upload or a link to a spreadsheet.

clarifying.question: Who operates it day to day?
clarifying.why: It decides what the operator screen must show.

steps.title: Requirements
steps.text: One query across all suppliers. Reads never block on a slow source. Each source runs on its own schedule. A person can override data by hand. Operators can see which runs failed.

steps.title: Architecture
steps.text: One adapter model with an acquisition method per source: live HTTP, an authorised B2B API on a daily sweep, a scheduled scrape, and an existing sync. Manual upload is an override on top, not a fifth source. EventBridge schedules Fargate tasks that run Playwright for the scrape, publish to SQS, and a consumer in the PMS writes snapshots.

steps.title: Data flow
steps.text: A schedule fires, the task fetches, results go on SQS, the consumer writes an availability snapshot and a run log. Sales reads snapshots. The live source can be called directly when needed.

steps.title: Key component
steps.text: The read path never blocks on a scrape. Snapshots are pre-fetched, so the slowest supplier can't slow the call.

steps.title: Scaling
steps.text: Each source scales by its own schedule and task count. In this design a new supplier would be a new adapter config, not a new pipeline.

steps.title: Evaluation and where I've built this
steps.text: A run passes only if every valid config passes, and the operator screen shows run history and per-config verdicts. I built this at Fresh Tracks Canada as the Trip Availability Assistant: four different availability sources behind one adapter model, with a PostHog per-supplier flag as the fallback when the client's BIM data slipped.

questions.whiteboard: Four suppliers on the left: BIM live HTTP, VIA Rail through Sqills B2B, Rocky Mountaineer by scrape, Jonview by sync. EventBridge on top triggering Fargate tasks, one running Playwright through a residential proxy. Arrows into SQS, then a PMS consumer writing AvailabilitySnapshot and AdapterRunLog tables. A ManualUpload box feeding in as an override. On the right, the sales screen reading snapshots, and an operator dashboard reading run logs.

tradeOffs.title: Pre-fetch against live calls
tradeOffs.text: Pre-fetching serves slightly older data. It means the call never waits on a scrape, which is what sales needed.

tradeOffs.title: Manual upload as an override against a source
tradeOffs.text: As a source, manual data would compete with the real feeds. As an override, it wins on purpose and is easy to see and remove.

tradeOffs.title: Feature flag against a code branch for fallbacks
tradeOffs.text: A per-supplier flag is reversible without a deploy. A branch would need merging later.

answer.label: Opening line
answer.text: I'd put every supplier behind one adapter model and pre-fetch the slow ones, so a sales call never waits.

answer.label: The decision that matters
answer.text: Manual upload is an override, not another source. And the read path never blocks on a scrape.

answer.label: Where I've built this
answer.text: This is the Trip Availability Assistant at Fresh Tracks. It started as a throwaway spike behind one output seam, and graduated to EventBridge, Fargate and SQS.

questions.remember: One adapter model, pre-fetch, override, flag.
questions.steer: Mention the spike-then-graduate seam. It shows how you go from feasibility to production without a rewrite.
questions.trap: The availability service itself had no AI. The AI at Fresh Tracks was the payment agents. Don't dress this one up as an AI system.

followUps.question: Why scrape at all?
followUps.answer: Rocky Mountaineer has no B2B API. Without the scrape, sales had no data for that supplier during a call.
followUps.remember: No API, so a scheduled scrape.

followUps.question: How did you prove the scrape was feasible?
followUps.answer: With an explicit throwaway spike, not even a git repo. The browser logic sat behind an output seam, so graduation swapped writing to disk for writing to SQS.
followUps.remember: Spike behind a seam, then graduate.

questions.question: Design an enterprise agent platform: shared tools, evaluation gates, cost control and governance for many teams
questions.simple: Many teams want to build agents. A platform gives them shared tools, a way to test changes before release, spending limits and rules about what agents may do. The aim is to let teams move fast without each one rebuilding the same controls.
questions.problem: A large company has many teams building agents. Leadership wants shared tools, release gates based on evaluation, cost control per team, and governance over what agents can touch. Design the platform.

clarifying.question: Do teams share one model provider or many?
clarifying.why: It decides whether a gateway sits between teams and providers to meter and route calls.

clarifying.question: Which actions are dangerous enough to block or need approval?
clarifying.why: It sets the policy layer and where human approval is required.

clarifying.question: Who owns a shared tool, and how are changes released?
clarifying.why: A shared tool that changes under a running agent breaks other teams.

clarifying.question: How is cost charged back?
clarifying.why: It decides the budget unit: per team, per agent or per user group.

steps.title: Requirements
steps.text: A shared, versioned tool registry. Per-team budgets enforced at call time. Evaluation gates on every agent release. Policy that blocks dangerous actions. Tenant isolation between teams. Traces for audit.

steps.title: Architecture
steps.text: A model gateway that meters and routes every call. A tool registry exposing tools through MCP, each versioned. A policy layer that checks tool calls before they run. An evaluation service that replays fixed cases and gates releases. Postgres with row-level security per team.

steps.title: Data flow
steps.text: An agent calls the gateway with its team identity. The gateway checks the budget, routes the call and logs it. Tool calls pass the policy check, then run. Traces go to the observability store. A release runs the eval suite and is blocked if it regresses.

steps.title: Key component
steps.text: Version pinning for shared tools and skills. A team pins the version it tested against, so a change by another team can't break a running agent.

steps.title: Scaling
steps.text: The gateway is stateless and scales out. Budgets are counters per team. Tools scale independently behind the registry.

steps.title: Evaluation and where I've worked on this
steps.text: Gate releases on regression against a baseline, and track cost per team. I have pieces of this, not the whole platform. At AML SoftServe, DeepEval scored retrieval and faithfulness on each change and Guardrails AI blocked ungrounded output. At Fresh Tracks, Guardrails AI checked every mail the agents wrote, DeepEval scored them and LangSmith traced runs. ai-gym runs Claude through OpenRouter under per-cohort cost budgets with an RLS boundary, though its production status is unclear. The fde plugin pins versions per engagement. PreToolUse hooks at Fresh Tracks block a coding agent from dangerous operations. org-memory is a locked spec for recalling governed knowledge through MCP, with no code.

questions.whiteboard: Teams and their agents on the left. All calls go through a model gateway in the middle that checks budgets and routes to providers. Below the gateway, a policy layer in front of an MCP tool registry with versioned tools. To the right, a tracing store and an evaluation service with a release gate. Underneath, Postgres with per-team row-level security holding budgets, versions and audit records.

tradeOffs.title: Central gateway against direct provider access
tradeOffs.text: A gateway adds a hop and a single point to keep healthy. Without it, cost control and audit depend on every team doing it right.

tradeOffs.title: Pinned versions against always-latest
tradeOffs.text: Pinning means teams lag behind fixes. It also means nothing changes under a running agent, which matters more.

tradeOffs.title: Hard blocks against warnings
tradeOffs.text: Warnings are easy to ignore. For destructive actions I'd block in a hook and require approval.

answer.label: Opening line
answer.text: I'd put every model call through a gateway that meters cost, and every tool behind a versioned registry with a policy check.

answer.label: The decision that matters
answer.text: Pinned versions. A shared tool must not change under a running agent.

answer.label: Where I've worked on this
answer.text: I've built pieces: evals and guardrails on shipped agents at Fresh Tracks and AML SoftServe, per-cohort cost budgets in ai-gym, pinned plugin versions in fde, and hooks that block dangerous coding-agent actions at Fresh Tracks. I haven't built the whole platform.

questions.remember: Gateway, versioned tools, policy, eval gate, budgets.
questions.steer: Name the pieces you have built and be clear the full platform is a design.
questions.trap: Don't claim ai-gym is in production, and don't claim org-memory has code.

followUps.question: Have you run evaluation gates in production?
followUps.answer: Evals and guardrails, yes. At AML SoftServe, DeepEval scored retrieval and faithfulness on each change and Guardrails AI blocked ungrounded output. At Fresh Tracks, Guardrails AI checked every mail, DeepEval scored them and LangSmith traced runs end to end. I'm not claiming a release-gate platform. Prepare how a failing score held up a change.
followUps.remember: Evals and guardrails shipped. A full release gate is not claimed.
followUps.trap: Don't describe a release gate you haven't confirmed.

followUps.question: Why MCP for the tool registry?
followUps.answer: It gives teams one protocol for tools across agents and harnesses. org-memory planned recall through MCP. That's a spec, not built.
followUps.remember: One protocol for tools. org-memory is a spec.

checks: Confirm whether a failing DeepEval score ever blocked a release at Fresh Tracks or AML SoftServe. The resume says scored, not gated.

answer.label: Prepared answer

I then spent about five years at EY, finishing as Senior Manager, Engineering. Since 2025 I've designed and shipped AI systems for clients in regulated domains as an AI systems architect, in travel, compliance and now environmental consulting, where I'm delivering 7 contracted deliveries covering 307 pages. I'm looking for a full-time, permanent role doing that work.
