questions.question: Function calling and tool use in LLMs

answer.label: What it is
answer.text: I give the model a list of tools, each with a name and a schema. The model replies with a tool name and arguments. My code runs the tool and returns the result.

answer.label: What I think
answer.text: The model proposes. My code decides. I validate every argument and I keep dangerous tools behind a check.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: I've built guardrails around an agent's tool calls: hooks that block certain calls. At Fresh Tracks I shipped LangGraph payment agents on Bedrock. I need to confirm whether they used model-facing tool schemas.

questions.remember: The model proposes the call. My code validates and runs it.
questions.steer: Move to the hooks that block the agent from running tests against dev RDS and from changing staging data.
questions.trap: The Fresh Tracks agents act through tools: they send payment requests and mails, issue refunds and adjust payment terms (stated 2026-10-22). MITCON has no model-driven tool choice. Its pipeline calls code tool steps (AutoCAD and Excel readers, AutoCAD to KML, SQL queries), so never say the model chooses them there.

followUps.question: How do you stop a model calling a tool with bad arguments?
followUps.answer: Validate against the schema before running anything. Reject and return the error to the model so it can correct itself. Never pass model output straight into a shell or a query.
followUps.remember: Validate first. Return the error to the model.

followUps.question: How do you limit the damage of a wrong tool call?
followUps.answer: Give tools the least access they need, make destructive ones need a human approval, and block the worst ones in code. That is the reason for the staging hook.
followUps.remember: Least access, approvals, hard blocks.

questions.whatItIs: Function calling lets a model request that your code run a named function with structured arguments, instead of only producing text. The model never runs anything itself. It returns a tool name and a JSON arguments object that matches a schema you supplied. Your code runs the function, then sends the result back for the model to continue. Most agent frameworks sit on this loop.
questions.opinion: Tool use is what turns a language model into an agent. It also moves the risk. The text a model writes is only an opinion, but a tool call changes things. So I keep the tool list short, validate the arguments against the schema, and put hard blocks on the dangerous tools. A block in code is stronger than an instruction in a prompt.
questions.cvConnection: The shipped case is the Fresh Tracks multi-agent payment system on LangGraph and AWS Bedrock. Deterministic code computes every amount. Agents read payment history, decide the next action and write the mail. The agents act through tools: they send payment requests and mails, issue refunds and adjust payment terms. Separately, the PreToolUse hooks at Fresh Tracks block an AI coding agent from running pytest against dev RDS and from changing data under the staging profile. That is governance of my own delivery tooling. MITCON uses structured output under a grounding contract. Its pipeline also runs code tool steps (AutoCAD and Excel readers, AutoCAD to KML, SQL queries) that the workflow calls in code, so the model does not choose them and it is not model-driven tool calling. stated 2026-10-21.
questions.example: How it works in principle: a PreToolUse hook inspects the tool call before it runs. If the command targets the staging profile or starts pytest, the hook rejects it and tells the agent why. The agent cannot talk its way past it.
questions.ifAskedUsed: Yes. At Fresh Tracks the payment agents act through tools for payment requests, mails, refunds and changes to payment terms. Code still computes every amount. I also wrote hooks that block an AI coding agent's risky tool calls.
questions.simple: The model asks for a tool by name with arguments. My code checks them, runs the tool and returns the result. The model never runs anything itself.

questions.question: MCP (Model Context Protocol)

answer.label: What it is
answer.text: MCP is an open protocol. A server exposes tools, resources and prompts. Any MCP client, such as Claude Code, can connect to it and use them.

answer.label: What I think
answer.text: It is a good standard for connecting an agent to many systems. The real work is still permissions, provenance and what the agent may do.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: I use MCP connectors for Jira, Linear, Outlook and Google Drive in my own Claude delivery workflow, not in a shipped product. I've also designed with it: the org-memory spec is locked and recalls knowledge via MCP, with no code yet. I have not built an MCP server.

questions.remember: MCP is the plug. Permissions and provenance are still my job. I have specified it, not shipped it.
questions.steer: Move to what org-memory governs: provenance-tracked knowledge, so recall can be trusted.
questions.trap: org-memory is a locked spec with no code. Don't say I built or shipped an MCP server, or that any deployed system has an MCP connector.

followUps.question: What are the security risks of MCP?
followUps.answer: A server can expose too much data, and a tool description can carry instructions that steer the agent. I would review each server, grant the least access, keep a human approval on risky actions and log every call.
followUps.remember: Treat each server as an access decision.

followUps.question: When would you build an MCP server instead of a direct API call?
followUps.answer: When several agents or clients need the same capability, so one server serves them all. For one agent calling one service, a direct tool is simpler.
followUps.remember: Many clients: a server. One client: a direct tool.

questions.whatItIs: The Model Context Protocol is an open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data. A server exposes capabilities in a common format. A client, such as an IDE assistant or a desktop app, discovers them and calls them. It replaces one custom integration per tool and per application with one protocol.
questions.opinion: It is useful, because I write the integration once and many clients can use it. It is also another route for data to leave a system and for an agent to act. I treat each server as an access decision: who authorises it, what it can read, and what it can change. The protocol helps with the plumbing, not with that judgement.
questions.cvConnection: It is not in shipped work. I specified org-memory, which turns coding-agent sessions into a governed, provenance-tracked knowledge base that agents recall through MCP. The spec is locked and no code exists. In my own Claude delivery workflow I use MCP connectors for Jira, Linear, Outlook and Google Drive. That is the delivery process, not a shipped product. No deployed system of mine has an MCP connector. stated 2026-10-21.
questions.example: Illustration from the spec: a coding agent asks the memory server for what the team already decided about a service. The answer comes back with its source, so the agent and the human can both see where the claim came from.
questions.ifAskedUsed: I use MCP connectors for Jira, Linear, Outlook and Google Drive in my own Claude delivery workflow. I designed with MCP too: org-memory is a locked spec with no code. No deployed system of mine has an MCP connector and I have not built an MCP server, and I say so.
checks: Stated 2026-10-21: the MCP connectors in your delivery workflow are Jira, Linear, Outlook and Google Drive. Do not name any other.
questions.simple: MCP is a standard way to connect an AI application to tools and data. A server exposes them and any compatible client can use them. It replaces one custom integration per tool.

questions.question: Agentic AI frameworks (LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen, Google ADK)

answer.label: What it is
answer.text: These frameworks give you the plumbing for agents: state, tool loops, memory, retries and multi-agent patterns. They differ in how much control they give you.

answer.label: What I think
answer.text: For anything consequential I want explicit control of state, checkpoints and human approval. That is why I use LangGraph. I judge any framework on those three things.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: LangGraph. At Fresh Tracks I shipped a multi-agent payment system on LangGraph and AWS Bedrock. techcirkle-agents is a deployed LangGraph prototype with human-in-the-loop interrupts and Postgres checkpointing. I haven't built with CrewAI, AutoGen or ADK.

questions.remember: LangGraph built. CrewAI, AutoGen and ADK understood. Judge on state, checkpoints, approvals.
questions.steer: Describe the Fresh Tracks split: deterministic code for amounts, agents for the next action and the mail. Then the human-in-the-loop interrupt and Postgres checkpoint on techcirkle-agents.
questions.trap: LangGraph only. Don't claim CrewAI, AutoGen or ADK. Don't name an agent framework for AML SoftServe, because I don't remember it. MITCON is a deterministic pipeline with no agent framework.

followUps.question: Why a graph and not a simple loop?
followUps.answer: A loop hides state. A graph names each step and each transition. So I can checkpoint, pause for approval, test a single node and see exactly where a run went wrong.
followUps.remember: A graph makes state and failure points visible.

followUps.question: When is a multi-agent design worth it?
followUps.answer: When the sub-tasks need different tools, context or permissions, and a single agent's context becomes unmanageable. At Fresh Tracks separate agents handled payment requests, overdue reminders, nightly reconciliation, invoices and per-country tax. Otherwise one agent with good tools is simpler, cheaper and easier to evaluate.
followUps.remember: Only when sub-tasks need separate context or permissions.

questions.whatItIs: Agent frameworks structure a loop in which a model decides, calls tools and updates state. LangGraph models that loop as a graph with explicit state, checkpointing and interrupts. CrewAI organises role-based agents into a crew. AutoGen centres on conversations between agents, and Microsoft has since folded that work into Microsoft Agent Framework. Google's ADK is Google's framework for building and deploying agents.
questions.opinion: I prefer the frameworks that make state visible. An agent in a regulated or customer-facing setting needs to pause for approval, survive a restart and show what it did. Role-play frameworks are quicker to demo, but I trust a graph more when a wrong step has a cost.
questions.cvConnection: Fresh Tracks is the shipped case. I built a multi-agent payment system on LangGraph and AWS Bedrock. Deterministic code computes every amount. Agents read each itinerary's payment history, decide the next action and write every mail in the brand voice. It is traced in LangSmith, with DeepEval and Guardrails AI around it. techcirkle-agents is a working, deployed prototype: a LangGraph 0.6 service on FastAPI that exposes the software delivery lifecycle as callable agents over server-sent events. It has human-in-the-loop interrupts and Postgres checkpointing, and it runs on Railway.
questions.example: How it works in principle: a LangGraph run reaches a decision point and raises an interrupt. The graph state is saved to Postgres. A person approves, and the run resumes from the saved checkpoint, even after a restart.
questions.ifAskedUsed: LangGraph, yes. At Fresh Tracks it runs the payment agents, and techcirkle-agents is a deployed prototype with interrupts and Postgres checkpointing. CrewAI, AutoGen and ADK I know from reading, and I haven't shipped with them.
checks: The Fresh Tracks agents are your own account, and the repo survey did not cover that code. Prepare the graph shape: which agents, what state, and how a run is checkpointed.
Confirm techcirkle-agents is deployed in the sense you will claim (the portfolio says "working prototype, deployed").
questions.simple: An agent framework runs a loop in which a model decides, calls tools and updates state. I prefer the ones that make state visible, so a run can pause, resume and be inspected.

questions.question: Open-weight LLMs (Llama, Mistral, Qwen)

answer.label: What it is
answer.text: The model weights are published, so a customer can run the model in their own environment. The licence terms vary.

answer.label: What I think
answer.text: They matter when data cannot leave the customer, or when volume makes a hosted API too expensive. Otherwise hosting costs and quality gaps often outweigh the benefit.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: No evidence yet. I understand the trade-offs. I haven't self-hosted a model in delivery work.

questions.remember: Open weights buy control. They cost operations. I understand them, I haven't run them.
questions.steer: Move to how I choose a model: the smallest one that passes the evaluation, behind one interface.
questions.trap: Don't claim self-hosting, fine-tuning or benchmarking open-weight models. There is no evidence of it.

followUps.question: How would you serve one in production?
followUps.answer: On GPU instances with an inference server such as vLLM, behind the same interface the application already uses. I would load-test it and compare quality and cost against the hosted model on the same evaluation set. I haven't done this.
followUps.remember: GPU, an inference server, the same interface, same evaluation.

followUps.question: What if a customer asks for one because of privacy?
followUps.answer: I would first ask what the privacy requirement really is. A hosted model inside their cloud account may meet it. If not, open weights are the answer, and I would plan the operating cost with them.
followUps.remember: Ask what the privacy rule really requires.

questions.whatItIs: An open-weight model has downloadable weights that you can run on your own hardware or cloud account. Llama, Mistral and Qwen are examples. Open-weight is not the same as open source, because the licence may restrict use and the training data is rarely published. You can also fine-tune them if the licence allows.
questions.opinion: The reasons to choose one are data that cannot leave the customer's network, predictable cost at high volume, and the ability to customise. The costs are GPUs, serving software, upgrades and often a quality gap on hard tasks. For most engagements I start with a hosted model and revisit only if a constraint forces it.
questions.cvConnection: It is not in my shipped work. MITCON uses hosted models through OpenRouter. A lightweight decision model narrows each document, and Gemini Flash-Lite extracts under a grounding contract.
questions.ifAskedUsed: No, I haven't run an open-weight model in a delivery. I understand when they fit, and I would prove it with an evaluation on the customer's own data before recommending one.

noEvidence.note: No evidence yet of running or evaluating an open-weight model.
prepare: Run one open-weight model locally (for example through Ollama) on a task from your own work, and note quality, speed and what broke.
Prepare a sentence on licence differences between Llama, Mistral and Qwen.

questions.simple: An open-weight model has downloadable weights you can run yourself. That gives control over data and cost. It is not always open source, because the licence may limit use.

questions.question: Reasoning models

answer.label: What it is
answer.text: The model spends extra tokens thinking before it answers. It does better on multi-step problems and costs more and takes longer.

answer.label: What I think
answer.text: I use them for hard, multi-step decisions and skip them for extraction and routing, where a small fast model is enough.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: Yes, in one place. At AML SoftServe the in-house reranker ran on o4-mini, a reasoning model. For anything else I'd judge a reasoning model with an evaluation first.

questions.remember: Reasoning models trade cost and latency for multi-step accuracy. I used o4-mini as the AML reranker. Prove any other use on an evaluation.
questions.steer: Move to the evaluation set: any model choice, reasoning or not, is decided by the data.
questions.trap: Don't claim I run reasoning models for extraction or authoring. The o4-mini use is the AML SoftServe reranker only. Don't treat longer thinking as proof of a correct answer. Prepare the latency and cost per event.

followUps.question: Would a reasoning model have helped on MITCON extraction?
followUps.answer: Probably not for pulling stated values out of a document. The risk there is inventing a value, which a grounding contract and a citation check control. I would test a reasoning model on the ambiguous cases only.
followUps.remember: Grounding beats thinking for extraction.

followUps.question: How do you control the cost of a reasoning model?
followUps.answer: Cap the thinking budget, route only the hard steps to it, cache where I can and measure cost per outcome.
followUps.remember: Cap, route, cache, measure.

questions.whatItIs: A reasoning model is trained to produce a chain of intermediate reasoning before its final answer. Examples include OpenAI's o-series and Claude with extended thinking. It spends more compute at answer time instead of only at training time. The reasoning may be hidden or summarised, and you pay for the tokens either way. Many current models fold this into the main model and expose it as a setting.
questions.opinion: They are strong on maths, planning and multi-step analysis, and weak value for simple tasks. For a task like pulling a value out of a document, extra thinking adds cost and delay without helping. The grounding contract matters more than the model. I would choose one per step, not per product.
questions.cvConnection: One case is shipped. At AML SoftServe the in-house LLM reranker ran on o4-mini, a reasoning model, in the agentic RAG over AUSTRAC documents. MITCON extraction is different: a lightweight decision model narrows each document and Gemini Flash-Lite extracts under a grounding contract. I use reasoning models in my own coding workflow, which is not shipped customer work.
questions.ifAskedUsed: Yes, in one place: the o4-mini reranker at AML SoftServe. For anything else I understand when they help, and I would test one against a smaller model on the customer's data before paying for it.

noEvidence.note: Evidence covers the o4-mini reranker only. No evidence yet of a comparison between a reasoning model and a smaller model on the same task.
prepare: Prepare the latency and cost per event for the o4-mini reranker, and why an LLM reranker beat a cross-encoder.
Pick one hard task from your work, run it on a reasoning model and a small model, and note the difference in quality, cost and time.

checks: "I use reasoning models in my own coding workflow" is our inference. Confirm it before saying it. The reason an LLM reranker beat a cross-encoder is also our inference, so confirm it too.
questions.simple: A reasoning model thinks through intermediate steps before it answers. It does better on multi-step problems and costs more and runs slower. I use it only where that trade pays off.

questions.question: AI governance and responsible AI

answer.label: What it is
answer.text: Governance is the rules, controls and records that keep an AI system safe, accountable and defensible. In a regulated setting it means grounding, human review and an audit trail.

answer.label: What I think
answer.text: I design for the failure I cannot undo. A gap on screen can be fixed. An invented number in a signed document cannot.

answer.label: Where I've built it
answer.text: The MITCON grounding contract and its hand-written gates. Clause-cited findings and Guardrails AI on AML SoftServe. Money computed only in deterministic code at Fresh Tracks. Hooks that block my own agent. Per-cohort cost budgets on ai-gym.

questions.remember: Ground it, gate it, record it. A gap is recoverable. An invented number is not.
questions.steer: Quote the comment above the MITCON contract: a gap on screen is recoverable and an invented number in a signed document is not.
questions.trap: Don't claim a formal compliance certification or an AI-governance framework adoption. I built controls, and I haven't claimed a certification.

followUps.question: How do you make a human-in-the-loop step real?
followUps.answer: Put it at the gate where a wrong output has a cost. Give the reviewer the evidence next to the claim. Make the system unable to proceed without the approval. At MITCON the expert checkpoints sit at every gate.
followUps.remember: Real approval blocks progress and shows evidence.

followUps.question: How do you keep an AI system auditable years later?
followUps.answer: Freeze the inputs and rules that produced a decision. On softserve360 the questionnaire snapshot is immutable, so scoring and the generated programme can be reproduced when a regulator asks.
followUps.remember: Snapshot the inputs, keep the rules versioned.

questions.whatItIs: AI governance covers who may build and deploy a system and what data it may use. It also covers how its output is checked, who is accountable and how decisions can be reviewed later. Responsible AI covers fairness, transparency, privacy and safety. In practice it becomes concrete controls: grounding, citations, human approval, access boundaries, evaluation gates and audit trails.
questions.opinion: Governance works when it lives in the design and the code. A policy document nobody can check does not help. I want the control to run on every call. Examples are a contract the extractor must obey, an approval step in the graph and a database rule that stops cross-tenant reads.
questions.cvConnection: It is in shipped work. On MITCON the extraction contract proposes a value only when the document states it and quotes the exact sheet and cell. Hand-written gates reject an invented citation, because the citation must be found in the source text. At AML SoftServe every finding cites its source clause, Guardrails AI blocks ungrounded output, and the questionnaire freezes into an immutable snapshot with tenant isolation in row-level security. At Fresh Tracks deterministic code computes every amount, so no LLM computes money, and Guardrails AI checks the mail. fde-os tags every claim as stated, artefact or ours.
questions.example: Illustration of the contract, not a recorded case: a value in a spreadsheet is ambiguous between two cells. The extractor proposes both with their sheet and cell references. A named expert picks one at a checkpoint. Nothing ungrounded reaches the signed document.
questions.ifAskedUsed: Yes. The MITCON grounding contract is the clearest case. AML SoftServe is the regulated-domain case: clause-cited findings, Guardrails AI, snapshot-bound scoring and row-level security. Fresh Tracks applies the same idea to payments.
checks: "Audit-first" came from the retired CV. Use "every finding traceable to its source clause", which the default resume says.
questions.simple: AI governance is the set of controls that decide who builds a system, what it can see and how its output is checked. It only works when the controls run in the code on every call.

questions.question: AI coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Kiro)

answer.label: What it is
answer.text: Coding agents read a codebase, plan a change, edit files, run commands and open a pull request. The quality depends on the context and the guardrails you give them.

answer.label: What I think
answer.text: The model matters less than the harness around it: context files, skills, hooks and a review gate. A small team with a good harness ships much faster.

answer.label: Where I've built it
answer.text: Five Claude Code skills with pre-execution guardrails, a verified-service-graph CLAUDE.md, a ROUTER.md and blocking hooks at Fresh Tracks. A team skill library, tc-skills, with 16 SDLC and 8 productivity skills. I work with People Equation's fde plugin. At TekMindz I introduced an AI-enabled delivery method and an LLM-maintained project wiki on every project. Sprint velocity rose 40 to 50% on the pilot project.

questions.remember: The harness beats the model: context, skills, hooks, review.
questions.steer: Lead with the hook that blocks the agent from changing staging data: a guardrail I designed against my own tooling.
questions.trap: Don't claim a measured speed-up beyond the quotable figure: sprint velocity up 40 to 50% on the TekMindz pilot project. Don't call the project wiki a "Memory Bank" or an "organisation brain". Don't confuse the AI in my delivery process with the AI in a shipped product. Never say "instead of talking about tools". Name the tools first, then the method.

followUps.question: How do you stop an agent making a destructive change?
followUps.answer: Block it in a hook, not in a prompt. The hook inspects the tool call and rejects it. The model can ignore a prompt, but it can't bypass a hook.
followUps.remember: Hooks block. Prompts only ask.

followUps.question: How do you keep a context file from going stale?
followUps.answer: Keep it short, verify the claims in it, and update it in the same change that alters the thing it describes. The Fresh Tracks CLAUDE.md carried a verified service graph for this reason.
followUps.remember: Short, verified, updated with the change.

followUps.question: How do you measure the benefit?
followUps.answer: I quote the resume figure only: sprint velocity up 40 to 50% on the TekMindz pilot project, after the AI-enabled delivery method rolled out. I describe how I measured it only if I can.
followUps.remember: Quote the stated figures, nothing newer.

followUps.question: Which AI tools do you use daily, for which use cases, and where have you seen a difference?
followUps.answer: I use Claude Code daily, with Cursor and Codex at times. My team skill library, tc-skills, has 16 SDLC and 8 productivity skills and works in Claude and Cursor. PreToolUse hooks block the agent from unsafe commands. I work with People Equation's fde plugin, which carries the method across engagements. The method is: context in files, steps as skills, hooks as hard blocks and a person in review. The difference comes from the skills and the hooks.
followUps.remember: Tools first, then skills, hooks, review.
followUps.trap: Never say "instead of talking about tools".

questions.whatItIs: AI coding agents work inside a repository. They read code, make a plan, edit files, run tests and commands, and propose changes for review. Claude Code runs in the terminal. Cursor and Kiro are editor-based. They use context files and tool permissions to know how a project works and what they may touch.
questions.opinion: The tool changes every few months, so I invest in what carries over. That is a short context file that is true, a router from task to files, and skills for repeatable steps. It is also hooks that block dangerous actions and a human review gate. Without those, an agent produces plausible changes that nobody can trust.
questions.cvConnection: It is the strongest area in my shipped work, and it describes how I deliver, not what a product does. At Fresh Tracks I authored five Claude Code skills with pre-execution guardrails, and a CLAUDE.md with a verified service graph. I also wrote per-repo bibles, a ROUTER.md, a RUNBOOK, ADRs and blocking hooks. tc-skills is a shipped internal library for Claude and Cursor. At TekMindz I led AI adoption across delivery and operations. I introduced an AI-enabled development method and a repeatable way to stand up an LLM-maintained project wiki on every project, which gives engineers and their coding assistants shared context. Sprint velocity rose 40 to 50% on the pilot project.
questions.example: Illustration of the setup, not a recorded session: a ticket keyword goes through ROUTER.md, which names the starting files. The skill /start-ticket loads that context. When the agent tries to run pytest against dev RDS, the PreToolUse hook blocks it.
questions.ifAskedUsed: Yes. It is the area I can show most evidence for. At Fresh Tracks that is skills, a context file, a router and blocking hooks. At TekMindz it is the project wiki and the AI-enabled delivery method.
checks: The 40 to 50% figure is on the resume. If an interviewer asks how it was measured, you need an answer.
Say "People Equation's fde plugin", not "I built the fde method". Confirm your part in it before you describe it.
Daily use of Claude Code, and Cursor and Codex at times, is your account on the 4 November call. Codex appears in no file. Confirm before you name it.
questions.simple: A coding agent reads a repository, edits files and runs commands. The model matters less than the context, skills, hooks and review gate around it.

tabs.title: Cloud
tabs.purpose: Practitioner-level cloud, AWS first, with honest answers on Azure and GCP.

questions.question: How do you deploy AI services on AWS using containers?
questions.simple: You package the service as a container image and run it on a managed container service. On AWS that is usually ECS on Fargate, so there are no servers to patch. A schedule or a queue starts the tasks. Each task gets its own IAM role and its own logs.

answer.label: The shape
answer.text: I package the service as a Docker image and run it on ECS with Fargate. A long-running API runs as a service behind a load balancer. A batch or scheduled job runs as a task that starts, finishes and stops.

answer.label: What starts it
answer.text: At Fresh Tracks an EventBridge schedule started Fargate tasks for the availability sweeps. Nothing sat idle between sweeps.

answer.label: How it hands off
answer.text: The task wrote its results to SQS. A consumer in the main Django app read the queue and saved to Postgres. The read path never waited on a task.

answer.label: What I would check before calling it done
answer.text: A task role with only the permissions it needs. Secrets from a secrets store, never baked into the image. Logs going to CloudWatch. A CPU and memory size taken from a measured run. An image tag pinned per release.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: Fargate, EventBridge and SQS on Fresh Tracks. Those tasks ran Playwright scrapes. They did not run model inference, and I won't say they did. The payment agents on Bedrock are a separate system.

questions.remember: Image in, Fargate task out, EventBridge to start it, SQS to hand off.
questions.steer: Move to the Trip Availability Assistant: four sources behind one adapter model, and a read path that never blocks on a scrape.
questions.trap: Don't say I ran model inference on Fargate. The Fargate tasks ran Playwright scrapes. Don't place the payment agents on Fargate unless you have confirmed where they ran.

followUps.question: Why Fargate and not Lambda for those sweeps?
followUps.answer: A browser scrape needs a full browser, more memory and a longer run than a function suits. Lambda caps a run at 15 minutes. A container task has no such cap and I control the image. For short event handlers Lambda would still be my first choice.
followUps.remember: Browser plus long run means a container task.

followUps.question: How would you run a model that needs a GPU?
followUps.answer: Fargate has no GPU. I would use ECS on GPU EC2 instances, a SageMaker endpoint or Bedrock, which I used at Fresh Tracks for the payment agents. I haven't self-hosted a model in production. I would start with a hosted API and move only if cost or data residency forced it.
followUps.remember: No GPU on Fargate. Hosted API first.

followUps.question: How do you scale it?
followUps.answer: A Fargate service scales on CPU, memory or queue depth. A scheduled sweep scales by how many tasks the schedule starts. On Fresh Tracks the scale came from the schedule: a daily sweep for one source and a more frequent sweep for another.
followUps.remember: Services scale on load. Sweeps scale on schedule.

checks: The portfolio shows the Fresh Tracks Fargate, EventBridge and SQS architecture under your flagship work. Confirm which parts you configured yourself (task definitions, IAM, schedules) and which a colleague owned, so "I" is accurate.

questions.question: What are EventBridge and Step Functions?
questions.simple: EventBridge routes events and runs schedules. It starts things when a rule matches or a clock fires. Step Functions runs a multi-step workflow as a state machine, with retries, branching and waiting built in. One starts work. The other coordinates it.

answer.label: EventBridge
answer.text: It is an event bus plus a scheduler. Services publish events, rules match them and send them to targets such as a Fargate task, a Lambda function or a queue. The scheduler runs cron and one-off jobs.

answer.label: Step Functions
answer.text: It models a workflow as a state machine. Each step is a task, a choice, a wait or a parallel branch. It handles retries, timeouts and error paths, and it keeps the execution history.

answer.label: How they fit together
answer.text: EventBridge starts the work and Step Functions coordinates the steps when there are several. For one step with a retry, a queue and a consumer is often enough.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: EventBridge only. At Fresh Tracks an EventBridge cron started the Fargate availability sweeps. No evidence yet for Step Functions: I have not built on it, so on that half I explain the concept and say so.

questions.remember: EventBridge starts it. Step Functions coordinates it. I have built the first.
questions.steer: Describe the cron to Fargate to SQS chain, then say the read path never waited on it.
questions.trap: Don't claim Step Functions experience. The evidence covers EventBridge only.

followUps.question: When would you choose Step Functions over a queue and a worker?
followUps.answer: When the process has several steps with different failure handling, long waits or human approval. A state machine shows each step and its history. For a single step with a retry, a queue and a worker is simpler and cheaper.
followUps.remember: Many steps, long waits, approvals: Step Functions. One step: a queue.

followUps.question: How does that compare with LangGraph?
followUps.answer: Both are state machines. Step Functions orchestrates AWS services and is language-neutral. LangGraph orchestrates an agent's steps in Python with checkpointing and human-in-the-loop interrupts. I have used LangGraph, and I would reach for Step Functions around it, not instead of it.
followUps.remember: Step Functions for services. LangGraph for agent steps.

noEvidence.note: No evidence yet for Step Functions. The portfolio shows EventBridge only.
prepare: Build or sketch a small Step Functions workflow (a retry, a choice and a wait) so the concept answer has a concrete example.
Be ready to say plainly that you used EventBridge and not Step Functions.

questions.question: What is SNS and how does it differ from SQS?
questions.simple: SNS is publish and subscribe. One message goes to every subscriber at once. SQS is a queue. Each message is read and processed by one consumer. SNS pushes. SQS holds messages until a consumer pulls them.

answer.label: SNS
answer.text: A topic with many subscribers. I publish once and SNS delivers a copy to each subscriber: queues, functions, HTTP endpoints, email. It is for fan-out.

answer.label: SQS
answer.text: A queue. Producers add messages, consumers pull them and delete them after processing. It buffers load and lets the consumer work at its own pace.

answer.label: Together
answer.text: The common pattern is SNS fanning out to several SQS queues. Each team or service gets its own queue and its own retry behaviour.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: SQS only. At Fresh Tracks the Fargate sweeps wrote to SQS and a consumer in the main app saved the results. I haven't built an SNS fan-out.

questions.remember: SNS pushes to many. SQS holds for one. I have used SQS.
questions.steer: Use the sweep-to-queue-to-consumer chain to show why a buffer keeps the read path fast.
questions.trap: Don't describe an SNS design as something I shipped. I used SQS.

followUps.question: Why put a queue between the scraper and the app?
followUps.answer: The scrape is slow and can fail. The app must stay fast. The queue decouples them, so a slow or failed scrape never blocks a read. The consumer processes at its own pace and the queue absorbs bursts.
followUps.remember: The queue decouples slow work from the fast read path.

followUps.question: Standard or FIFO queue?
followUps.answer: Standard gives high throughput with at-least-once delivery and no strict order. FIFO gives order and deduplication at lower throughput. For sweep results where each message is a full snapshot, standard with an idempotent consumer is enough. I would say that as a design choice and check it against the real queue type.
followUps.remember: Standard plus an idempotent consumer, unless order matters.

checks: Confirm the Fresh Tracks queue was a standard queue before you say so in an interview.

questions.question: How do you handle failed messages in your queues?
questions.simple: A message that fails should be retried a limited number of times, then moved aside to a dead-letter queue so it stops blocking the rest. Someone then looks at it and replays it. The consumer must be idempotent, because the same message can arrive twice.

answer.label: Retry first
answer.text: A failed message returns to the queue when its visibility timeout ends, and the consumer tries again. I limit the attempts. Transient errors such as a timeout usually pass on the second try.

answer.label: Then a dead-letter queue
answer.text: After a set number of receives, the queue moves the message to a dead-letter queue. A poison message then stops blocking healthy ones.

answer.label: Make the consumer idempotent
answer.text: SQS delivers at least once. The same message can arrive twice, so processing it twice must give the same result.

answer.label: Make failures visible
answer.text: I alarm on dead-letter queue depth and keep enough context to replay a message after the fix.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: I used SQS at Fresh Tracks and kept a run log of every sweep. No evidence yet for a dead-letter queue configuration, so I describe this as the approach I would take.

questions.remember: Limited retries, dead-letter queue, idempotent consumer, alarm on depth.
questions.steer: Bring it back to the run log and the rule that a run passes only if every valid config passes.
questions.trap: Don't say I configured a dead-letter queue unless I confirm it. The evidence shows SQS and a run log, not the redrive policy.

followUps.question: How do you make a consumer idempotent?
followUps.answer: Give each message a stable key, such as the supplier, config and sweep time. Before writing, check whether that key was already processed, or write with an upsert on a unique constraint. A repeat then changes nothing.
followUps.remember: Stable key plus upsert.

followUps.question: How do you replay messages from the dead-letter queue?
followUps.answer: Fix the cause first. Then redrive the messages back to the source queue, in small batches, and watch the error rate. Replaying before the fix only fills the dead-letter queue again.
followUps.remember: Fix, then redrive in small batches.

noEvidence.note: No evidence yet for a dead-letter queue or a redrive policy on the Fresh Tracks queues.
prepare: Check the Fresh Tracks queue setup (or ask the team) for a dead-letter queue and a max-receive count. If one exists, add it as evidence.
Prepare one real example of a failed sweep, from the AdapterRunLog or ScrapeRun history, and what you did about it.

questions.question: What is AWS Bedrock and how does it compare to calling a model provider directly?
questions.simple: Bedrock is AWS's managed service for foundation models from several providers behind one API. You pay through AWS, use IAM for access and keep traffic inside your AWS account boundary. Calling a provider directly gives you the newest features first and fewer layers.

answer.label: What Bedrock is
answer.text: A managed API for models from several vendors. Access goes through IAM. Billing sits on the AWS invoice. It offers extras such as guardrails and knowledge bases.

answer.label: Why a customer picks it
answer.text: Their data stays in their AWS account and region, their security team already trusts the controls, and procurement is one contract. For regulated customers that often decides it.

answer.label: Why I might call the provider directly
answer.text: New features and models often reach the provider's own API first. There is one fewer layer to debug. Some features are not available through every route.

answer.label: How I decide
answer.text: I ask where the data may go, which models are needed, who pays and who signs off. Then I keep the model call behind one interface so the route can change.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: Yes, in shipped work. The Fresh Tracks multi-agent payment system on LangGraph used models on AWS Bedrock. I keep to that level and don't go into model choice, quotas or throughput until I've confirmed them.

questions.remember: Bedrock: AWS-side controls and one invoice. Direct: newest features, fewer layers.
questions.steer: Move to the MITCON model-route decisions: why Anthropic was dropped, and how extraction moved to Gemini through OpenRouter.
questions.trap: Describe the payment system, not Bedrock internals. Don't state which models, quotas or throughput Fresh Tracks used until you have confirmed them. Check a model is really on Bedrock before you name it.

followUps.question: What did you learn from switching providers on MITCON?
followUps.answer: At the time, Anthropic's document block accepted only PDF among binary files, so spreadsheet inputs returned a 400 before reaching the model. ADR-003 dropped Anthropic. Extraction first ran on gpt-4o-mini, then moved to Gemini after a golden-set spike on 110 uploads, all through OpenRouter. I filed the 400 reproduction as a session note. The lesson is to test each input type against the provider early.
followUps.remember: Test every input type against the provider early.

followUps.question: Does a managed route change your evaluation?
followUps.answer: No. I evaluate the same task with the same data on each route. A route change can still move quality, latency or refusals, so I rerun the evaluation before switching.
followUps.remember: Rerun the evaluation on every route change.

checks: The Fresh Tracks Bedrock work is your own account, and the repo survey did not cover that code. Be ready to say which models ran on Bedrock and why Bedrock was chosen.
Confidence stays at understand until you can describe the Bedrock work in detail. Raise it to built when you can.
The repo survey does not show Bedrock code at Fresh Tracks, so only your own account supports it.
The review's claim that Bedrock doesn't host Gemini or o4-mini is general knowledge and unverified. Check the current Bedrock model list before you say it.

questions.question: How do you handle IAM and access control?
questions.simple: IAM controls who and what can call which AWS actions. Give every workload its own role with only the permissions it needs. Prefer roles over long-lived keys. Keep application-level access control, such as user roles and tenant isolation, as a separate layer.

answer.label: Roles over keys
answer.text: Each workload runs under its own role, such as an ECS task role. No access keys sit in code or images. Credentials are short-lived and rotate on their own.

answer.label: Least privilege
answer.text: I start with no access and add the specific actions and resources the workload needs. Wildcards are the exception, and I review them.

answer.label: Separate the layers
answer.text: IAM protects the cloud resources. The application protects its users and tenants. I don't treat one as a substitute for the other.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: No evidence yet for AWS IAM policy work. At the application level, the Fresh Tracks platform used shared-cookie JWT access across its services. Row-level security was the tested tenant boundary on softserve360 and ai-gym. The psql policy tests I can show you are on ai-gym.

questions.remember: Roles not keys. Least privilege. Cloud IAM and app access are separate layers.
questions.steer: Move to row-level security as the tested boundary, and name the psql policy tests on ai-gym.
questions.trap: Don't present the application-level JWT and RLS work as AWS IAM experience.

followUps.question: How do you give a service access to a secret?
followUps.answer: The task role gets permission to read that one secret in Secrets Manager or Parameter Store. The service reads it at start-up. The secret never lives in the image or the repo.
followUps.remember: Role reads one secret. Nothing in the image.

followUps.question: How do you test an access boundary?
followUps.answer: I write tests that try to cross it. On ai-gym I had psql policy tests for row-level security, and RLS was the tested boundary on softserve360 too. They assert that one tenant cannot read another's rows. For IAM I would use the policy simulator and a deny-by-default review.
followUps.remember: Test the denial, not only the allow.

noEvidence.note: No evidence yet for AWS IAM policy work. The evidence covers application-level access only.
prepare: Write down one concrete IAM setup you can describe (a task role and its policy for the Fresh Tracks sweeps), if you configured one.
Know the difference between a task role and a task execution role.

checks: The portfolio lists shared-cookie JWT access across the Fresh Tracks services as a theme and does not say who built it. Confirm how much of it you wrote, and the service count, before you say "I built" or quote a number.
The portfolio theme line says RLS is tested on softserve360 and ai-gym, but only ai-gym records the psql policy tests. Confirm how the softserve360 tests were run before you describe them.

questions.question: How do you think about cloud costs for AI workloads?
questions.simple: For most AI workloads the model calls cost more than the servers. Cost scales with tokens in and out, so it depends on prompt size, retrieved context, model choice and call volume. You control it with budgets, smaller models where they are good enough, caching, and measuring cost per task.

answer.label: Where the money goes
answer.text: Model tokens first, then storage and compute for retrieval, then the usual hosting. A long retrieved context on every call multiplies the cost.

answer.label: Put a budget in the design
answer.text: I want a cost limit per tenant or cohort that the system enforces, not a figure someone checks monthly.

answer.label: Right-size the model
answer.text: Use the smallest model that passes the evaluation for that task. Keep the expensive one for the hard step.

answer.label: Measure cost per outcome
answer.text: Cost per document, per answer or per booking tells you more than the monthly bill.

answer.label: Where I've built it
answer.text: On ai-gym, Claude calls went through OpenRouter under per-cohort cost budgets. On MITCON, a lightweight decision model narrows each document before Gemini Flash-Lite extracts. On a 78-upload golden set, narrowing raised recall from about 61% to 68% and added no net cost per file. I chose Gemini for accuracy: on the same first stage its wrong values were 11.1% against 24.0% for gpt-4o-mini. At AML SoftServe the agent screened every onboarding and transaction, so cost per event is the number to have ready.

questions.remember: Tokens drive cost. Budget per tenant, smallest model that passes, cost per outcome.
questions.steer: Describe the per-cohort cost budget on ai-gym as the control, not the dashboard.
questions.trap: Don't say ai-gym is in production. Its production status is not stated. Don't say the MITCON model route was chosen for cost alone, or for accuracy alone. It was chosen for both: narrowing was the cost step and Gemini was the accuracy step. Anthropic was dropped for input format.

followUps.question: How would you cut the cost of a RAG system?
followUps.answer: Retrieve less but better: a re-ranker and a tighter top-k shrink the context. Cache repeated queries and embeddings. Route simple questions to a smaller model. Then measure quality on the evaluation set after each change.
followUps.remember: Smaller context, caching, routing, then re-measure quality.

followUps.question: What do you do when a customer's bill spikes?
followUps.answer: Find which tenant, task and prompt caused it, using per-call tracing. Then apply the budget limit and fix the prompt or the loop. Add an alert on cost per task so the next jump shows within a day.
followUps.remember: Trace to the call, cap it, alert on it.

checks: ai-gym has no stated production status. Describe the cost budgets as a design you built, not as a system with live spend.

questions.question: What is a VPC, and how would you deploy into a customer's private network?
questions.simple: A VPC is your own private network inside a cloud account. You split it into subnets, control traffic with route tables and security groups, and decide what reaches the internet. For a customer's private network you deploy into their VPC or connect to it privately, and you design for no public exposure.

answer.label: What a VPC is
answer.text: A logically isolated network. Public subnets can reach the internet. Private subnets cannot, except through a NAT gateway. Security groups act as per-resource firewalls.

answer.label: Reaching a customer's network
answer.text: I would ask which model they want: deploy into their account and VPC, or connect ours to theirs through a VPN, peering or PrivateLink. I prefer the one with the smallest exposed surface.

answer.label: What I would ask first
answer.text: Which data may leave their network, who owns the network team, how a change gets approved and which logs they require.

answer.label: Where I've used it
answer.text: No evidence yet. I haven't designed a VPC for a customer in my evidence. What I have is the discovery habit: name the security decision-maker and data owner early, which the fde-os charter does.

questions.remember: Private subnets, security groups, private connectivity, and ask who approves network changes.
questions.steer: Bring it back to discovery: the charter names the security decision-maker and the data owner before any build.
questions.trap: Don't invent a customer network story. If asked for one, say I haven't done it and describe what I would ask.

followUps.question: How does a private subnet reach an external API?
followUps.answer: Through a NAT gateway in a public subnet, or through a VPC endpoint when the service supports it. A VPC endpoint keeps the traffic off the public internet.
followUps.remember: NAT for the internet, endpoints for AWS services.

followUps.question: What if the customer won't let you into their network at all?
followUps.answer: Then the work happens on exported data in a controlled environment, or through a narrow API they expose. I would agree the data path in writing, as the charter records the data owner and security decision-maker.
followUps.remember: Agree the data path in writing before building.

noEvidence.note: No evidence yet for VPC design or deployment into a customer network.
prepare: Draw a simple VPC with public and private subnets, a NAT gateway and a security group, and practise explaining it in 60 seconds.
Check whether the Fresh Tracks RDS or Fargate setup sat in a VPC you configured, and if so add it as evidence.

questions.question: Tell me about your experience with Azure OpenAI and Microsoft Foundry
questions.simple: Azure OpenAI hosts OpenAI models inside Azure, with Azure's identity, networking and compliance controls. Microsoft Foundry is the wider workspace for building, evaluating and deploying AI apps on Azure. Customers who already run Microsoft 365 often choose it for those controls.

answer.label: The honest summary
answer.text: I have designed for Azure. I have not deployed on it.

answer.label: What I designed
answer.text: The sandvick-agents pre-sales architecture: a SharePoint RAG chatbot inside Microsoft Teams, on FastAPI and LangGraph, with pgvector and the Graph API on Azure. It is a design with no code.

answer.label: Why Azure suits that customer
answer.text: Their documents sit in SharePoint and their users sit in Teams, so I would expect their identity to sit in Entra ID too. Staying inside that estate keeps the access model and the audit trail they already trust.

answer.label: What I would learn first on a real project
answer.text: Which models their tenant has approved, regional availability, quotas and how content filtering behaves.

questions.remember: Azure: designed in sandvick-agents, never deployed.
questions.steer: Use the design to show I start from the customer's existing estate: SharePoint, Teams and identity.
questions.trap: sandvick-agents is design only, with no code. Don't call it built, deployed or shipped.

followUps.question: How would the chatbot respect SharePoint permissions?
followUps.answer: Retrieval must filter by what the asking user may already see. I would carry the user identity through to the Graph API and apply permission filters at retrieval, not after generation. This is design reasoning, since nothing was built.
followUps.remember: Filter at retrieval by the user's own permissions.

followUps.question: Azure OpenAI or the OpenAI API directly?
followUps.answer: If the customer needs their own tenant's controls, data residency and Entra ID access, Azure OpenAI. If they want the newest features first and have no such constraint, the OpenAI API. I keep the model call behind one interface so the route can change.
followUps.remember: Controls and residency: Azure. Newest features: direct.

checks: The portfolio says the design targets "Azure" without naming Azure OpenAI or Microsoft Foundry. Open the sandvick-agents design and confirm which Azure services it names before you say so.
Entra ID is our inference from the SharePoint and Teams design. The design evidence does not name it. Confirm before you say it.

questions.question: What do you know about GCP's AI services: Vertex AI, Gemini and ADK?
questions.simple: Vertex AI is Google Cloud's platform for models and ML workflows. Gemini is Google's model family, available through Vertex AI. ADK, the Agent Development Kit, is Google's open-source framework for building agents. I know Vertex AI and ADK as concepts. I have used Gemini through OpenRouter on MITCON.

answer.label: The honest summary
answer.text: No evidence yet of GCP or Vertex AI work. I haven't built on GCP. I have used Gemini through OpenRouter. What follows on Vertex AI and ADK is what I understand, not what I've shipped.

answer.label: Vertex AI
answer.text: Google's managed platform for model access, tuning, evaluation and deployment, with IAM and regional controls like the other clouds.

answer.label: Gemini
answer.text: Google's model family. I use Gemini Flash-Lite for extraction on MITCON, through OpenRouter and not Vertex AI. It is also known for very long context windows and strong multimodal input. I would test that against my own evaluation set before trusting it for a task.

answer.label: ADK
answer.text: An open-source framework for agents, in the same space as LangGraph. I know LangGraph from building with it, so I would judge ADK by how it handles state, checkpointing and human-in-the-loop.

questions.remember: GCP: understood, not built. Gemini used on MITCON through OpenRouter. LangGraph is the framework I have built with.
questions.steer: Move to what carries across: a clear model interface, an evaluation set and a checkpointed agent graph.
questions.trap: The Gemini NL to SQL feature in bms-fe-pms is a colleague's work. Don't claim it as mine. My own Gemini use is MITCON extraction through OpenRouter, not Vertex AI.

followUps.question: Have you used Gemini?
followUps.answer: Yes, on MITCON. Gemini Flash-Lite does the extraction through OpenRouter. On the same first stage it beat gpt-4o-mini, with 11.1% wrong values against 24.0%. Not through Vertex AI. A separate Gemini feature in a project I touched was a colleague's, and I don't claim it.
followUps.remember: Gemini yes, on MITCON. The NL to SQL feature is not mine.

followUps.question: How would you compare ADK and LangGraph?
followUps.answer: I would compare state handling, persistence, human-in-the-loop support, tracing and how easy it is to test a graph. I know the LangGraph answer from experience and the ADK answer only from reading.
followUps.remember: Compare state, persistence, interrupts, tracing.

noEvidence.note: No evidence yet for GCP, Vertex AI or ADK work of your own. Your Gemini use is through OpenRouter on MITCON only.
prepare: Read the Vertex AI and ADK documentation enough to explain what each does in one minute.
Prepare one sentence on Gemini that uses the MITCON spike numbers and does not claim the colleague's feature.

questions.question: If you had to choose between AWS, Azure, and GCP for an AI project, how would you decide?
questions.simple: Start from the customer, not the cloud. Use the cloud where their data, identity and approvals already sit. Then check model availability, region, cost and the team's skills. Keep the model call and the deployment portable so the choice is reversible.

answer.label: Start with the customer's estate
answer.text: Where does their data live? Which identity system do they use? Which cloud has their security team already approved? That usually decides it.

answer.label: Then the models
answer.text: Which models do I need, and are they available in their region and tenant? Quotas matter as much as availability.

answer.label: Then cost and skills
answer.text: Pricing, committed spend they already hold and what their team can operate after I leave.

answer.label: Keep it reversible
answer.text: Put the model call behind one interface and run on containers, so a move is weeks, not months.

answer.label: What I have run
answer.text: AWS at Fresh Tracks (Fargate, EventBridge, SQS, and Bedrock for the payment agents). Railway on AML SoftServe and techcirkle-agents. OpenRouter as the model gateway on AML SoftServe and MITCON. An Azure design for sandvick-agents. I have no GCP deployment.

questions.remember: Customer estate first, models second, cost and skills third, keep it reversible.
questions.steer: Frame the answer as a forward-deployed habit: fit the customer's estate rather than bring mine.
questions.trap: Don't pick a favourite cloud before asking about the customer. Don't imply I have run all three.

followUps.question: Is multi-cloud ever the right answer?
followUps.answer: Rarely by design. It doubles the operational load. It is right when a customer already spans clouds or a regulation demands it. Portability through containers and a clean model interface gives most of the benefit at a fraction of the cost.
followUps.remember: Portability yes, multi-cloud operation rarely.

followUps.question: Why did you use Railway on some projects?
followUps.answer: It is fast to deploy and fits a small team. softserve360 moved from Vercel to Railway, and techcirkle-agents runs on Railway. For a customer with enterprise controls, I would move to their cloud.
followUps.remember: Railway for speed and small teams. Their cloud for their controls.

checks: The reason for choosing Railway is our inference. The portfolio records where it was used, not why. Confirm the reason before you give it as yours.
Your account puts AML SoftServe on Railway, with Supabase for the database. Older CV versions said AWS, so be ready if an interviewer has one.

questions.question: Walk me through your deployment pipeline and how you manage environments
questions.simple: A pipeline takes a change from a pull request to production through checks you trust. Separate environments let you test safely. Feature flags and blue-green deploys let you release without downtime and roll back fast. The record of why a decision was made matters as much as the pipeline.

answer.label: The path
answer.text: A ticket becomes a branch. The change is checked, reviewed and merged through a pull request. At Fresh Tracks I authored skills for that path: /start-ticket, /ready-for-git and /post-pr.

answer.label: Environments
answer.text: Development, staging and production, each with its own data. I put guardrails where a mistake would be costly. A PreToolUse hook blocked the agent from running tests against dev RDS and from changing data under the staging profile.

answer.label: Safe releases
answer.text: A PostHog feature flag per supplier let us swap the BIM lookup for an Excel fallback when the client's data slipped. It was reversible and needed no code change. At Ernst & Young I ran Kubernetes blue-green deploys, with 99.9%+ uptime.

answer.label: Keeping the record true
answer.text: I kept a RUNBOOK, ADRs and a ROUTER.md that maps ticket keywords to starting files. On the FDE method, an engagement pins its plugin version so the process can't change mid-milestone.

answer.label: Quality gates
answer.text: SonarQube ran on the Fresh Tracks platform. I would describe exact gate thresholds only after checking them.

questions.remember: Ticket to skill to PR, guardrailed environments, flags and blue-green for releases, a runbook for the record.
questions.steer: Lead with the hook that blocks the agent from mutating staging data: a guardrail designed against my own tooling.
questions.trap: Don't describe a CI/CD tool stack I haven't confirmed. Don't imply the Ernst & Young blue-green work and the Fresh Tracks work overlapped in time.

followUps.question: How did you roll back a bad release?
followUps.answer: With a feature flag I switched the behaviour off without a deploy. With blue-green I switched traffic back to the previous version. Both are faster than rebuilding. I haven't got a specific incident in my evidence, so I would explain the mechanism and not a story.
followUps.remember: Flag off or traffic back. Faster than rebuilding.

followUps.question: Why guardrail your own agent?
followUps.answer: Because the agent acts with my permissions. Containers pointed at dev RDS, so a test run could change real data. A hook that blocks the call is stronger than a rule in a prompt, since the model can ignore a prompt.
followUps.remember: Block in a hook, not in a prompt.

followUps.question: How do you manage environment drift?
followUps.answer: Keep configuration in code, build one image and promote it through environments, and compare staging with production on a schedule. The ADRs record why an environment differs on purpose.
followUps.remember: One image, config in code, ADRs for deliberate differences.

checks: Confirm the CI tooling and any quality-gate thresholds at Fresh Tracks before you quote them. The portfolio names SonarQube but gives no thresholds.
The Ernst & Young blue-green figure (99.9%+ uptime) is from the quotable numbers table. Do not attach it to a date range beyond the profile career table.

tabs.title: Coding round
tabs.purpose: What to expect in a coding round, how to approach it and what to practise.

questions.question: Common coding tasks in AI and forward-deployed interviews
questions.simple: AI and forward-deployed coding rounds lean towards practical tasks: calling a model safely, parsing messy data and building a small service. Some companies still add a classic algorithm question.

blocks.heading: Practical AI tasks
items: Call an LLM API with retries, backoff and a timeout, and validate the JSON it returns against a schema.
Write a small agent loop: the model picks a tool, you run it, you feed back the result, with a step cap.
Build a tiny retrieval step: chunk text, score chunks by cosine similarity on given vectors, return the top k with sources.
Extract fields from a messy CSV or Excel file into a typed structure, and report rows you could not parse.

blocks.heading: Backend tasks
items: Add an endpoint that starts a long job and returns a job id, plus a status endpoint.
Make a handler idempotent so a retried message doesn't double-charge or double-write.
Write a SQL query with joins, grouping and a window function, then explain the index you'd add.

blocks.heading: Classic algorithm questions
blocks.text: Expect medium-level problems on hash maps, two pointers, intervals, BFS and DFS, and heaps.

blocks.heading: Forward-deployed twists
items: Debug or extend an unfamiliar repo in a short time.
A take-home that wants a small working service and a short write-up of trade-offs.
A customer-style prompt with vague requirements, to see whether you ask clarifying questions.

questions.remember: Expect practical tasks first, one classic algorithm question second.
checks: The degree-as-gap point is tagged ours in profile.md. It is why the classic algorithm block is here.

questions.question: How to approach a coding round
questions.simple: Interviewers mark how you think as much as whether the code runs. Clarify, say the plan, write the simple version, test it out loud, then improve it.

blocks.heading: The order
items: Restate the problem in one sentence and ask about inputs, sizes and edge cases.
Work one small example by hand.
Say the plan and its complexity before you type.
Write the simplest correct version first.
Test it out loud with a normal case, an empty case and an edge case.
Then improve it, and say what you're trading.

blocks.heading: Habits from my own work that help here
blocks.text: Name the failure path. In my extraction work a missing value stays a gap rather than a guess. In a coding round that means returning a clear error rather than a silent default.

scripts.say: Let me restate it to check I have it right.
scripts.effect: Buys a few seconds and catches a misread early.

scripts.say: I'll write the simple version first, then optimise.
scripts.effect: Shows judgement, and gets working code on screen.

scripts.say: This is O(n log n) because of the sort. I could get O(n) with a hash map at the cost of memory.
scripts.effect: Shows you know the trade-off without being asked.

scripts.say: I'm not sure of the exact library call. I'll write what I mean and we can check it.

blocks.heading: If you're stuck
blocks.text: Say what you know and what you're missing. Try a smaller case. Ask whether a brute-force version is acceptable as a first step.

questions.remember: Clarify, plan, simple version, test aloud, then improve.

questions.question: What to practise: Python, TypeScript, SQL, an LLM API call with retries, a small agent loop
questions.simple: Practise the tasks you will be asked, in the languages you used on the job. Practise some of them without a coding agent, because many interviews ban one.

blocks.heading: Why without the agent
blocks.text: Agentic coding tools are my daily driver, and many coding rounds forbid them. Practise a few drills by hand each week so typing syntax from memory feels normal again.

blocks.heading: Python drills
items: An LLM call with retries, exponential backoff with jitter, a timeout and schema validation with Pydantic.
A small agent loop with two tools, a step cap and a repeat-call guard.
Parse an Excel workbook with openpyxl and return each value with its sheet and cell.
A FastAPI or Django endpoint that queues a job and a status endpoint.

blocks.heading: TypeScript drills
items: A typed fetch wrapper with retries and a discriminated union for the result.
A small Next.js route handler that validates input with a schema.

blocks.heading: SQL drills
items: Joins with grouping, and a window function such as a running total or rank.
Read a query plan and say which index fixes it.
Write a row-level security policy and a query that proves it holds for another tenant.

blocks.heading: Algorithms
blocks.text: Do a short daily set of medium problems on hash maps, two pointers, intervals, graphs and heaps. This covers the CS-fundamentals probe a metallurgy degree invites.

questions.remember: Drill the real tasks, and some by hand without the agent.
checks: The point that coding without an agent may feel rusty is our inference from your CV line on agentic tools. Confirm it applies to you.

tabs.title: Tactics
tabs.purpose: How to deliver answers: pacing, unknown questions and saying exactly what you did.

questions.question: Pacing and timing

blocks.heading: Target lengths
items: Tell me about yourself: 60 seconds for HR, 90 seconds for a technical panel.
Behavioural STAR: about two minutes. Situation in one sentence.
Technical concept: 60 to 90 seconds, then stop and let them pick the follow-up.
System design: ask your clarifying questions in the first three minutes.

blocks.heading: Answer first
blocks.text: Give the answer in your first sentence, then the reason. If they want more, they will ask.

scripts.say: Shall I go deeper on the grounding contract, or move on?
scripts.effect: Hands control back and shows you're watching the clock.

scripts.say: The short version is this. I can expand on any part.
scripts.effect: Sets up a crisp answer and invites a targeted follow-up.

questions.question: Buying time and handling questions you can't answer

blocks.heading: Buying a few seconds
blocks.text: Repeat the question in your own words, or ask one clarifying question. Both are normal and both earn thinking time.

scripts.say: Let me make sure I have it. You're asking how I'd keep the agent from looping?
scripts.effect: Confirms scope and gives you five seconds.

scripts.say: Is this for a single tenant, or many?
scripts.effect: A real clarifying question that also buys time.

blocks.heading: When you don't know
blocks.text: Say so in one sentence. Then reason from what you do know, out loud. Never make up a project or a number to fill the gap.

scripts.say: I haven't used that in production. Here's how I'd approach it, based on what I built at MITCON.
scripts.effect: Honest, and moves to your evidence.

scripts.say: I'm not sure of the exact figure. I can tell you how I'd find it.

blocks.heading: Items marked "No evidence yet"
blocks.text: Some behavioural and HR items in this prep have no story yet. Prepare a real story for them, or use the honest script above.

blocks.heading: Answer the literal question first
blocks.text: Answer the question as asked in the first sentence. Then add the context. If asked for the difference between two things, give the difference before you talk about how you use them. If asked which tools, name the tools before the method.

scripts.say: The prompt is what I send. The context window is the model's whole limit. Now here is how I manage it.
scripts.effect: Answers the literal question, then adds context.

questions.question: Saying exactly what you did: built, evaluated or understand

blocks.heading: The three words
items: Built: you wrote it and it ran. Say "I built".
Evaluated: you designed it, specced it or ran a spike. Say "I designed" or "I evaluated".
Understand: you know how it works but haven't used it. Say "I understand" or "I've read".

blocks.heading: Where you're on each
items: Built: the MITCON extraction pipeline and grounding contract; the Fresh Tracks multi-agent payment system on LangGraph and AWS Bedrock; the AML SoftServe agentic RAG, snapshot design and RLS boundary; the Fresh Tracks Trip Availability Assistant; techcirkle-agents on LangGraph; the Fresh Tracks skills and hooks; fde and fde-os for People Equation.
Evaluated: sandvick-agents (SharePoint RAG design), org-memory (MCP spec) and the healthcare supply proposal. All are designs with no code.
Understand: fine-tuning, GraphRAG, open-weight models.
Confirm before you go deeper: Braintrust's tracing role at AML SoftServe, and the AML agent framework, which you don't remember. Name no framework.

scripts.say: I designed that one. It never went to code.
scripts.effect: Stops a design being mistaken for a build, before they find out.

scripts.say: That feature was a colleague's. My part was the availability service.
scripts.effect: Protects your credibility on shared work.

checks: Fresh Tracks payment agents: know the flow end to end from the story bank (payment request, overdue reconciliation, nightly reconciliation, rebalancing). The only outcome on record is refund turnaround of about two business days down to one.
AML SoftServe agentic RAG: Braintrust's tracing role is our reading, and the agent framework is not remembered. Don't state either as fact.

questions.question: The bridge from engineering manager to hands-on engineer

blocks.heading: The doubt you're answering
blocks.text: Five years as an engineering manager can make an interviewer ask whether you still write code. Answer with commit numbers, not adjectives, and say that coding agents wrote a share of them.

blocks.heading: The numbers
items: AML SoftServe: top contributor, 327 of 986 commits on the team of 8 he headed.
Fresh Tracks Canada: 218 merged commits across 10 repos, for a 2-engineer team.
MITCON: the repos recorded 773 commits across 3 repos in about 10 days. A share were written by coding agents under my direction.

blocks.heading: Turn the manager years into an asset

scripts.say: I ran client delivery for 8 enterprise accounts at EY. Now I do the same work as the engineer who builds it.
scripts.effect: Frames management as client experience, which the FDE role needs.

scripts.say: Happy to take a coding exercise. I write code every day.
scripts.effect: Invites the test instead of arguing.

checks: The commit counts are repo totals. Authorship is not recorded, and a share was written by coding agents under your direction. Know the split between agent-written and hand-written commits before you quote a count as your own work.

questions.question: Questions to ask the interviewer

blocks.heading: About the work
items: What does someone in this role ship in their first 90 days?
How much of the time is spent on customer sites, and how much in the core codebase?
How does what you learn in the field get back into the product?

blocks.heading: About quality and risk
items: How do you evaluate model changes before they reach a customer?
When a customer wants a demo more than a working system, who decides?
How do your agents reach production, and what breaks most often?

blocks.heading: About the team
items: How many people are on the team, and who do they report to?
What would make someone great in this role after a year?

questions.trap: Never answer "Nothing" when asked if you have questions. Ask at least one.

tabs.purpose: The terms interviewers use for this role, grouped by topic.

tabs.title: Quick reference
tabs.purpose: Scan this before the interview.

cards.title: Tell me about yourself: the triggers
lines: AI systems architect. 10+ years in production software. Forward-deployed AI engineer at MITCON now.
Co-founded Spotmentor, acquired by EY in 2020. About five years at EY, finishing as Senior Manager, Engineering.

cards.title: Confidence map: what is built, evaluated and understood

cards.title: Questions to ask the interviewer
lines: What does someone in this role ship in their first 90 days?
How does what you learn in the field get back into the product?
How do you evaluate model changes before they reach a customer?
How do your agents reach production, and what breaks most often?

cards.title: Delivery reminder
lines: Answer first, then the reason.
Stay under two minutes, then offer to go deeper.
If you misspeak, correct yourself out loud. It builds trust.
Say built, designed or understand. Never blur them.

terms.oneLine: The neural network design that nearly every current language model uses.
terms.meaning: Introduced in 2017, it replaced recurrent networks for language work. Each layer uses attention to let tokens weigh the other tokens they can see. In decoder models like GPT, a token sees only earlier tokens. It trains in parallel on GPUs, which is why models could grow so large.
terms.example: GPT, Claude, Llama and Gemini are all transformer-based models.
terms.whyItMatters: It explains the limits you design around: a fixed context window, and a compute cost that grows quickly with input length.

terms.oneLine: The mechanism that lets each token decide which other tokens matter for its meaning.
terms.meaning: Every token produces a query, a key and a value. A token's query is compared with all keys, and the scores weight the values. The result is a context-aware representation of each token. Standard attention cost grows with the square of the input length.
terms.example: In "The trophy would not fit in the suitcase because it was too big", attention helps link "it" to "trophy".
terms.whyItMatters: It explains why long inputs are slow and costly, and why a model can lose detail in the middle of a very long prompt.

terms.oneLine: The most tokens a model can handle in one request, counting the input and usually the reply.
terms.meaning: The window holds the system prompt, the conversation, any retrieved documents and the model's own reply. Providers often cap the reply separately and lower than the window. Anything outside the window is invisible to the model. A bigger window costs more per call and does not guarantee the model uses all of it well.
terms.example: A 200,000-token window fits a long report, but you would still retrieve only the relevant pages for a question.
terms.whyItMatters: It decides how you chunk documents, how much history you keep and how you summarise. It also sets a cost ceiling for each call.

onYourCv.text: I manage context deliberately in my delivery work: a short CLAUDE.md, a ROUTER.md that maps ticket keywords to starting files, and an LLM-maintained project wiki on every project at TekMindz.

terms.gloss: Unit of text a model reads
terms.oneLine: A chunk of text, often a word or part of a word, that a model reads and writes.
terms.meaning: Models don't see characters or words. They see token ids. In English a token averages around four characters, so 100 tokens is roughly 75 words. Other languages and code often use more tokens for the same meaning.
terms.example: The word "unbelievable" may split into three tokens, while "the" is one.
terms.whyItMatters: Providers charge and set limits in tokens. Your cost and your context budget are token counts, not word counts.

terms.oneLine: The component that converts text to token ids and back.
terms.meaning: Each model family has its own tokenizer, often built with byte-pair encoding. The same text gives different token counts on different models. Using the wrong tokenizer gives wrong cost and limit estimates.
terms.example: A page of text may count as 600 tokens on one provider and 700 on another.
terms.whyItMatters: Count with the tokenizer of the model you will call. Chunk sizes and cost forecasts depend on it.

terms.gloss: Text as a vector of meaning
terms.oneLine: A list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text, so similar meanings sit close together.
terms.meaning: An embedding model maps text to a vector, often with hundreds or thousands of dimensions. Similar texts get nearby vectors. You compare vectors with a distance measure such as cosine similarity. Queries and documents need the same embedding model.
terms.example: "Refund my booking" and "money back for my trip" produce nearby vectors, though they share no words.
